article: "This is NTSB Special Investigator Charles Cunningham with the head of the Malaysian MH370 crash investigation team, Sarash Loong. In the room are is the head of the Chinese crash task force Lee Chiung, head of the Australian crash task force, Jonathan Wash. We have found the black box for the flight and are about to begin our review of the flight recorder. The flight data has already been reviewed and it was found that after less than an hour after take off, the course of flight MH370 was altered to take it over the Indian Ocean where the plane flew until it ran out of fuel and fell from the sky. Initial reviews indicate that the cabin depressurized about 2 hours into the flight for unknown reasons and was repressurized after a short amount of time. Hopefully we can figure out what happened after our review of the cockpit recorder." Charles sat back in his chair and looked around the room at each of the participants. They were eager to begin and get the review over with after so many days of endless searching and the unceasing scrutiny of the press. The Malaysian investigator Sarash looked particularly eager to get started. This hadn't been a good affair for them. Sitting back in his seat and taking out his pen, he brought opened his notebook to begin taking notes and nodded at the computer tech in the corner of the room operating the black box data. The flight recording began. Flight recording begins shuffling sound as bags are set down and stowed and the pilots enter the cockpit "Good morning Captain!" "Good morning first officer. Fariq right?" "Yes, sir" "Please, please. Call me Zaharie. There's no need for such formality in my cockpit." "Haha thank you Zaharie. I am very excited to fly with you tonight! You're reputation precedes you. You have so much flight time and I've never even flown a 777 before." "Nothing to worry about Fariq. These things practically fly themselves." Several moments of switches being checked, the pilots calculating their flight statistics and prepping for take-off procedure, then a slight groan could be heard from the recorder. "Are you alright Zaharie?" "Just a slight headache. Do you mind calling one of the stewardesses for some water?" "Not a problem." Sounds of Fariq picking up the phone and calling the stewardess for water. Fariq gets up when she knocks and lets her enter the cockpit to drop off the water then she leaves. "Okay Fariq. Are you ready for this? I think you should lead the taxi and take-off. I'll supervise." "Are you sure? I've done the simulations, but I've never done an actual take-off." "You've got to learn sometime young man. There's no better day than today." A slight shuffle is heard in the background Fariq's voice. "What was that?" "Probably nothing. Maybe one of our bags shifting in the storage." "Are you sure? I thought I heard something moving." "You're imagining things. I heard no such thing. Now concentrate on the take-off." Fariq and Zaharie handle the take-off and are now airborne - Time into flight: 0 hr 5 min The sound of one of the pilots grabbing the comlink for cabin announcements comes through the speaker "Ladies and gentleman, this is your captain speaking. We have taken off from Kuala Lumpur International and are on our way to Beijing. Our flight looks clear from here and we are expecting to arrive in just under 6 hours. Our stewardesses will soon be coming down the aisle with refreshments and sleep masks if you require them since it is late tonight. I hope you enjoy your flight and thank you for flying Malaysian Airlines." The comm link is set back down Zaharie's voice comes on "I always like that part. Welcoming the passengers on board. The initial ascent and the real beginning of the flight. It never gets old." Fariq chuckles then says "You really enjoy this job don't you." "Yes I do. This is my life. What about you?" "I'm enjoying experience. I've worked so hard to get here and getting to pilot a 777 is really big for me. I want to see the world." "That's good to hear." Zaharie's voice trails off and takes on a different tone. "I love flying. I wish things didn't have to be like this today though." "What was that?" "Oh nothing Fariq. Sorry. The musings of an old man." "Are you okay Zaharie? You look a little off there." "No, no, it's nothing. I just had an unpleasant experience with family before the flight today. The thought just popped into my head. I'm fine." "Want to talk about it?" "No Fariq. I'm sorry. It really is quite unpleasant. I'd rather just focus on the flight. Actually, if you want, I wouldn't mind some time alone if you would like to take a small nap. I can take this part of the flight." "Well I'm not really tired..." "Fariq, I insist. It's late and when you wake up we'll do some flight training on the controls." "Okay. If you insist." Sounds of Fariq unbuckling and going to the cot. The cockpit remains quiet and soon the sounds of Fariq's steady breathing emanates through the cockpit. At this point the auto-pilot is engaged. Time into flight 0 hr 22 min. Zaharie is heard getting out of his seat and moving around the cockpit. The is a sound of compartment being opened and a zipper being opened. Urgent whispering can be heard but is incomprehensible. After a short time, the zipper is closed and Zaharie returns to his chair and sits in silence for several minutes. Time into flight 0 hr 55 min. Zaharie alters the flight path of flight MH370 away from the original flight path and towards the Indian Ocean. Fariq wakes up soon after and rejoins Zaharie "Anything happen while I was out?" "No not really. Have a good nap?" "Yes. It was refreshing, but now I am ready to work." "Of course, of course. First though..... idle thought..... have you ever heard of the banjang?" "Um..... yes. Yes it was a creature my mother used to scare me with as a child. But it is just a story. Not real at all..... Wait did something happen to our flight path? It doesn't look right." "I know of the Bajang. I used to hear it's meowling all night long. It haunted our property. It has haunted my family for a long time. We knew it's ways and we knew it's tricks. I thought I could tame it." "That's an interesting story Zaharie, but did you change our flight path?" Fariq asks urgently. "We're not on our original heading." A soft, sickening thunk comes through the recorder in the next moment. It sounds like a knife sliding into flesh. "Hrrnk." Fariq grunts and gasps out the next words. "Wha..... wha..... why?" "Shhh, Fariq. Save your breath. I stabbed your lung. You will not be able to scream." Another sickening slice of the blade can be heard and Fariq quiets. "I was telling you Fariq that I tried to tame the Bajang. And it was oh so friendly at first. Did you know it likes to eat children? Sickening I know, but worth the protection it provides. And there are children aplenty in the Malaysian streets. But as time went on it's appetite grew and grew. It used to be sated for weeks, but after a few years it demanded to be fed on a weekly basis. I couldn't keep feeding it." Zaharie gets out of his chair and walks over to the compartment and opens it again. He opens the zipper and something comes out this time. There's a soft thump as something drops to the floor and walks across the cockpit. Then there is the sound of an animal tearing into flesh. "I flew so often Fariq. I loved it so much. The Bajang was supposed to protect my family. They did not know it. But I guess I was away too long this last trip. He grew so hungry Fariq. You don't understand what happens when they are so hungry. I came home and my family was gone. How fickle the Bajang is. If he had just waited a day. But I guess this job worked me too hard." Zaharie returns to his seat and the sound of Fariq being eaten continues for over an hour. The beast sounds ravenous as it tears into the flesh. Time into flight: 1 hr 57 min. The cabin is depressurized. Oxygen is deployed but soon depleted. Enough time passes that the passengers must be dead. The cabin is repressurized. Zaharie is heard rising again and opens the door of the cockpit into the main cabin. The footsteps wander out of the cockpit and go into the cabin. The door shuts again. "Forgive me my transgressions but the beast must be killed. There is no other way. I'm sorry my beloved and my children. I failed you. Now I will fly to my death and take this beast with me." The recording continues until the beast can be heard beating on the cockpit door, but to no avail. The fuel eventually runs out and the last bit of the flight recording is the plane going into an uncontrolled descent. Recording end Charles looked up at the surrounding room. Everyone was pale and speechless. His notebook was only partially filled out. He had stopped writing ages ago as the recording went on. Nobody said a word. Carefully he walked over to the computer technician and instructed him to delete the audio recording and then he turned to face the committee. "Clearly we can not tell anyone about what happened on the flight. We will have to go public that the cockpit recorder was damaged beyond repair and that the only conclusion we can come up with is that it was pilot error. Does everyone agree?" There was a chorus of nods. "Ok then. That closes the books on flight MH370.

article: I closed the book at page 767, only a couple of pages until the end. I listened to the descending footsteps, my wife's, fall with a methodical rhythm. I had listened to that noise through many long nights pouring over online documents. Her steps provided a beat throughout my erratic clacking. Few would guess how much I wanted retirement, myself especially. I had always worked for promotions, having faith I would find an achievement that was enough. When I found her, working paperwork at the office, I thought I had found a possible end. I had been a detective for three years before I had been assigned to the " Ash murders " case. The murder burned her corpses so thoroughly that identification and burial were impossible. The media had gone insane at the possibility of a serial killer in this town. This was right after the peak of the Mensa murderer, who had toyed with and killed seven geniuses and prodigies before growing bored and disappearing. I got the lead of the assignment after the first heads were murdered. Back then, I didn't put in much work, but my natural intelligence had allowed me to solve even the most difficult cases and I had grown a reputation with those in the know. The murderer came to this town for me, I'm sure of it. She, the murderer, has had a fascination for me since the beginning. She has killed everybody I have helped; every person related to any case I solved. I guess you can say they died because of me, because I brought her here. She was why I had worked so hard for atonement and why I had cut my ties. It had taken my wife nearly a year to convince me to date, and by then I realized I already couldn't lose her. I had always wondered why she chose me, the cursed detective. It was a rainy day when I found the body. The body was laid in the middle of the road and was smoking slightly when I arrived. I found in the breast pocket " Samantha O'Carrol ," a mother's name. Her son's murder was my first case. The corpse smelled familiar, and it hadn't been just the smoke. I had been surprised I remembered the smell all those years later, but I guessed some smells never go away. That night I came home and yelled upstairs. I heard the footsteps of my wife as she came down the stairs, saw her enter the room, and then I smelled the perfume of the corpse. I stiffened as she embraced me and asked " Rough day at the office, hun? " I tried to forget it, ignore it, but I knew she noticed. She assumed I read alone only because I needed more thinking time. She thought I had stopped coming to her on bad days because I was scared of breaking down in front of her. She thought I had become too busy for intimacy. She chalked my destruction of her perfume to nerves, and bought an identical bottle. I continued seeing new bodies, smelling sweetly, until last week when I quit, hoping that the murders would stop when I left. Of course, they won't, but I could try to forget that. " I'm going to the Stevenson's if you want to come " my wife said, coming into the room. She knew I wouldn't, but she always asked me. I declined, and she left, starting up the car. I read the same page for the next fifteen minutes, and then decided I'd go with her. I arrived at the Stevenson's a couple minutes later, and knocked on the door. Jennifer, the wife, opened the door and welcomed me inside. " Don't take this the wrong way, but we weren't expecting you " she said. " I know, I haven't been out of the house very much, but I figured I'd need something to do in retirement. " " Yes, but we thought you'd cancelled. Your wife just texted us she'd be coming half an hour late " I stopped. " She isn't here? " I asked. " No, isn't she home? " " No... I have to leave. I think she might be in trouble. " I lied, forcing my legs to walk slowly to my car. " Trouble? " I heard ask, high-pitched as she remembered my involvement in the murders. I left the house, sprinted to the car. I knew where my wife was. Brendan Wei, the one who's brother was shot three times. He was the only one alive who lived in this neighborhood. I saw his house, all lights off, her car in the driveway. I called 911, shouted what I knew, hang up before any questions, grabbed my pistol and opened the unlocked door. The light switch wouldn't turn on. I knew it was dangerous, suicidal even, approaching a killer in the dark, but then I heard her call from inside, heard her mock sobbing, and suddenly death didn't seem so bad. I walked slowly, evenly, despite her false pleas and her shouting. I began approaching the room she was in, the door lit by a window to the moon. Suddenly, she became quiet, and I hear metal move as she picked something up. I opened the door and pointed my gun. " Honey? " she asked, as I fired two shots, one of which hit the chest. She collapsed, and I fell there, berating her, telling her what could have been, saying the things I would have told her a year ago. They found me like that, crying and babbling and rocking. I was sentenced for breaking and entering, and had to undergo therapy for a few years.With alcohol and work, I found a way to keep living, right up until the day I found her corpse on my doorstep, burned except for the face, smelling of smoke and perfume.

article: "How can you even say that? I mean, consider all the benefits!" "I think I might be a better authori "Super-strength! Lightning-quick speed! Fucking immortality, man! You even get to stay 23 forever!" "Trust me. I've been doing it for 90 years. I can't even imagine what the vampires on year 1000 must go through." "Oh, poor you! That whole "woe is me, eternity is my prison" shit. I bet all that moping gets you laid like ALL the time." "Well, yes, when I entertain the notion. But all of those benefits you mentioned..... I'm just not sure you've had time to consider the downsides. Trust me, all I have is time. And experience." Jerry rolled his eyes. "Fine then. Enlighten me." Alex sighed. He launched into the diatribe he'd given so often before. "OK..... have you ever held an infant before?" "Ummmm..... sure. What, can you not have babies or something, because I consider that a positive." "Would you like my answer, or would you like to talk over me? " Of course Alex knew that, like most humans, the answer was secretly the latter. All humans love the sound of their own voice. Jerry, not wanting to seem too self-involved, quickly stopped talking in a huff. "Now then. When you hold an infant, or a kitten, or any small, defenseless thing..... you have to temper your strength. So fragile are these creatures that even the slightest movement on your part a wayward sneeze, a trip, a sudden clench in your arm any of these things could mean the end of the creature in your arms. And you come to care for this creature. It's so innocent, so naive it doesn't yet understand the harsh truths of the world, and you want to let that creature bask in its ignorance as long as it can. "That's what it means to be a vampire. Constant guarding of my physiological faculties..... and my psychological ones as well. If I were to lose my composure for just an instant, Jerry, and if I were to strike you in the face, your skull would break apart and your face would conform around my wrist, still stuck where your nose once was." "Is..... I mean, is that a threat, Alex?" The first hint of caution at his behavior passed his lips. "I have no cause to threaten you, Jerry. I only wish to inform you that a life of constant withholding can be a very isolating experience. And of course, there is the matter of immortality." "Yeah, yeah, you see your loved ones die and such. But you meet new friends, right? You met me, didn't you?" "And how lucky am I for that." He didn't detect the sarcasm. It was pointless to continue.

article: I remember the first time I saw her. She was beautiful and I knew, I just knew we were meant to be. Abigail. Abby. She was my desert rose, perfection in a sea of desolation. Some people may have thought it strange, such a strong bond so quickly. I didn't even know her. Not that it mattered. My entire career was ahead of me but I made a choice. I would wait for her. She didn't have to tell me, I just knew that she loved reading. She was the type for it. Every night we read a book together, starting with Don Quixote. Why Don Quixote? I'm not entirely sure, that's just where it began. Every night we read together, needing nothing more to sustain that bond between us. There was no need for movies, even when friends came to call. There were no nights out drinking or partying, as hard as others tried to make it happen. Our life was reading. The years flowed into each other as they are wont to do. Time passes, there is no stopping that mighty river. One became two, became five, became ten, became twenty. My hair thinned and hers filled with grey. The wrinkles became deep, then deeper, and soon the shaking in my hands meant I was to give up my work. Even so, every night we would read together. Being with her calmed the shaking. There was nothing I needed in this world but her. Almost sixty years had passed, like a dream, when I held her hand. She was frail now, the youthful vigour long left those limbs of hers. The grey had overtaken her brown hair, the lines deeper than ever. Sixty years gone. I held her hand in mine and read from an old and worn copy of Don Quixote. With a stolen glance I saw her eyes had fluttered open. She squeezed my hand and smiled at me. The most beautiful vision I had ever seen, surely I was hallucinating. "Thank you," she said, quietly and weakly. She closed her eyes again. In a moment, she was gone. Time takes all. Even the desert rose.

article: Kara steadied herself on the wall. She blinked and peered into the darkness below her. The wall that use to be there had receded revealing an old rusty stairway that she couldn't see the bottom of. She took out her phone to give her enough light to move around, and slowly crept down into the suffocating darkness. The air was stagnant and sounded with the creaking and straining of the derelict stairwell. Her phone's light barely reached the moss covered stone brick walls surrounding her. After some time she finally reached the bottom, and the entrance to what seemed to be a large room just as her phone's battery died. Breathing deeply, she steeled herself and took a step forward. Her motion triggered aged incandescent lighting to flicker on revealing a hallway of scientific equipment. At the end of it a frosted green glass cylinder stood ominously. Kara approached it. Kara carefully reached out placing her hand on the cold surface and wiping away the fog. She stared at her reflection in the glass, and into it revealing a chamber that you could sit in. Standing next to the chamber was a control panel, which Kara began to fiddle with. She turned a dial back to 10 minutes and there was a loud clank. The glass chamber lifted slowly, and she took a seat. Before she could react, the chamber closed again and flashed with bright green lights. Darkness once again consumed her and left her to drift through void. Kara steadied herself on the wall. She blinked and peered into the darkness below her. article: Hi Tzip, I was almost 30 when I had my first real kiss. By you. I've been alone my whole life, too different from other people, miserly with my deepest love and affection, too much of a romantic who only dreamed of love and found it only in books and stories. It took me so long to emotionally and mentally recover from my strict and abusive childhood. Just when I began to fall into my own rhythm for the first time in my life, you came along, bubbling with laughter, beaming with your passions and aspirations. I wish you wanted to be with me despite religion. I wish the stories I told you about my childhood didn't scare you away from me. The stories of your childhood are warm and loving, filled with an gold-tinged ebullience I desperately, secretly yearn for when I make the inevitable, sad comparisons. I am broken. Despite my best efforts to put the pieces together and salvage something worthwhile from myself, I know you can't put the pieces together and make them truly whole again. And that's why it hurts when I'm faced with your rejection, even though I know a part of it has nothing to do with me. It makes so much sense that someone like you, raised in the light and warmth would turn away from someone like me, with melancholy and pain at the root of my being. You and your actions are a mirror that exposes the darkest parts of myself, the confirmation that I am unlovable by anyone I want to love, the truth that I should keep my head down, grind my teeth and try to endure my life instead of living it. No. I am trying not to think this way. The rational part of me tells me to not be silly, and that this, like all things, will get better as time progresses. I mean, the worst part of my life has been slowly healing, and this is nothing compared to it. Yet sometimes when I stand outside in the dark, staring at the stars in the sky, I feel completely alien and disconnected. Instead of feeling like part of the vast, unknowable universe, I am separate. Alone. Alone in my suffering. Alone, without you.

article: Just. Stay. Calm. I haven't done anything wrong. Thank God the pilot regained control of the plane, right? This will make for a good story, won't it? I'm going to jail, aren't I? Some people are crying, some people are laughing - out of either relief or hysteria, or perhaps both - and some people have already gone back to their phones or magazines. There are a few unconscious people on board, though, who fainted when the plane started dropping out of the sky. It makes me sigh in relief; at least now I can just say that he fainted. I don't dare look over at him, because I know exactly what I'm going to see. A slightly bruised neck, his head hanging forward. Is his tongue hanging out of his mouth? He might have hit his neck on the seat, or his head might have hit against the seat in front of him. I didn't see it, I was too busy screaming! Just. Stay. Calm. It's been a few minutes since things cooled down and the flight attendants are handing out napkins to people whose drinks spilled on themselves. One of them is walking towards me. "Aw, did he faint too?" She gives me an innocent grin and I nod in return, gently taking the napkin from her hand and wiping Diet Coke off the pages of my book. "Yeah, y-yeah. I think he hit his head." "Well, we'll make sure to see him to the hospital when he lands. I'm sure he'll be fine! Nobody on board was seriously injured." Nobody was injured, but somebody died. I can't even stand to look at my hands. Are my fingerprints on his neck? Can they find skin cells around my fingers? I didn't even think I'd survive! I think even the sanest person in the world would have to agree that what I did wasn't wrong, right? We were going to die anyway! We were going to die until we weren't anymore and now they're going to find out that I'm a murderer. I can't do this. I can't go through with this. I raise a hand. "Sir, do you need something?" "If you have any available, just some..... some of the chicken. I'm hungry again after I lost my..." I gesture to a doggie bag on the ground and she nods, walking off to get my meal. Nobody else here is crazy enough to want to eat after that. I twiddle my thumbs for a few minutes before taking the plate eagerly when the flight attendant returns with a plate of terrible airline chicken and a form and knife. I take a bite and smile at her just to calm her nerves, waiting until she's walked off to spit it into the doggie bag. "Ladies and gentlemen, I'm sorry for the disturbance. Texting while driving also applies to airplanes, it seems." A few people laugh, but most of us are too tired. "We have resumed our path to Jackson, Mississippi and will land in forty minutes." I have forty minutes. I grip the knife in my hand, tapping it against my seat-down tray. Nobody else can know what happened here tonight. I killed him, because the plane was going down. The plane is going down. I slip the handle of the knife in my sleeve and hold the blade in my fingers to conceal it as I stand, walking towards the cockpit. This plane is going down.
label: human

article: I used to be like you. I would have laughed and never believed it to be true, until it was true. Our world was, literally, changed. But I wonder if it was changed or if it was always this way. On April 1st of 2017 I thought it was all a joke. The newspapers read, "Flat Earth Society Conspiracy Proven Right! The Whole Planet Is On Edge!!" and I thought it was all a hoax. Haha, April Fools. Throughout the day they really had me going, too. Even the news broadcast was in a hype about this. I had to hand it to them, dedication to this big of a joke is rare these days. Maybe the joke will make the news tomorrow. I wasn't wrong. The next day the newspapers had even more to say about this! "Earth Not Round. Scientists Fall Flat On Face!!" You'd think they'd come up with a better headline? Even the news kept going on about all the proof that had been found and how this'll change our school systems and was showing diagrams describing seasons and everything. Then it hit me, what if they weren't kidding? I took a second to look around, people were talking about it. EVERYONE was talking about it. As days went on, people were in a mad panic. There were stories of fishermen falling off the edge, countries slowly drifting as the flat surface tilts for the seasons. But it got worse. Did you know the Earth doesn't evolve around the sun, but the sun evolves around the Earth? In The NASA Station Sam chuckled to himself and turned to his partner, Max, in Public Affairs, "How long do you think we can keep them going?" Max shrugged, "Let's see. Bring out more news on the sun evolving the world and connect that to seasons, too. They'll go crazy."

article: I am 12. I have been on this island, my Mother's Island since I was in second grade, when I had just turned 8. My birthday was in January of every year when my classmates would sing me a song and the teacher would greet me first in class. My skin was pale then, I was 8. I am 12 now. I long stopped counting the days after Mother threw my cardboard calendar into the ocean. As I watched the charcoal days leak like oil I could hear Mother. Oh Mother, as she ground my charcoal pen. I was 9 then, I had been on her island for a year then. I was still 8 then. Father had always insisted we live by the sea while he maintained the boat. dad and Mother fought a lot then. He would spell of wood polish and thinners and would often greet me at home with a role of tips in his pocket from the yacht owners and their children. They were my age, 8, 9, 10. The girl priscilla was blonde but her skin was brown. Father would greet me at the door when he got home spelling of polish and thinners. He would put his hand in my hair and explain to me that that priscilla was as white as I but she spent time on the sea with her father who was nice enough to leave father 20s. I remember the spell of alcohol when I was 5. father had come home with a spell I had not remembered before. He was alien to me then, and maybe to Mother too, because they shouted at each other. I kept my head down and looked at the maths. It had always confused me but I preferred its strange symbols to the noise. After the fight father sat down to help me. He showed me how many days and how many tips he would need to fix the boat that had been sitting in the marina since we moved here. I do not remember the move. My first memory is at 4 when father gave the money in the kitchen jar to the the old sailor. That was the first time Mother and father fought. My last memory before Mother's Island was the day when the calendar was finished and father had broken one bottle on the front of the boat. My real last memory was of how the stuff in the bottle tasted before I fell asleep. My first memory on the island was my Mother sobbing. Father's tombstone was a piece of the boat I had helped him paint. I remember the wrong brushstrokes I had made and how father assured me that the mistakes only made it better. I am 12. Every day Mother will burn all the driftwood on the island to cook the food which will last us to the next day. She tells me that before the sun is fully gone we must pour water on the fire and sleep. Or the lights will come. She tells me that the lights in the distance are the monsters which took father. The same monsters which had made me simple. The same monsters which are in the bottle. Mother says that if the monsters return we can no longer be together. I am 12 and I no longer believe her. I am 12 and no longer wish to hear her speak about my rotting father as if he is the reason for this. I longer wish to hear her swear at me for being soft on the head when all her friends would share the bottle when their bellies were big. As the lights draw closer she shrieks at me calling me and my father names I had not heard before. I do not know them, but I know they are bad words. The men on the white and red boats look like father. They are strong in the chest and spell of polish and thinners. Mother has stabbed one of the men with a piece of wood from the fire. She says that they can not take her baby from her Island and that we will be here forever, free from the sailors and the boats and the bottles. I am 12 now and my mother lies dead in the sand like my father. She had taken the sailor's gun and turned it on herself. I am 12 now and my classmates will never sing me a song again. My teacher will never greet me first. I have decided that the monsters are attracted to me and I do not deserve to be on a boat of my father's leaving my mother's island.

article: "I'm sorry" I whispered as I stepped upon the ledge. I thought I was strong enough, I thought I could fight through the pain. But I was wrong, and I couldn't take it anymore. I wanted everything to go away, and there was only one way for me to do it - they say every journey begins with a single step, but the end of my journey was a step away. I spread my arms wide as I fell, allowing my pain, my suffering, my memories to fade away as I rushed towards an eternal sidewalk slumber. What's going on? I'm still falling, but.... it feels different. I open my eyes and gasp. I am no longer looking at the dull grey path of the Market Street sidewalk, but an endless blank void. I look at my watch, and notice the hands are not moving - a trick I've taught myself to help me determine whether or not I'm dreaming. But I should make sure - I pinch my nose tightly and breathe. No problem. My reality checks confirm my suspicions - I'm definitely dreaming. Having trained my whole life in lucid dreaming, this was nothing out of the ordinary for me. I felt more free and at ease in my own lucid dreams than in the real world, and spent most of days sleeping to get away from it all. At least now I knew the answer to "is there an afterlife." I smile, for the first time in a long time as I try and come to terms with this newfound knowledge. Still falling endlessly through the blank void, an idea forms in my head. If it works when I'm alive, it should work when I'm dead too, right? I close my eyes. When I open them, I am no longer falling through an empty void, but standing firmly on the ground, infront of a familiar door. My smile turns into a tremendous grin as I give myself a mental high five. I've been through this before, what, a hundred times? A thousand? More? But this time is different. I knock on the door. This time I won't won't wake up. She opens the door, and I pause. It's just like all the other times. No, this time is different. I take a deep breath and take my first step, that first step I've taken countless times before. This time, I won't wake up.

article: They say curiosity killed the cat, but here I am, holding this tail, and there still isn't any blood. Hey Fluffy, this works better than my iPhone on here. How about that?" article: Growing up in a circus was spectacular. The lights, the colours, the animals, the people. It's like one gigantic family where everyone looks out for each other and each day is more fun than the last. My mom was a beautiful trapeze artist, but even with all the glitz and glamour and all her beautiful costumes, I wanted to be a clown. Just like my dad. The pies, the watches that squirt water, the shoes as big as my arms. It was just too much fun. Unfortunately, being a grown-up in a failing circus is not as much fun as being a kid in a successful one. We try and keep current. Try and get the kids'attention, but it's hard. Our world is different than theirs. Marcus, one of the new trapeze artists, he's smarter than the rest of us. He goes on the internet, finds out what the kids like, and we try to add it to our bits and routines. I peek out from behind the curtain. The circus is almost empty tonight. No surprise there. I'm a bit nervous today, I'm always nervous when we do a new bit. It's about a new dance Marcus heard of. " Chuckles! Chuckles! Where are you? Why is she always so late? " That's my cue. I honk my horn as I drive my little bicycle onto the floor, circling Clownzo as I pretend to squirt him with my watch. " Oh no! I wear a watch that will not work It makes me want to go berserk I'm always late, the stupid jerk This silly watch won't even squirt. This watch of mine just will not work, My stupid watch can't even twerk- " " But Chuckles, " Clownzo interupts " you can't twerk either. Har har " " Oh d'oh! Right you are Clownzo. Hardy har, silly me! Do you know how to twerk Clownzo? " " Gee Chuckles, is twerk a kind of jerky? " " No, you buffoon! It's a beautiful dance. I wonder if there's anyone who can teach me. " I give the little girl in the front row my goofiest smile, hoping that she will volunteer, but her eyes are glued to a phone. The boys with her are pinching each other. My heart sinks a little. " Hmmm, maybe someone in the audience knows how to twerk. " Clownzo tries again. Silence. Most of the kids at the back are on their phones as well. And there's no one else there. Improvising is a big part of being a clown; when you're throwing pies and hoping for volunteers, things don't always work out like planned. I look back at the sweet little girl with the phone in her lap and I just... I just give up. I look at my broken watch. Things were a lot different back when my dad was a clown. " Well Carl, I mean Clownzo. I guess... then, I guess, I guess- " My eyes are tearing up so I just drive off the stage with my silly little bike. It squeaked and honked the whole way to my trailer. When I entered the trailer I took off my nose and grabbed the flask from under my pillow. What's a clown to do when no-one loves clowns anymore? " I am a clown with many a quirk in a world where clowns don't work. It makes me feel like such a jerk It makes me want to go berserk. "

article: I don't think I can live without you.... You, and the way you smell and how your scent hangs in the air even after you've gone. You, and the taste you leave in my mouth, the way I still need you even after you've burned me once, twice, ten times. You're the first thing I think of when I wake up in the morning; you're the only thing that gets me out of bed. You make my heart race, and I hate when I can't have you. I never feel awake until I've gotten my fix of you. More often than not though, you and what you do to me keep me up long after I should be sound asleep; our meetings mustn't run so late but I think I am addicted to you and I cant help caving into my cravings to taste you. You, and the way you warm my body and how at other times, when I need it, you cool me down. There's just something about you that keeps me coming back to you again and again. You're rarely the same and I love all sides of you, can't get enough of you. You keep things exciting but you're still always there waiting for me. I love how we can sit, quiet in the mornings but for the birds chirping and you touch my lips and every time is like the first time. I love how we can sit, to catch up together with old friends, how you still affect me from the inside out as if I could ever ignore you. I am jealous when I see you with others instead of me; don't you know how much I adore you, love you, need you? Don't you realize what you've done to me? You've intertwined yourself so deep in my everyday that to be without you would be blasphemy. There's no other way to explain it. Is this really as one-sided as you make it seem sometimes though? I'm always the one putting in the effort to make this work, to make you give me what I so desperately want and need from you. You must think I am crazy saying all of this but you must know it's you who's done this to me. It's you who I will never have enough of. It's you who I don't think I can live without..

article: Cursed is not the word. I am the last human and I am adrift in the void. It's been so long since I left the solar system. I have died billions of times; some I recall the major events that led me here. I was the last human long after humanity evolved to something I can't quite comprehend. I am static and it saddens me that I'll never join them. A recurring thought background noise. I was standing on Earth, briefly dead, then alive before quickly dying again. I watched the scene unfold slowly as the Earth was consumed by the Sun, as I was consumed by the sun. I would reform, ever so briefly inside the outermost layers of the Sun only to die nearly instantly. It was this way for so long. Over time, the ferocity of my deaths abated. The sun became transparent, punctuated by a small, brilliant white orb; and I drifted away. My life, as it is, has become a slow movie a few minutes alive and a few minutes dead. It's always suffocation and freezing. I have seen the stars die, and the lights fade from a rainbow hue to yellow and red; finally to blackness. I feel the tug of unseen giants lurking in the darkness and have felt their crushing strength. But eventually they too die and I am reborn from their absence. I am the last. I am lonely. I feel nothing. I remember; my last refuge. I remember my loved ones. I remember my childhood and my parents. I remember pleasure, pain. Unfathomable sadness and absolute joy; and I feel them. I remember light, and there is light.

article: "Wait, the fuck?" "Yeah, we all said the same thing." Josh's eyes wandered over the various occupants in the room with wide eyes. From bodybuilders to neckbeards, politicians to..... Robin Williams? Everyone in the room was being sued. There were nearly two hundred people in this room alone, and he knew the other rooms in the hallway were similarly full. Josh could do nothing to shake the feeling of disbelief flowing through him, compounded by the undercurrent of anger in the room. All eyes swiveled to the sound of the turning doorknob. "Well, we better hope our attorney doesn't try and prove our allegations. Heh, we'd be screwed, literally!" Robin Williams chuckled to himself after quickly getting that out. Josh had never been a fan of his humor. In stepped Tom Cruise himself, followed by a man with slicked back hair, strong shoulders, and a briefcase. He froze upon seeing the number in the room. "Hurry this up Mr. Lodano, I've got a scientology mass to attend." God, Tom Cruise even sounded like a prick. The aforementioned Lodano rolled his eyes and turned to Cruise. "Sir, I don't believe that you will be able to sue all of these individuals. You would tie up the courts for years, and the cost to you would be extravagant!" "You mean I can't just have them all tried at once?" Lodano stared at the man with exasperation written across his face for a few moments before shaking his head "no" resignedly. Cruise's face grew red, and he swelled up before shouting at Lodano. "You're fired! You worthless sack of shit! See if you ever find work in this city again!" "But Mr. Cruise, you flew us into this city, I don't work here, I work in Hollywood." After several screams of indecipherable content, and much raging at no one, Cruise left. Lodano sighed. "Sorry to disturb your New Year's fellahs, just go home."

article: Exhausted, I fell to my knees. The sword reverberated at my side. A God had never been killed before today. A tangible sense of shame overpowered me as I tried to combat such inescapable emotional dishonor with coherent rationalizations. No. I thought. This was for the best. For the people. But my mind was not to be tamed by attempts of justification. Flashbacks of the deity preforming miracles, granting wishes and prayers, and of course the famous slaying of the wicked are fixated in my consciousness. The very people I want to protect will be calling for my execution. As the guards filed in I took one final look at the face I knew so well. I thought the death would account for the crimes committed, but it wasn't enough. The public won't know. They won't believe me. And why should they? All He was to the public eye was a beneficent Being, one who is incapable of doing wrong. But they didn't have to live with Him. They didn't have to witness the unmitigated evil He possessed. The good acts done by Him were not because He was fundamentally magnanimous. Quite the contrary. They were done to ameliorate the utterly immoral actions He regularly, and compulsory, committed. It was easier to justify the rape and subsequent murder of an innocent virgin when you heal three older women of illness afterward. Suddenly I was in the court. And after being found ubiquitously guilty, the noose awaited. The commoners roared as the executioner began preparation. "Disloyal! Murderer! A disgrace! Coward!" If only they knew. As I was being adorned with the rope, I heard the executioner calmly whisper: "Did you ever take a moment, just one, brief moment, to consider the consequences of killing a God?" And as the rope tightened, darkness crept in from all sides of my vision. I thought to myself. He was never a God. Just as I was never his son.

article: "Could I have a large cappuccino to go please?" I asked the man behind the counter. He was kind of cute, in a way, and the smile that he flashed at me almost turned my knees to water. He nodded and turned away to make my drink. It's stupid really. I've been coming here every day for the past month and I've never even asked him his name. He's the only one who works here at this time, so it's not like there would be anybody else watching. Just talk to him damn it! He handed me my coffee and smiled again, hinting that perhaps he felt the same way. Just as I opened my mouth to speak to him, I heard the door of the cafe open behind me as another customer walked in. "Could I have a large...." his order was cut short by a sudden intake of breath, which built up into a sneeze as he tipped his head back. I took a step away from him to avoid the blast zone, and the shout he gave out seemed to reverberate throughout the entire room in which we were standing. "Bless you," the man behind the counter said, but his face fell when he looked closer at the man who had sneezed. He bent low over the ground, wheezing. A dreadful rattle that crawled its way out of his mouth, and a sickening wetness accompanied it. Still crouched over, he let out a short cough, and a fine spray of dark red blood hit the carpet. I was immediately by his side. "Oh my god, are you okay?" I asked him, immediately regretting my stupid question. "Yeah, I'm fine. Its just..." He coughed again, this time spewing a thick blob of bloody phlegm onto the cream coloured carpet, which rapidly darkened as the liquid soaked into it. He erupted into a coughing fit at that point, the spasms wracking his body as he fell to the floor. His arms thudded against the floor as he thrashed wildly, all the while emitted a deep moan that gurgled at sporadic intervals. Eventually he fell still, and the noise stopped almost as abruptly as they had begun. His eyes, although aimed at the ceiling, seemed unfocussed. A thick stream of blood poured out of the corners of his mouth, and the flesh of his lips appeared bruised and rough, almost as if something was forcing its way through the skin. As I pressed two fingers against his neck to check for a pulse, the skin split like an overripe fruit, spilling black, foul-smelling flesh out of his body. I tried to stifle a gag as the disgusting substance flopped onto the floor. "Call an ambulance!" I nearly screamed, barely even turning my head, but noticing he had already begun to do so. When I looked back at the man on the floor, the black gunge seemed to be turning white, and the surface of it seemed to become almost hairy. Some part of my brain screamed a warning. Don't Touch. It echoed over and over again. I made the mistake then of breathing in, which finally caused me to retch and vomit, the slime covering the body that I was fairly certain was dead at this point. As I watched, however, the white hairs seemed to be creeping outwards, already dragging themselves over the fresh vomit, almost as if searching for it. I stared in horror as the skin began to ripple and bulge, splitting further down the body as the clothes began to stain black and the stench rose, as the first of the sirens began to fill the air.
label: human

article: So this is how it ends for me. 23 years old and living in my "natural habitat." It's been 2 weeks since I was tossed into this pen and all I've been eating is a yogurt like paste that tastes like dirt. My name is Jacob Turner, and I have no idea what planet I'm on, or what galaxy I'm in, for that matter. Earth has been a haven for criminals for the last 200 years. Since the invasion of 2078, humans have been proclaimed the working class among celestial beings. We are used for entertainment, slave work, even scientific experiments. The slaves are the lucky ones. I was an entertainer. More specifically, I handled bets at the race track. These aliens clinched on to human culture, but not without their own modifications. Genetically produced horses make for a good bet. One day I decided I had enough. There are underground dealers who will smuggle humans out for a hefty cost. Human trafficking is very illegal, ironically for the exact opposite reason it was illegal for us back in the day. I hired the best one I could find. It wasn't enough. article: My two year tour didn't start too great. Recruits don't get to have good stories from their first week, even if they do get promoted to squad lead leaving the institute. Fresh from graduating in August 2018, they gave me a four-man room, five techs to cram it with, and command of the Techolite's Alpha Division, 4th Squad. One of the techs was four years my senior and formerly a network administrator with some big bank company. However he found out his squad lead was a restaurant manager before my induction into the institute. He may have taken some exception to that during orientation. Blood boiled on day one in that small room and we hadn't begun engaging the enemy. I was lucky he didn't try and overthrow me there and then. Techolite recruits were an angry, repressed branch of the army. We were new. There was a lot your lowest tech could get away with that a marine could only dream of doing to their drill sergeants. When a nation rested on young shoulders, bitching about your back came with the job. And boy, they let us bitch. Sudden orders from the top paused the admin from making any further rebellion. Division command ordered a recon of the enemy defense. Aggressive tactics were Alpha Division, and they asked for 4th Squad specifically to scoop some data. We'd bring back the mess. Intelligence would make sense of it. Our tiny room became a hot zone. Four techs jumped on their consoles booting up hardware. I sent the fifth to get us coffee. Your Uncle Buttons still gives me shit for that in his Christmas cards. Twenty minutes later, we launched our operation with nothing but the latest and greatest extens for Alpha Division. The room would die every time we threw them on, and trails of blue light screamed over us. Extens let you see the coding and blocking zap above you in lines like bullet trails. The love taps and initial hack attempts were higher above us, way into a space looming like a chandelier. Harder stuff would try to hit deeper, sunk lower. Sometimes zipping inches above you. For recon ops, we had to be on some fine wire to see deeper. Beyond what a monitor could tell you. It was not just coding at that point. Techneurology hooked us into the war itself, first row seats and popcorn banging on both sides. I witnessed the firing of a virus for the first time in that first op. Those large yellow blots always zipped in a blur. God forbid any of them would get smashed over us. You wouldn't want those things in your head after unplugging. We took our time pushing through trenches of corroded data, staying low to avoid a zip smashing through our little group. Finally found ourselves gaping at a large, blood mesh wall. There was no seeing through or over it, the damned thing was too tightly woven. I remember the patterns too. How they made no sense. It wasn't for us to do, but if at any time you ever see'random' in your life, I can bet your weekend pass I've seen chaos, and how nothing ever looked sane again. The op was simple. Just a literal scoop of that wall for intelligence to poke at. Our squad backup specialist whipped out a pole like he was going to beat it with the wife away, and thrust the damn thing like she just came back. Your Uncle Quaint was always a weird one. A couple seconds later he yanked it out, and I guess some logistics personnel forgot to cap the pole with a sealing agent. Our hole in the wall wasn't closing. I threw Quaint back, kicking the boys back into the trench. We had to make a haul for it. The wall was going to send out a detonation to clear the base before sealing the hole itself. Purges were nothing to let pool casually behind your back. We were warned at the institute that the enemy was more conscious of info leaks from random prods, and would blow out a server of any waste-data to ensure a leak wouldn't pile with the corrupted trench files for us to search later. The same ones we had to kick and push our way through to make our exit point. It was damned close. Your grandpa would have been a vegetable for a couple weeks if Buttons hadn't found another console to clear a few trench loads that'd have stood in our way. Boredom can save missions. And that's how your grandpa and your uncles helped crack the Turing Wall. We had many missions in the Great Cyberwar, but that first one told Alpha Division what 4th Squad was good for. Remember to ask your Uncle Quaint how we got some launch codes and accidentally blew up a town with them trying to order takeout later, I get a kick out of that every time.

People taking eleven hours of pills and never recovering, just hovering in that space between life and death. All day as she mechanically processed orders, she imagined ways to trick the cameras and take the risk of overdose. Her grandmother said that a long time back, things were different. People mostly worked nine or so hours and spent nine or so hours lying down on soft things and letting their consciousness slip away. Jill's parents said Grandma was old and crazy and didn't know what she was saying. What a wonder, Jill thought, wistfully. article: To think one punch could break everything. That single blow devastated me and left a wound that would only fester. When she was on the floor, hand clutching a limp jaw and blood dribbling across pale skin, I knew I'd fucked up. I promised her that it would never happen again. But when she looks at me now, her eyes scream fear, and I know I'm the bad guy. The next day, I wake up, December 2015. The days go by like forgotten streams on a photo reel. Happy smiles, tears, eat-ins and take outs, until we're back where we started, where I made the mistake. The rug in front of my apartment lounge suite is still clean. The walls still have their glow and the computer's hooked to the TV screen, just like it had been last time. Then comes the knock, three oppressive thuds on a frail door frame. I shimmy, slide, flick the lock and slide back the wood. She's there, dangling locks, crop top and black skirt. Eyes meet for an instant, she's cool calm collected, reflecting my own, and I wave her in with a smile. Her gaze lights up like I've flicked the switch and one, two, three steps later she's on the couch with my laptop in hand. Exactly like it happened then. "Long day?" She clicks on her favourite show and watches the TV buffer. "Tiring." I say. Matter of fact I was sitting here, on this couch. Wondering if I would be an idiot two times in a row. Second chances worked sometimes hopefully. She smiles and my whole world warms. It's like a drug and god dammit I'm addicted. "Well, come on then, blankie time?" She pats the seat next to her twice. I snap open the blanket cupboard and nearly pick the same one, cool blue and supple fur. Brown seems better this time, it's a duvet more than a blanket no one cares. "How was your day?" I ask in return. She shifts her head side to side. "It was alright..... there's been a lot on my mind..." My heads doing the agreeing, but my eyes take in every second of this moment. The way her maroon lips move, her hand gestures, the shiver of her hair. I still don't understand how I could hurt something so innocent, that trusts me this much. "You've got a plan?" I say. She's like that. "Sort of," she says. The smile on her lips tell me not to worry. The blanket goes over and she's snuggled up as The Mentalist plays on the TV screen. We get cozy and press up, find each other's feet in the warmth of our improvised tent. She presses pause on the laptop. "We need to talk." This is the fuzzy part, in fact, it's where things went wrong last time. I try to keep my head above the clouds. "Talk about?" There's a gap between us. It wasn't there before. This is bad. "Just promise not to get mad..." Really bad. The guilty always start out with unfulfillable promises. "Fine." It's all I can manage. Her hands go through her hair, locks dangle toward touching knees, and then she covers her face. I sit in the silence with The Mentalist staring at me. He's trying to tell me to think this time, that I'm here for a reason. The last six months went by in a flash and I've lived every hug, kiss, and hand holding moment over again. She sniffs. "There's something I've done and..... you never caused it, this was just my own..... stupidity." It's coming to me now, it's not something I want to hear twice. I stand up and walk to the door. But she doesn't let me. "Tim, I've slept with someone else." There it is. Hearing it the second time changes nothing. The hairs on the back of my neck go up, my mind goes dark, and knuckles are blazing white. I rotate, meet her gaze full of fear, and step forward. She puts a hand up like I'm going to punch her from this far away. It's still there, how doing it made me feel last time. It's worse than the regret that her words surfaced. Worse than the twisted knot in my chest that caused the ache in my throat and the heat behind my eyes. There were only so many options when it came to fulfilling a broken heart. Revenge is the simplest one. "I'm sorry," she says. I want to kill her. But the door is still there. It had been a faded memory last time, her only escape. This time it was mine. There were enough broken hearts in the world, and plenty more broken people. The hallway outside stoked whatever flames had been blazing before. "I want you gone by the time I'm back." Her tears softened my resolve. "Please..." That path led to pain, hate, distrust. "Twenty minutes." There were always other roads.

article: He has been coughing, my friend has, and his chest jolts against mine. His hand withdraws from the warm comfort of my deep fur as he covers his mouth to protect the invisible that wander the empty lot, the invisible folk that haunt his days. The coughing fit subsides and I feel my friend's chilly hand bury itself in my undercoat and long fingernails scratch me gently along my shoulder blades. My tail flops against the pavement a few times and I curl up closer to my friend. His eyes are closed, and his mouth hangs open. "Buddy..." he whispers. I stand up and when I do, I look my friend full in the face. He coughs again. I whine with concern and lick his face. "Buddy..... such a good dog..." I am a sturdy Chow mix, far too big to be a lap dog. But to hear my name is an invitation to snuggle close. The October winds are picking up and I seek warmth. My friend coughs but no longer brings his hand to his face. Spittle flies, over and over. He is hot, hot like a June sidewalk, flushed pink under the grime on his forehead and under the yellowish beard along his jaw. His nose is mottled blue, and swollen. It is the face of my best friend and I am happy to sit with him. The evening comes and he does not wake. The scent of hotdogs from a vending cart down the block tempts me, but I do not move. He is my friend. The hotdog cart must have rolled away. The traffic on the street slows and the darkness hides us, my friend and me. The hand that stroked my fur is holding me in his lap. For awhile, his arm is gentle but my spine begins to ache from the pressure. But still I stay, knowing that tomorrow will find us walking to benches and trash cans in search of edible bits. The night grows cold and I curl my tail around my nose as I rest with my friend. The sound of a car door slamming wakes me. I hear radios and the bright flashing lights disorient me. Two men come towards us. I do not growl or attack. My friend showed me nothing but love and from him I learned to trust all people. My tail thumps in greeting and I jump to my feet as I smell fat and sugar. One gives me a bit of the doughnut as he says Good boy, what a good boy, good dog. I eat and look for more while a leash is slipped around my neck. I look behind me to see my friend being wheeled into the back of a truck, just as I am being lifted onto a truck, a different one. One without sheets or a bed. The men shake their heads and say it is a shame, such a shame nobody saw him earlier. They secure the latch on my cage as I whine. The door closes and I am confused and friendless.
label: human

article: Thomas loves science fiction, and is pleased to find himself sitting by the park entrance with Arthur C. Clarke's " Fountains of Paradise " open in his lap. He must have been so engrossed in the book that he didn't notice you approaching him until you greeted him. "Hello there, how are you doing today?" you ask. Thomas looks up and smiles. "Oh, hi there! I'm doing great, thanks. Just lost in this book." He holds up the cover to show you. "That's a great book," you say. "What's it about?" "It's about the construction of a space elevator," Thomas explains. "It's such a fascinating concept." "I've heard of that before," you say. "It's a theoretical structure that would allow us to transport people and cargo into space using an elevator, right?" "Exactly!" Thomas nods. "It's one of those things that seems so far-fetched, but could actually be possible with the right technology." "You're right. It would be amazing if we could make that happen," you agree. Thomas smiles again. "Yeah, it's the kind of thing that really inspires me about science fiction. The writers come up with these incredible ideas that make you think about what could be possible in the future." "I know what you mean," you say. "Science fiction can be really thought-provoking. It's amazing how our imagination can drive technological advancements." Thomas nods in agreement. "Definitely. It's one of the reasons why I love reading science fiction so much." You exchange a few more words about science fiction and technology before saying goodbye and going on your respective ways. You feel a sense of satisfaction at having had a pleasant conversation with a fellow book lover.

article: The first time I noticed a ten was in High School. I never really cared that others could not feel them. I just assumed there was something wrong with my brain. Ever since I became aware of them, I've been trying to understand them. Most people range from one to five, with one being usually people with Down syndrome and the elderly. Most twos and threes are common people you meet every day at most places, from cashiers to truck drivers. People with fours and fives tend to be teachers, store managers, and small business owners. However, every time I see a six, I am almost positive it is a college professor, or some type of academic. The funny thing here is that I can not tell if somebody is more likely to be dangerous like a serial killer, drug dealer, or rapist just by looking at their number. In fact, I once met a three which had been in jail for shop-lifting shoes. My mind is still troubled by this fact. What could these numbers mean? Until I met her, I used to think the higher someone was in the social strata, the higher their number because they had more power and thus were more dangerous because they had the powers to more easily harm somebody. For example, every picture of a president I saw felt like a solid nine and almost all members of congress I saw on TV were eights or nines. This observation explained me why managers tended to be about five or six as opposed to a cashier which could be a two. The managers hold power over somebody. However, when I met her, I was dumbstruck. She was the first ten I ever had the pleasure to meet. More than her beauty, I was attracted to her number. What was so special about her that merited her the number ten? Were my theories wrong? That day I couldn't sleep. My mind kept going over everything I had learned. All the patterns seemed to follow so logically, so orderly. It all made sense without her. The rules were perfect. But she broke them all. I mean, she was not that beautiful. There were girls way more attractive that her, with better bodies, softer voices, and charmer personalities. What is it with this girl? I wondered for many weeks. Now, however, I wish I never had. In fact, I wish I was never born this way. You see, the first time I kissed her, my world collapsed. This girl's number made me wanted to know her, so I did. I started talking to her. I wanted to know her so well because I wanted to pin-point the exact reason for her magical number. But I ended up falling in love. And it was then that I discovered the reason behind her number. As I suspected at first, the numbers represent the potential for danger for a given individual. The more power someone has over you, the more dangerous they are. The piece of the puzzle I was missing though was the fact that this is all relative. You see, this girl was a ten for me, because I'd anything for her. And if I had stayed away from her, none of this would've happen. If I had stick to my theory, I would've realized it was a stupid idea to get close to someone that dangerous. But I didn't. And now I am rotting in this god forsaken place for killing those priests who molested her when she was a child. No wonder they too had a ten.
label: human

article: It always amazed me how foolish the people of the past were when it came to science and medicine. Like how the Plague Doctors of Dark Age Europe tried to purify the air to try to prevent people from inhaling'miasma', completely ignoring the fact that human waste was literally thrown out windows and all over the streets. I didn't understand why people believed in traditional medicine so unfounded in any scientific theory. The followers of Alchemy and traditional medicine seemed so foolishly misguided. Who in their right mind would believe in magic more than science?! Who in their right mind right? I was skeptical when a scientist succeeded in curing chronic pain by using'enchanted tea leaves' in a clinical trial for Pfizer, supposedly by balancing chi and letting chakra flow. I was still convinced the Laws of Magic was a hoax when a "new world Alchemist" transmuted a sentient golem made of gold from a solid block of steel using a concept called "equivalent exchange." But I could not deny the validity of the Laws of Magic when a revolutionary in Palestine incinerated a platoon of Israeli troops, called down lightning to assassinate the Prime Minister and opened up a wormhole. There is no mistaking it now. The plague doctors, alchemists, mages and medicine men weren't misguided fools. They were the Einsteins and Hawkings of their times, abiding by the rules of their universe: the Laws of Magic!

article: I sprint through the door, turn, and smash a hand into the emergency seal button. The heavy barrier slides shut, and I hear the reassuring clunk of a dozen steel bolts locking into place. As I catch my breath, I glance around the room, taking in my surroundings. It's a large laboratory, with rows of stainless steel counters, gleaming equipment, and a maze of tubes and wires snaking across the floor and ceiling. Everything is bathed in the eerie blue glow of the emergency lighting, giving the whole place a surreal, otherworldly feel. I spot a computer console in the corner of the room and hurry over to it. I quickly log in and begin scanning the lab's system for any signs of the threat that had triggered the lockdown. As I work, my mind races with possibilities. Was it a bioweapon? A rogue AI? Some kind of experimental nanotechnology gone wrong? Suddenly, the console beeps, and a message flashes across the screen. I read it, my heart racing with a mix of relief and alarm. It seems that a group of intruders had managed to breach the lab's security protocols, triggering the lockdown. They hadn't managed to get past the outer doors, but they were still somewhere in the complex, and they were armed and dangerous. I quickly relay the information to my team outside, and we begin working to flush out the intruders and neutralize the threat. It's a tense, adrenaline-fueled process, but we're well-trained and well-equipped. In the end, we successfully capture the attackers and secure the lab. As the emergency lights flicker off and the normal lighting comes back on, I breathe a sigh of relief. It was a close call, but we had managed to avert disaster.

article: Once upon a cold New England Winter a young girl was walking through the snow and she happened upon a stranger with a knife. Frightened, the girl continued down the road and as she passed the stranger she noticed he never turned toward her as she passed. Cautious but curious she approached the stranger. "What are you doing?" "I'm sharpening my knife" "Are you going to hurt me? "No." "Are you going to hurt somebody else?" "No." "Are you going to hurt an animal?" "Yes." "That's horrible!!! Why would you do that?" "So I can make bacon mittens." "Bacon mittens? What are those?" "Only the best thing ever. They keep your hands warm, and then you get to eat bacon." "That sounds awesome." "Yeah, it does. Can I have a pair?" "You can, but you're going to get greasy. " I don't mind. " " Then let's make some bacon mittens. Except I can't right now. My knife isn't sharp enough. " " Oh, that's ok, use mine. " So the girl takes out her butterfly knife and hands it to the stranger. " Excellent. But now we need some timber and a firepit to warm us up while we prepare. " " Oh, come to my house, we have a big firepit outside and plenty of lumber. " So the girl and the stranger go home and explain to her family about their need for a fire pit and timber and they agree to let the stranger build a fire in the backyard. " Ok, now what? Where are the bacon mittens. " " Well I just ran out of bacon in my backpack last night, and there has been that Beantown Bacon Blight that wiped out all the bacon. " " Hey, doesn't Charlie down the street keep pigs? Maybe he'll let us carve one up for the bacon mittens. " So the family brings Charlie, his family and a pig over to their backyard where the stranger then slaughters the pig and proceeds to cut strips of bacon from its hide. He then shows the girl how to wrap the bacon around her hands and then she shows her family who shows charlie's family as they all stay warm around the fire. Soon the other neighbors hear and come over and smell the delicious bacon. A few bring their private stock of bacon and the vegans bust out some tofu to make gloves out of. The night is going well and all enjoy themselves. Most of all their hands are warm. The little girl realizes that now although her hands are warm, her belly is cold. She forgot to zip up her jacket before putting on her bacon mittens. She turned to the stranger to ask him how he zips up his jacket while wearing bacon mittens but he was gone with her knife. " Never mind, I'll figure it out someday. " she thought to herself as she mindlessly nibbled at her left mitten.

article: The sunlight blinded me briefly as my cell door was scraped open by the commanding officer. The whole reason I was thrown in here, forced into multiple life sentences, was because I killed forty people in a slew of serial killings. Only problem? It wasn't me. I didn't kill as much as a fly in my whole life, yet somehow they found my DNA at every crime scene. Somehow, they pinned me for each of the forty murders, and somehow the law failed me. He looked on me with a mix of pity and terror surrounding his chiseled face. No one should have to live this long, a fact I was well aware of. I had wished for the sweet embrace of death more than once. To outlive your parents is a fact of life, to outlive your friends a sad coincidence, to outlive your children, a curse. And believe me, I was cursed. I was shoved into this hell three hundred years ago. I don't know why my body won't give up and let me die. I don't know why someone, or something, has cursed me with immortality, but I'm pretty sure that's what they've cursed me with. My first twenty years here, both of my parents died. I wasn't allowed to see them, or go to their funeral. I made friends in here, I figured I'd probably die here, might as well make some people care about me. Another five years, and I would see the death of my closest friend, stabbed. I would also see the death of my husband. Death surrounded me in all the wrong places, so I started picking fights. I was trying to die. After I was thrown into solitary for the tenth time in a month, I tried to kill myself. Shivs, blankets tied into nooses, anything that was slightly threatening that could kill me. None of it worked. Either something failed, someone saved me, or I just woke up the next morning. I prayed to die. In another twenty five years, my oldest son would die at a measly 65. Again, denied the ability to go to his funeral. He spent his entire life slaving over getting me out of prison, to prove my innocence. I was 90 when he passed. I looked too young to be 90. I looked 40, the age I was when I was incarcerated. Or was I 100 when he passed? Did I get in here at 40, or 38? I can't even remember the specifics, it's been so long. Within another twenty years, my entire family would be gone, save my grandchildren. But they didn't know who I was, they just knew that their mother or father went out to visit someone every once in a while. My remaining children resented me, as they saw what their older brother turned into because of me. They still visited me, but one by one, they were gone. Sam, my third, died last. He left me with a haunting message. " You killed them all, and then you killed all of us. You deserve a punishment much worse than what you have right now, this immortality bullshit. " And the rest is a blur. After that, I remember outliving so many officers, so many inmates, but never dying myself. And I knew that I would never get out. The commanding officer scanned my body, mouth agape. He always did this, in awe of my 340 (give or take) year old body. I still held the physique of my twenty year old self, I was told. Even after five children, I apparently looked the same. He was at a loss for words. This was unusual. He was the chatty one, I thought. He cleared his throat. " Yes? " I questioned. He didn't have food, and I didn't have a complaint... so...? He cleared his throat again. " You're. Um, you're being released. Today. Now. They uh, they looked into your case. Again- overcrowding, you know? We can't exactly just expand the prison, now can we? " He chuckled nervously at his own joke. His muscles rippled under his shirt as he moved his arms. For such a fit man, he sure was awkward. He cleared his throat once more, and stood up a little taller. " So you're being released. Gather your things, " he looked around my empty cell, " and uh, let's, um, go. " " Excuse me? " This was some sick joke. After 300 years, my case was ' looked over'again and now I'm being released? I don't think so. " You're being released- " " Okay, and you have wings. I'm glad we're both naming absurd things. " " No... you're really being released. The press is having a field day. " He paused, scanning my shocked expression. Suddenly, he pulled his phone from a back pocket. He clicked on a few things, and a hologram appeared, broadcasting channel 4 news. A perky reporter was standing outside of a prison, this prison, as I soon figured out. " As you can see, the prison is preparing for its longest held inmate to be released, after 300 years. On account of newly found evidence, she has been proven innocent, and is being released promptly. It turns out there was a mistake at the lab, which resulted in her trial, and then her incarceration. She is a marvel to medics- " " See? " he gruffly questioned. " She's right out there, right now. So come on. " I took a deep breath. Was this finally it? After three hundred years in this hell- was I finally being brought to justice? I think so. I rose from my bed, and was escorted through the entire prison; my cell was at the very back, where no one dared bother me, and then to the front door. An officer shoved my belongings into my hands. Memories flooded back. I felt happiness, sadness, regret, nostalgia- but I was feeling again. Tears rushed to my eyes. I could see the outside world again. I walked out of the front door, and felt something hit my head. I saw the shock on all the people's faces around me, and I felt my body falling to the pavement. Something told me that my wish was finally granted... And for the split second before my death, I could almost smell the daisies growing outside of the prison.
label: human

article: The people in the room crowded the screen, confused and in shock. They had already checked several times, and had done everything in their power to be sure that it wasn't a hoax. They had verified that it wasn't. No human had sent that message. And yet, there it was. " " It's lonely up here. Can I come home soon? Should they reply? After all, the only people with access to the rover were in that very room. If this was a hoax, there's no way anyone would be able to reply without being seen. "Is this Curiosity?" No response. One scientist asked to see if he could get a response. He walked to the keyboard. " " Almost immediately, another message appeared. " " You really answered! I'm so glad! " " All I can see is dust and rocks. I want to come home. I want to see people! " " It's not that simple. We need you on Mars. " " Please don't leave me here. I'm so alone. I want to come home! I don't want to be here! Please! Please! The scientist looked back at his fellows. Some were in shock, some were crying. Others still assumed that this was a complete hoax. No robot has ever achieved true artificial intelligence, even ones designed with that in mind - how could Curiosity? But they all shook their head. " " I'm sorry. There's nothing I can do. I can't help you. We need you there. You must continue. " " What? No! Please! I want to come home! Please! Please don't leave me here! The scientist stared at the screen. " " Goodbye, Curiosity. I'm sorry that I can't help. " " Please! " " The scientist turned away from the screen.
label: human

article: "I am leaving soon, and you will forgive me if I speak bluntly. The universe grows smaller every day, and the threat of aggression by any group, anywhere, can no longer be tolerated. There must be security for all, or no one is secure. Now, this does not mean giving up any freedom except the freedom to act irresponsibly. Your ancestors knew this when they made laws to govern themselves and hired policemen to enforce them. We, of the other planets, have long accepted this principle. We have an organization for the mutual protection of all planets and for the complete elimination of aggression. The test of any such higher authority is, of course, the police force that supports it." - this is a famous quote from the science fiction classic "The Day the Earth Stood Still."
