article: "The hell kind of question is that? Look, when you said we needed to meet and talk about work on a frickin' Sunday afternoon, did I care? No. Did I bitch and complain? No. I put on my big kid pants, left my wife at home, and came here to this ratty-ass diner just for you." "Jim, you and I both know you'd have left your wife alone tonight anyway." "That's not the point and hey, what the fuck man? Who are you talkin' to right now, huh? YOUR BOSS. I swear, you mention one more thing about my wife or what I may or may not do later tonight and you're gon na find yourself with a lot of free time this time next week. Got it?" "Yeah Jim, I gotcha." He smiled a smile that showed itself as something between bemused and pitying. A long drag of his cigarette resulted in the not-quite-finished smoke stick being smashed among the corpses of its long-before extinguished brethren. The man exhaled only slightly away from the face his non-smoking counterpart and gazed apathetically around the smoking section of the diner. It was a 50's style diner much like you see next to a Stuckey's in the middle of New Mexico, or imagine to be the setting of a Hunter S. Thompson book. Man, people have weird fantasies. Of all the places..... "So what is it you wanted to talk about? Or was that stupid question all you wanted to bother me with?" Jim looked about the room while chastising the image of his subordinate in front of him, hoping to find the waitress so he could encourage her to get a move on those pancakes. "Jim, why do you like Pulp Fiction?" Jim gave him a look as if to say If you aren't going to talk about work, thank you for talking about something I like. "It's a great movie, ya know? Amazing dialogue, the camerawork is just masterful..... and I've got a thing for diners anyway. Like this one! Say, how did you know to invite me here? I didn't even know this place existed! It's pretty nice - very retro and..... well, kinda like from Pulp Fiction!" "I have a gift for this kind of thing. Also, the file helps." he said after firing up another cigarette. After taking that long, pleasurable first drag he grabbed the file folder on the table and waived it in Jim's general direction. "File? Holy shit man, have you been stalking me?" Jim's coworker started to laugh. Not a normal laugh; more like a laugh you have to force yourself into, but in the midst of your feigned joviality you find some hilarious irony to your laughter and thus burst into an altogether new level of hilarity. "You might say so," he managed to squeak out after taking a sip of his coffee, "and you could even say I do this for a living." Jim's muscular structure fired off in dramatic fashion, effectively doing everything but actually stand up from the table at which they were seated. "The FUCK man!" Jim noticed his voice travelling to the ears of nearby customers and tried to quell his furious anger. "What are you after? Is it money,'cause you sure as fuck know I've got none. We work at the same shitty company for nearly the same shitty salary so you know what I'm lookin' at in my bank. I do a fucking Irish jig when I see a comma in my checking account." As Jim came to the realization that his subordinate wasn't after anything like that, he become both more calm and more aware of his surroundings. The customers he thought were hearing his exclamations weren't there. The waitress hadn't been on the floor in 10 minutes. In fact, to the best of his knowledge, there was nobody in the building but them. So it begins. He's finally realized..... "Jim, I'm going to ask you two questions. If you answer them correctly I will give you what you want - even if you don't realize you want it now. It's something more precious than you wife, your job, or those commas you so desire. Hell, I'll even let you fire me!" He put the cancerous tube to his mouth and leisurely took a drag. "And if I don't?" the slightly less than belligerent boss asked. A terrible smile sauntered its way across the lower-ranking man's face. "If you don't, I have what I would call an'unending' surprise for you." Jim tried his best to look stern and intimidating. He failed miserably, but kept up the act and decided he'd had enough of this. "Alright, ask the questions." "How did you get home last night, Jim?" What? Of all the questions..... "I got in my car with..... uh, with a friend. And we - I mean, I took he I took her home. That's all." "You didn't answer my question, Jim. How did you get home?" Jim looked at the bottom of his empty, stainless coffee cup. "I dropped her off. And eventually I got home." "Are you sure?" "The fuck do you mean'am I sure?' Of course I'm sure! How the hell am I here if I didn't get home?" Jim was nearly at his breaking point. He glanced nervously at the file across the table sitting next to his far-too-calm underling. "One last time, Jim. How did you get home?" "I DROVE HOME. OKAY?" Jim thought about this statement as soon as it left his lips. Actually, he had no idea. He and that girl had had a hell of a night at her place and kept drinking through the night. Kept drinking. How did he get home again? He got in the car and....... "Ah, I see you've realized something, Jim." "Why can't I remember how I got home?" Jim desperately inquired. The man in front of him clapped. Not a genuine applause, but a sarcastic, slightly too slow clap. "Jim, James, Jimmy boy! You've got it. You figured it out." Jim was teetering of insanity trying to figure out what was going on, when his companion piped up: "So, Jim. My second question." The suddenly bright red-eyed man inhaled a tar-filled breath of smoky air. "Are you dead?" "What? Of course I'm not dead!" Jim lost all color in his face. His subordinate smiled a devilish smile.
label: human

article: This is my first time commenting on a writing prompt. All opinions and criticism is welcome. I haven't written (in real life) in a while so bare with me as I am rusty. "Carey..... It's time" said Win as he opened the door to the dressing room where Carey had prepared his speech for his piece he was unveiling at the gala. Carey had become an overnight sensation in the realm of media for capturing seemingly unreal or perfect photos of wonders and relics long since passed. "Tonight in front of all of you, I am proud to show my new picture that encapsulates the times before modern technology. The times before we had cameras that had auto set He pauses for a moment mid sentence to realize the crowd fell completely still. He looked down at his watch, "Damn." he says realizing that the watch was the cause of time standing still. The watch needed to be wound back up every 9 hours or else time would freeze on it's own. This nifty worn down unsavory piece of metal was how he got his pictures in the first place, along with the help of a photo album he bought at a little shop of gilden street containing the images of ancient ruins and wonders of the world would change his life forever. He first found out about the power when he touched slid his hand across the picture of The House of Virgin Mary in present day Turkey. A flash of light and a few moments later he was standing in Ephesus just outside of the house where he saw Mary walk to the front door, then just as quick as she appeared in the flesh he was brought back to his time with only the memories of what happened. Carey thought of a plan to show the true essence of life before his time. This is where the watch makes it's appearance. A traveling man on day when Carey was taking pictures in Spain sold him the watch for a few coins, Carey felt the watch was strange as the minute hand would rotate counter clockwise. One day while collecting photos around the city he noticed a bird perfectly still on a fence. He quickly realized that somehow time was standing still. He looked at his watch and all hands stopped at 6:30:30. After winding for a few turns time gradually began flowing again. Carey starts to walk a few blocks and a woman with black hair walks up to him and says "Welcome to Unravel."
label: human

article: The Rhythm filled me. The Rhythm filled us all. We were invincible. Arrows stopped at arm's length, before falling to the ground in front of me. The war drums filled my ears and flooded my body. All the earth followed the rhythm. The beat pushed us onwards. Each resounding boom was a command. Charge. Fight. Win. Arrows flew back and forth overhead. It didn't matter. No one would die in this battle until one side or the other lost the rhythm. That was how wars were fought, and that was how wars were won. Destroy the beat, you destroyed the entire army. I could hear the hideous sounds of the sawtooth instruments of our enemy. It was impure and wretched. Our empire had adopted the drums of war. We did not require melody. Every man knew the Rhythm, and that was our strength. I closed my eyes and exhaled slowly. I absorbed the Rhythm, and it became me. My heart beat to the Rhythm. I fought to the Rhythm. Every step, every blow, every parry, was directed to the Rhythm. The ground shook. To one side of us it began to crack and roar. The earth spewed out fire upon the enemy, and their screams and wails only joined our Rhythm. Such was the power of the drum. My squadron and I charged forwards. Perfect unison. I raised my shield to block the blow of an enemy solider. Even if I hadn't, he couldn't kill me. I was completely invincible. I should have stumbled to the ground long ago in exhaustion. This battle had gone on far too long. I swung my sword low, to his knees, and he leapt back. I saw my chance. I surged forwards, slamming my shield against his chest. He grunted, eyes widening.He collapsed beneath me. His heart stopped. He had lost his rhythm. I focused on the Rhythm, trying to block out the rhythms of the enemy. They faded down to almost nothing, and I once more began my assault. I could hear our Rhythm speeding up. A dangerous tactic, to be sure. It could easily cause your entire army to lose the protection of the beat, but it, when used properly, could easily catch the other side off guard, causing them to fall, revoked of their powers. It worked. I could see hundreds of them collapse from exhaustion, trampled beneath the tidal forces of both armies. I caused many men to lose their rhythm that day. Each one got to feel the cold bite of my sword deep in their chests. The Rhythm sped up. Sometimes it slowed. But every time I faithfully followed where it led me. Then, there was nothing. Where I expected the boom of the drums, there was only silence. We fought as one, and now we fell as one. Our heart stopped. They had stopped our Rhythm. I could feel the darkness closing in. Weakly, I gripped my sword. With all my strength, I pounded it against my shield Bang. I closed my eyes, expecting to die. But then, I heard another clang of sword against shield. Then another. And another. The Rhythm had died But now we made a new song. And we rose again. As one. I know I'm kinda late to the party, but this was what came to mind when I read this prompt. article: The world is a different place when you are five. Bedtime at eight, sharp. Diet dictated by your parents. Entertainment is demoted to colourful flashes of colour and high voices talking to you from behind a screen, asking you to find the red bridge that is clearly right behind her. Freedom is limited to the toys you can play with when you are finally told that, yes, you can go and play with them. Toys... When was the last time you played with toys? With nothing you talking to them and waiting for a reply. After a certain point in life, you begin to seek out more than toys. You want something more to fill in your time. You want books, television. You want something with more thought behind. Maybe a narrative. Or something with a high level of effort put into it. That's when toys stop being fun. When you're forced back into them, they seem empty and hollow. The characters you imagined are all gone and you're left holding their static remains. You have no peers. No one is at your level. No one is anywhere near you're level! Everyone talks about cartoons and superheroes and Barbies and all the other things you think you're over but it's all you have. They aren't smart enough. They're aren't emotional mature enough to give you anything more than a headache and a sour mood. Adults don't talk to you. You can offer up the conversation you want to have, filled with all the maturity and sophistication that you can manage from your tiny, underdeveloped vocal chords. They just smile and pat you on the head. Or maybe the nod and think you're being cute. You know everything. School becomes a pointless drag with no difficulty. Even the subject you've long forgotten are too basic to offer a challenge. You hope something comes along to test you, but it doesn't. Colour in the Roman armour. Join the dots to make a cat. Draw arrows to the leaves and petals of the flower. Read the books you can manage in under give minutes. Now do the next one. But then enough time passes and you do manage to get that little bit extra. Your parents give you weird looks, telling you that the book you want is ' too hard for you ', but you persevere. You get that novel you never read and always thought sounded fun. You find out you love it. Your parents are impressed. Six years old and reading books that are usually for teenagers. They talk to your school, asking if you can get into harder material. Everyone agrees and the books you get for homework are better than the ones from before. Spot the Dog is replaced by The Lord of the Rings and Discworld and, suddenly, parts of your life become bearable. School gets ever so slightly harder as your other subject follow suit. There's challenge in life again. Adults treat you as some sort prodigy and offer conversation that, while dulled and softened for your little ears, entices you to go back. They offer a social life. Not a fulfilling one, but something. You go up a year in school. You still find everything entirely too easy. You're almost seven and something is very wrong. Your parents are spending more time with you, pleased with your progress. They go out of their way to give you mental stimulation, making sure they help your gift flourish. They want you to succeed. They love you. It's three months until your little brother's birthday. Your mother is not pregnant.

article: I sat on the floor of my tiny studio staring at my hands that were still shaking violently. I clenched my fists tight taking in a deep breath. "Just a dream." I said trying to calm down. I stood up and walked over to the pantry and found the last of my Jack Daniels. I put it into an Owl shaped mug and within a few swigs it was gone. I felt my eyes get tired again and laid on my bed. "No dreams." I said to my brain of course it didn't listen. It had been only a few months since I was approached by a homeless man who wanted to give me a "gift" for buying him a hot meal. Some gift. I hadn't slept in days and when I did sleep the dreams came. Horrible visions of what could happen not would but could. I could see the future but there were two flaws to this. The future wasn't set in stone so say someone wants to shoot up a school, they go to bed believing they are going to shoot up the school kill whoever then kill themselves but they wake up and something changes their mind, maybe they're favorite cereal was on sale, doesn't matter cause they choose not to shoot up the school. I get to see them actually do it, the people screaming for mercy, the jock pissing his pants when faced with death all of it. When this gift first happened I would cry wolf every time. Most of the time I was right but of course the media only got wind of when I was wrong and it wasn't long before I was written off as a crazy person who lucked out on a few right calls. The second was that the only time the dreams stopped was when I drank heavily, which made me develop a drinking habit that would put an Irishman to shame. I rolled out of bed seeing the clock say it was almost 10:00 am. I sat up and got dressed grabbed my wallet and started my walk to the store. I had moved twice since getting the " gift " and now lived off of whatever money my parents sent me. They were sure I was having a mental breakdown and forced to go to counseling to get their checks every month. My head spun back and forth as I made it to Albertsons. I filled my cart with Gatorade, bread, peanut butter, jelly, bananas and of course whiskey. I must have smelt horrid because people made sure to avoid me as I checked out. I walked out the store and walked through the parking lot. I didn't hear it but a car backed up beside me and bumped my hip. I turned and screamed at it. " Watch where you're fucking going! " I screamed. I looked at the rearview mirror and saw a set of very familiar piercing green eyes. I felt my heart sink and I dropped my bags. I wanted to be angry but the pure shock was still racing through me. He stepped out of the car and I barely recognized him. The skinny, smelly homeless man with a scraggly beard and stringy hair was now standing tall. His face was clean and he wore a polo shirt and jeans. " Hello, Sarah. " He said. He voice wasn't as raspy as it was and I swore he even looked younger. I felt the shock begin to wear off and rage replaced it. " You! " I screamed and ran at him. I grabbed his shirt. " You fucking piece of dog shit! Do you know what you've done to me? " I yelled at the top of my lungs. He wasn't fazed. " Yes. " He said. No remorse or guilt just a stern affirmation. I let him go and put my hand out. " Take it back! I can't take this anymore! Please! " I screamed. He sighed and shook his head. " I'm sorry Sarah but no. " " Take it or I'll make you! " I screamed. He smiled and laughed a little. " Sorry but you can only receive the gift if you want it. I don't want it. " He went to get back in his but I grabbed him. I fell to my knees my eyes swollen with tears. " Please! I can't do this! " I said. He pulled his arm away. " You think you have it rough! I was stuck with that thing for five year! I lost my wife, kids, and job and was fucking living on the streets eating garbage! " He grabbed me by my hair and tossed me away from his car. " You've had it for five fucking months! You want to get rid of it find some sad sap to take it just like I did! " He jumped in his car and sped away. I got to my feet and started walking. I felt my feet moving as I contemplated what he said. Was I willing to put this burden on some poor new sap? I got home with only the bottle of whiskey and sat on my bed. I walked to the medicine cabinet and pulled out a bottle of Tylenol and one by one took every single pill. I laid on the bed and started to cry not from the fear of dying, it couldn't be all that bad, but from relief that pretty soon it would all be over. My eyes finally grew heavy and I went into my dreamless sleep.

article: "YOU'RE GOING TO LOSE, YOU KNOW." "Come on, bones," said the mugger through the bullet hole in his throat, his voice decidedly less melodious than gravel on a chalkboard. "You said so yourself, this was a special occasion." The reaper of Humans sighed and adjusted the bow-tie of the ridiculous tuxedo he'd dressed in for the game. At least he could stop time, he thought as he stared at the three cards facing up in his hand. He'd been kind and let them each have a single face-down card. "DEALER HITS." A three of spades. Death had seventeen; a queen of clubs, a four of spades and his new three. The top card was a jack of hearts. The card two down from the top would be a four of hearts, bringing him to twenty one. One from the top was a four of clubs, also bringing him to twenty one. That was how it always ended. He could count cards for infinity, calculate dozens of statistics per draw and could read the kinks in the cards to know what had been drawn. Not that he needed to; even if they brought in their own deck he could just stare through his opponent's cards and continue to win. Sometimes he liked to humor his opponents; give them the hope that they might win, especially if they'd led a particularly good life. Usually they were good sports about leaving after that. This wasn't so clean-cut. A mugger, a freshly-snorted pile of cocaine, a dark alleyway, a woman, her date and a Mexican standoff over her body. It was the third time in the last hundred years this had happened. Most of the time, the criminal shoots first. It was a rare but impressive occurrence when two people died within the exact same millisecond. It had happened, by Death's count, fourteen thousand, eight hundred and forty three times at this point. Three people had died simultaneously six hundred and ninety one times. Four had died twenty eight times. In his entire career, five people had died at the same time only once. He hosted a tea party, congratulated them, and then promptly tore their souls from their corpses. It was convenient that they were all in the same room, he mused for what felt like a millennium. Finally, his opponent made the choice. "I'll stay." The mugger coughed as he said it, blood spraying onto his hand. He flipped his face-down card. A ten of hearts and a jack of spades. Twenty. The reaper mused for a moment, wondering if maybe the mugger thought he was lucky instead of the product of an elaborate scam. "Hit me." The date plucked the jack from Death's hands with a finger covered in the blood of his stomach's entrance wound. Eleven or twenty one, depending on how you interpreted the ace on the table. Death considered for a moment, looking back at the woman in the alley, the terror on her frozen face. She had a good time that night. "HARD 17. DEALER STAYS." "No shit?" The mugger spat. "You got 17. You lose, bones." "Hit me again," the date said, his voice growing nervous. The four came to him. Fifteen showing. "FOUR OF HEARTS. YOU HAVE FIFTEEN SHOWING, YOUNG MAN." "Thank you, sir." The young man peered over the table, over Death's shoulder, at the woman. "Sir," he said, his wavering voice hardening, "what will happen if I lose?" The skull that was the reaper's head didn't blink. "YOU WILL DIE." "And you're just going to let this guy live?" The man half-asked, half-yelled as he slammed his fist on the tabletop's green velvet. Unable to speak further, the mugger just cackled as more blood spewed out of his throat. Death said nothing for a while. "FIFTEEN SHOWING, YOUNG MAN. WILL YOU HIT OR STAY?" "Fuck it, then! Hit me!" The young man gritted his teeth and waited for the card. The second four came and he froze in fear. "FOUR OF CLUBS," Death said, his skull still unblinking. "YOU HAVE NINETEEN SHOWING AND FIVE CARDS." The man's eyes widened. He looked at Death and, with pure terror on his face, began to realize what the number meant. The mugger saw his face and continued to laugh, a raspy, clogged sound that grew louder as Death raised his hand. "FLIP THE LAST CARD." Shaking, the man turned it over. A two of hearts. Twenty one. The mugger choked and spat out what would be his last words. "You son of a Death snapped his bony fingers and the mugger evaporated, nothing but a pile of ash remaining. Back in the real world, his body lay motionless. It would never move again. "Wh what do I do now?" The man asked, still holding the bloody card. Death gathered the cards and tossed him the deck. "NOW?" There was a long pause. "YOU DEAL." The skeletal man pulled a dark cloak around himself and disappeared, leaving the new Death to his own games.

article: "A lot of people are calling you a hero." "A lot aren't." I tear the velcro cuffs of my gloves, tossing them across the table - they land on the other side near the newspaper. Jerald continues to force his nose in my face, as if I wanted to hear what he had to say. I already know what I did. Nothing can change my mind. That conscious being, that genetic'person' that we transferred..... I don't even know what it is anymore." "But Rob, you do know! article: "But are you sure the Master will be ok?" My pack sister stared at me, nervous and frightened. It had been three days since the Master had left our home, leaving inside the humans metal beast that ran faster than any bird could fly. It was known by all dogs that humans could live for many generations, sometimes for seven or more. Such was the way with our Master. My mother's mother told stories of her grandfathers mother growing with our Master as pups, but we had only known him as the slow but loving human he is today. My pack sister barked again impatiently, and I was drawn from my reverie. "The Master will be fine," I growled, making my aggravation for her incessant worrying known "he has survived the blood fields and fire rain. This sickness inside will not be his end." This seemed to calm her for a moment, her ears raised back up and her tail slowed its fearful wagging. "Beware!" barked Alpha, his massive frame rising from then ground, "There are humans in our land!" My pack sisters rose frantically, barking up a storm as they propelled themselves to the opening wall. Our Masters Pup came in through the opening wall, bringing with her her own pups, and their pups as well, the smell of cleaning sprays and dead things heavy on their removable fur. Alpha bowled into Masters Pup's daughter, she had barely been more than a pup when he had been brought from a world of cages and fear into our home, and they had spent much of their time together. Slowly I pushed my way into the greeting; my joints ached from the strain of keeping my body up, but I had grown old, very old by our standards. So had our master, but I could not smell him on their skin or removable fur, only the smell of clean and death. Their eyes were red as we licked them, and their cheeks tasted of salt. Humans do this when they ate sad, its their way of coping. They spoke in great sobs as they scratched us, saying words of theirs. A few of them I knew, and I knew more words than any of my pack sisters even more words than our Alpha. They said words like "come," "walk," "good dogs" "gone." Their voices broke when they said their word for master "Rick," barely able to get the noise out, but my ears were still very sharp. They were grabbing our neck-lines even as fresh salt-water began to form around their eyes and sobs racked their bodies. Our humans led us to the metal beast, silent but blasting heat around itself into the frigid air. We got in as it roared to life and we went very fast towards the sun. My young pack sisters were overjoyed to stick their noses into the rapid winds to smell the world in snippets, and even our Alpha bit at the air as we flew across the land, but I remained in the back. The metal beast had always made me queasy as we flew, its awesome speed pulled on my stomach and I had to try very hard not to lose it and make the humans clean up my mess. Plus, something was deeply wrong. Our humans could not say their father's name, as I could not say my mothers after she stopped breathing and was buried next to her mother on our land. The Master could not have stopped breathing, it was to soon in his incredible lifespan. Many humans lived for seven generations, and ours was only the sixth. Surely it was too soon? Then we slowed and turned onto a hill. I almost lost my stomach on that turn, the lurching so sudden I tipped over into Alpha, but he was nearly twice my size and helped me right myself. The door opened and we were assaulted by smells of flesh and blood and feces, all muted by a viceral chemical that burned my nose. The beast stopped, and we exited, Alpha being the first after the humans, and I being the last, my old legs threatening to fall beneath me as I landed into the hard black stone. Alpha stopped and waited for me to catch up, looking at me with a deep sadness in his eyes, and suddenly I knew. He knew it as well, and wanted to pay me the respect owed to the oldest pack member. Our Master was dying, and I had spent the most time with him, it was only right for me to give the first good bye lick, but oh I did not want to. Suddenly I felt old, like all of my nearly twenty winters had happened all at the same time, and I did not want to enter this great home of death and chemicals. But my Master's Pup pulled gently on my leash and I obeyed. We came into our Masters room, and there he was hooked to many whirring beasts with long tongues, hooking into his wrists and chest. His eyes opened dully as he saw his family, but they glowed like embers with a gentle breath of air, and a smile eclipsed his face. His body was dying, I could smell it beginning to fail even as his breathing rattled and slowed and his heart beat erratically. Wearily I brought my head to rest next to his hand, the hand that had held me before I could open my eyes, the hand that brought me such wonderful treats and excellent scratches, the hand that was now cold upon my tongue as I licked it gently. He scratched my eat weakly as the others began to push their way in. Master coughed and spoke words, many I could understand, but a few I couldn't. "It's my time, pups. You've been good to me, but now I need you to be good to my Sophie. She's gon na need all of the love she can get, ya hear?" I did hear, Master had given us a new order, be good to Sophie, take a new Master. But I didn't want a new Master.

article: John wrinkled his nose and cleared his throat. Pausing, he put down his briefcase and adjusted his tie. It was a red tie with white stripes. This was one of his favorite ties. He picked up his briefcase and walked to his car. It was the last car in the lot, as was common on every night for John. A black Ford Taurus, 1998. He walked with his head held high, and his left hand fumbled for his keys in his pocket. There were many things on his mind at the moment, one of which was pulling out those damn keys without his wallet hanging on to them like an unexpected prize from a claw machine. But the larger thought that had taken residency in his mind, was the voice. The voice that told him that he would never step foot in that location again. A small smile cracked at the thought of this, but was quickly hidden with a deep breadth. Now John was never too keen of nature, but this air tasted sweet to him. Something he had never noticed before. Finally, he reached his car. Unlocking the door, he placed his briefcase in the passenger seat. He thought of his daughter and of his wife. He thought of all the hours of work, and how it had finally got him to the point he was today. He replayed in his mind what his boss said to him, You are getting a promotion, no more floor work for you now, now you will manage your own branch of factories. You are your own boss now. As John turned the ignition nothing happened. After five twists, the Taurus sputtered to life. If there was a form of car bronchitis, this car was definitely patient zero. After the drive home, John was ready to unwind in his small apartment with his family. By the end of the month, John would never step foot in that beat down car, or that run down apartment again. He would hear that first, from the voice.

article: A static buzz gave way to fluorescent light and chatter as she awoke from her slumber. The oppressive light above seemed to force her eyes shut again. But the lights only grew brighter, and the bed sheets heavier. "We failed," she caught someone say as he left the room. The other attendants followed shortly after, leaving her alone. - "What do you remember before you woke up?" The old man's wide smile and round face projected kindness. But under that brown, old-fashioned suit, she could see he was stiff. She remembered remembered a few faces, a place here and there. "Nothing," she said. "There's no need to be nervous," he said with a plastic smile, eyes pointed not at her, she just realized, but at the loop of hair she was tugging at. She casually let go, then gathered another brown loop around her fingers. "I'm just glad my hair was kept in good shape," she said. "It's standard procedure, with a coma patient, for the nurses "I'm sorry, but I have to go," she said. - Slowly, more memories returned to the patient. She remembered her home address and where she grew up, her name and what she did for a living. She wasn't a celebrity or noteworthy person. She returned to the hospital defeated, but the doctor and the psychologist she spoke to earlier were already in the lobby. - "You were watching my dreams with a machine?" She asked. article: X-Posted between here and rnosleep, here's my story: I grew up in Oregon, right on the cold, dismal edge of the Pacific Ocean. Fifteen minutes in any direction would take you to a beach, an open expanse of sand dunes, a National or State park, or one of about a dozen permanent lakes. For years, every summer we'd go to a family friend's house to use their lakefront property and their dock. Looking back it doesn't seem like much, but I can remember spending countless hours there swimming, kayaking, paddle-boarding and snorkeling. When I was twelve years old, I refused to go again. I hated the lake, I hated that house. I had nightmares for years and never explained to anyone why it happened. I still don't like to talk about it. Whenever I do, I feel like I can smell that lake again. People don't realize, but lakes are dirty places. Animals piss and shit and die in them, all kinds of plants rot on the surface, people dump their garbage. There's so much water that stays clear that people think that it's clean. It's not. All the lakes I've been to have a certain smell like they're not totally pure. This lake - my lake - slowly developed a smell like death. That sounds dramatic. It's not like you could just sniff the air and think "That's death." No one would have gone to the lake if it had been like that. It was just a subtle thing that you caught a whiff of once and then it was gone. Maybe you looked around you for a dead fish or squirrel or something and then you forgot about it. I probably only noticed it was getting worse because on most days I was there from sun-up to sun-down. The dock our friends owned was a simple hand-built thing that involved Styrofoam and treated two-by-fours. A few times it had come loose from the rope that held it and had drifted across the lake. It sat sandwiched between two bigger and more impressive boathouses. As you faced the lake from the shore, the boathouse on the right was freshly painted bright red and housed a small white fishing boat. A simple pulley system allowed the boat to be lifted out of the water while it was stored in the majority of the year when it wasn't being used. We never saw inside the boathouse on the left, and we also never saw anyone use it. It was made of plywood that had once been painted dark green, though years of weather had warped the edges of the wood and it had shed about half its paint. That summer when I was twelve, it disappeared and we all assumed that it had just been torn down so that it wouldn't be such an eyesore. That summer was the first one that I got really into snorkeling. I had explored the surface of the lake many times before in a boat, but that summer, I got to see a whole other world hidden below the surface. My friends and I caught salamanders, built things out of cinder blocks on the sandy bottom and found everything from fishing lures and golf balls to pieces of old boats and docks from the past. As you might have guessed, the lake was pretty small but it was frighteningly deep. Huge trees would fall into it on occasion, become waterlogged and would turn vertically with only their roots or broken bases poking above the surface. A swimmer drowned there once and even though they used scuba equipment to try to find the body, it was never recovered. At a depth of about ten feet, the water was already as cold as it was in the winter. At about fifteen feet, it was dark enough that a thick forest of weeds were able to grow on the bottom. Beyond was just cold and darkness. My friend and I devised a plan to use an upside-down plastic barrel full of air and a boat anchor to allow us to dive much further than we could while only holding our breaths from the surface. We'd go out to the dive spot using a surfboard, then, with the barrel covering our heads and masks, we clutched the anchor and jumped off, quickly sinking to the bottom of the lake. You basically dove blind, since you had the bucket over your head. We could go far enough that the pressure would compress the air in the barrel to half its original size. All we had to do in order to surface was to release the anchor, and the barrel full of air would propel us quickly to the surface. Then we'd reel up the anchor with a rope and start again. This was fun for us to see how far we could go, and we got pretty good at it. The only bad times were when we would land in the deep weeds, which instantly tangled around our legs and ankles. We never got seriously stuck, but it would freak you out when you were expecting to land with both feet on the sand and instead landed in the weeds. On a successful dive, you could see about five to ten feet in any direction, and looking up, you could see the outline of the sun, and the long shadow of the surfboard. The last time I ever dove into the lake - the last time I ever swam in open water - was when I found the remains of the neighbor's boathouse. It was the first dive of the day, and we had paddled the surfboard straight out from the dock, a bit further than we normally did. It was about 10:30 am, and the water was still slightly cold from the night before. I put on my mask and snorkel, put the bucket over my head and curled my legs around the anchor like normal. This day, my friend had brought his father's underwater flashlight, so I readied that as well as the bucket above my head and took the plunge. I remember falling a long time. Too long, because the pressure was pressing my mask against my face uncomfortably, and the air in the barrel was compressed to smaller than I'd ever seen it. The rope, holding the anchor pulled taut, and I almost lost my grip. I don't believe in the little voice inside of a person that tells them the difference between right and wrong. I did, however, experience a very loud message from inside myself telling me that this was not a place I should be. It was too cold, too dark, and the pressure crushed in from all sides. It wasn't the first time I'd realized the absurdity of our little diving system, but it was the first time that it had struck me as being truly stupid. My body gave me the message loud and clear that I was an idiot, but my curiosity ultimately won out. Just a quick peek. I lifted the barrel above my head, and got my first sight of how deep I'd come. I was suspended on the rope between a gradient of graygreen above me to only blackness below. If I could have looked at myself from the outside, I'm sure I'd have resembled a worm on a hook. I had to let go of the barrel with one hand in order to grab the flashlight tucked into my swim trunks. The air in the bucket strained to float up, and the container tipped at a dangerous angle, but the bubble of air, being so compressed, stayed intact. I clicked on the flashlight, shining it down right in front of me. The thin beam of harsh white light sprung into existence like a camera flash, and what I saw there..... People. Pale faces through thick, motionless black hair staring up at me from inside the remains of that old green boathouse, flipped upside down or fallen apart. They were there, right below me. I screamed, and dropped the flashlight at the same time as I kicked off from the anchor. The barrel started pulling me up to the surface, faster and faster. In a complete panic, I thrashed my remaining arm and legs in order to try to go faster. I had expelled all my air and I felt like this was the moment I was going to die. I felt sure that they were right behind me, their pale hands inches from my ankles. From one moment to the next felt like an eternity. The end of the rope fell past me. Ten more feet. Nine. Eight. Fire in my empty lungs. I don't remember breaking the surface. I do, however remember being on top of the surfboard, alternately breathing so hard that I couldn't cry and crying so hard that I couldn't take a breath as my friend pushed my to shore. Once I reached dry land, I left without looking back. I felt then that it was so crazy, that I couldn't tell him, or my parents or anyone. There were people down there, not living people, but dead ones, with empty eyes, staring up at the gray, faraway surface. They must have been weighted down, or restrained. I don't remember. What I do remember is that as the flashlight fell into the weeds, it shone on the most horrible part of all. The legs of one of these..... things had been roughly sewn together to create the image of a grotesque mermaid, including a large and elegantly shaped black tail. For a long time after that incident, I tried to pretend that it hadn't happened - that I hadn't seen what I thought. Trees, or logs, not twin female bodies. A patch of sand through the weeds..... Anything to not have to accept a reality that that scene could exist in. As an adult, I've had to accept it. I still see it in the dark. I can't escape it. I've realized that whoever owned the boathouse, must have been experimenting. The swimmer who disappeared was probably one of those victims. I don't know who the other woman might have been. Somehow, the bodies would have to have been preserved. The only evidence of decay being from the eyes, which still stare at me in my nightmares. I'm still torn between wishing I'd investigated and learned more about it, and wishing to hell that I'd never, ever seen it.

They walked out of the back room towards the front of the store, where the non-magical weapons stood arrayed on simple wooden racks. The boy thanked the salesman and was about to walk out of the store when the man called him back, hesitating briefly. "There is..... one weapon you might want to try. You see that one over there?" article: "Hallo?" I heard a child's voice calling in the forest, "Hallo?" Great, I thought. Red Riding Hood's lost. But as I continued down the path, I saw that it was two unfamiliar children, headed towards the Witch's house. The children were clearly brother and sister: thin with button noses and freckles. One was a girl, in a ragged gray dress, the other a boy in suspenders. I stalked in the shadows behind them. I could smell the softened caramel of the Witch's roof tiles before the house came into view. The kids must have spotted the house too, because they stopped shouting for help, and went running so fast towards the candy house their arms flapped behind them. I paused. It was a pretty picture: the gingerbread house, framed in dark chocolate pillars. The children fell to eating it. From where I stood, in shadows at the edge of her yard, I could see the Witch inside the window. She stood when she heard their munching, and crept towards the door. The sounds of their feasting echoed throughout the forest: smacking of lips, grunts, and (most terribly of all) the crunch of the little girl's teeth against the peppermint doorknob. It was a pleasant spring day, and I had things to do. But I couldn't help but watch for a moment. I heaved my axe up against my shoulder, blade up. I straightened my spine a little and wiped my runny nose on my sleeve. A wolf appeared the Big Bad Wolf lured by the smell of the children as surely as the children were lured by the house. He was a big, dark gray wolf, with teeth as jagged as broken glass. When he smiled at the children, his lips rolled back, revealing gray gums. Interesting, I thought. Witch vs. wolf? Let's see where this goes. The witch finished creeping to the doorway. She and the wolf spotted each other, but the children kept eating, oblivious. The wolf's low growl reverberated through the handle of my axe. Yet the children, the little dummies, still didn't hear or see either of them. I wondered how long it would take them to realize they were in danger. I've always thought of myself as a highly capable person, although lately I've had a bit of a cold. I took two steps forward into the yard, when the wolf lunged at the Witch. I backed up again, hiding behind a bush. The witch and the wolf grappled, tumbling down the slope of the yard and towards the woods. Towards me, in fact. The wolf tore at the witch's dark cloak, white teeth flashing The Witch clawed back with long fingernails. Within a minute, the Witch flipped over on top and sucker-punched the wolf right in the gut. The wolf yowled and fell limp, and the Witch pulled out a knife and cut his throat. This commotion, finally, roused the children from their feast. They stared at the dead wolf, melted chocolate smeared on their faces. The Witch turned towards them. Before she could open her mouth, I threw my axe in the Witch's back. She dropped to the forest floor. (If the witch's back hadn't been turned, I wouldn't have stood a chance. I've been ill lately, and I'm weak. I'd hate to think what would happen if I had to face the wolf.) "Hey, dummies!" I stepped over the witch's dead body and nodded a greeting to the two grubby kids. They stared at me. "Why do you have an axe?" the boy asked. He looked me up and down. "I was chopping wood," I said. "But you're old." I shrugged. I was a little petite lady, it was true. I sneezed. "And you're sick." "When you live out in the middle of the woods, you've got to chop wood for your fireplace everyday," I said, "Even when you're old and sick." "Isn't there a lumberjack around here?" "He's a rip-off," I said, "His prices are too expensive. And besides, he's never around when I really need him. He always comes too late to help." I turned my head and coughed into my sleeve. Soon as I got home, I was going to take a nap. "That candy crap's no good for you," I said, "Little Red Riding Hood's on her way to visit, want to come to my house? She's bringing a basket of wholesome food with her, I'll share it with you." "Wholesome food?" the girl asked, her little teeth smeared brown with chocolate, "What's that?" "Apples and shit, you know?" I said, "C'mon. Let's go. I hope Red Riding Hood didn't get lost." I grabbed them both by the elbow and ushered them through the yard, giving the dead bodies of the Wolf and the Witch a wide berth. The breeze rustled the leaves overhead as we hurried down the path, leaving our bad endings behind us.

Take over X, where X equals the landmass or society desired. Bureaucracy is pretty simple, too. The people who manage the empire directly after the conquest are usually pretty disciplined, and have a source of pride to maintain. Then comes stagnation. For whatever reason, people think that what they have isn't all that good, or that it runs itself, and they get lazy. This is typically where another conquest comes into play, but sometimes the stagnation gets so bad that there isn't even an empire to speak of anymore. I managed to conquer the world. Scientific research is going along swimmingly. Research on what is anyone's guess, but things are most certainly being researched. And I'm bored. Bored out of my skull. article: Jimmy was always the brave one. He wasn't the least bit shy and was never afraid to talk to anyone. article: " WAKE THE FUCK UP RIGHT NOW! " My head shoot upwards at the sound of the woman screaming at me from the phone on my lap. What the hell? I look around and find myself sitting in my car, seatbelt on, and keys in the ignition. It's nighttime. " FUCKING RESPOND! ARE YOU AWAKE? " " Ye-yeah, I'm here- " I manage to mumble before I am rudely interrupted. " DRIVE. START THE FUCKING CAR AND DRIVE, " she screams at me. I obey and start driving down the road. I realize I am in the middle of butt-fuck nowhere and that it's pitch black outside. " Could you please tell me what's happening right now? " I politely ask the woman, hoping she would calm down (calming me down in the process) and provide a logical explanation as to where I am, who she is, and why the fuck I am driving in the middle of the night to who knows where. " You don't know me, " she starts, in a much milder tone (thank goodness). " But you know me, " I reply. Silence. " Listen, lady. I'm not in the mood for your spooky, mysterious bullshit right now. Tell me what's going on. " I've been driving for some minutes now and surprise surprise, I'm still as clueless as when I first woke up. " You just need to drive. Trust me, " she says, wavering in the end. Is that fear I hear? " Lady, tell me where I am, at leas- " I impatiently say, before I notice a constant, regular booming behind me. I look in the rear-view mirror but nothing can be seen in the moonless darkness of the night. " What is that, " I whisper, not daring to speak over the booming noise. " I'm so sorry- " the woman whimpers, starting to sob. What is happening?! " I'm so, so sorry, " she says again. " Sorry for what? " I inquire. Do I want to know? Am I dreaming right now? " Forgive me, please forgive me. It's too late... Oh dear God, I'm sorry- " she continues in her nonsensical cries. " SORRY FOR WHAT!? " I scream into the phone, desperately looking around the outside of the car. The car starts to lift from the ground - yes, lift, like levitate off the surface of the planet - and that's when I see it. I stare in utter disbelief for a moment before I am brought back to reality by the woman's increasing sobs on the phone. " I'm sorry. I had to. I had to protect myself and this buys me time to get away for a little bit, " she wails, but I barely process what she's saying. The giant gnome peels the roof off of the car like a sticker, plucks me out from the car, brings me to his horrible gnomish mouth, and bites off the bottom half of my body. It grins its impossibly wide, gnomish, evil grin, licking at his blood-covered teeth and lips before he throws the rest of my body into his mouth. " I'm sorry, " I hear the woman cry before the gnome crushes me between his teeth.

article: "How do you feel?" Great. Here we go again. My therapist is convinced he can fix me by asking me stupid questions like this, without really comprehending how fucked up I really am. How can you fix someone who is feared by everyone they love because they know my disorder? My moms answer to this question was to take me to therapy. She belongs to the category of people in my life who know what I can do but refuse to believe I can not be cured. Not only is she afraid of her own daughter, but she is convinced its some sort of demon inside me, ravishing my soul and disrupting Gods plans. She hovers over me, making sure I dont make any friends, homeschooling me until high school, making me go to church and watching me fearfully, wondering if the next time I step foot inside I will incinerate spontaneously. I cant believe I got stuck with this woman as my mother. Regardless, the question remains unanswered, and I quickly realize the extended silence is a bit disconcerting. "Im good!" I say, using my best smile and over exaggerating my happiness, attempting to beat this shrink at his own game. I scan his face for some sort of relief, but he looks quizzical still, meaning I will need to up my game. "I have started my senior year, and I am really fitting in with my classmates." Good, good, lie as much as possible. Dont tell him you saw three of your classmates mauled faces, with massive pieces of flesh torn from their cheekbones and dangling from their bones, and skulls broken, with their brains spilling from their near decapitation. At the time I guessed car accident, which was confirmed three months later. Its hard to be normal in a world where everyone tries so desperately to enjoy life, yet no one understands how imminent death really is. I see it, on the faces of my classmates, in my mother, even when I look at my shrink. I see what they try to avoid their entire lives. I see what they will become. I try to make friends, but its hard when everyones expiration date is so clearly labeled. The one guy I had a brief crush on would later become addicted to heroine, and die rail thin with a needle stuck in his arm. Gross. My shrink dies of an overdose, or at least thats what I suspect. His corpse is pale, with dark circles around his eyes, and his stomach is covered in ulcers. It isnt a pleasant way to go, and sometimes I want to ask him how he is doing for a change. He is so concerned with me, yet he is the one who dies alone surrounded by empty pill bottles. Such a shame, how quickly we dismiss others and forget lives. We see death everyday in the newspapers and simply turn away. Sometimes people ask why I dont try to save people, but I am no worse than the millions of other people turning away. I have been over stimulated with this idea of death, and it no longer frightens me, it just continues along with everything else. That is, of course, until I saw my own death. My mom knew my abilities since I was one years old, and both my grandparents came to visit. I climbed atop my grandfather lap and started to touch his chest. "Boom Boom!" I kept repeating over and over. Then I looked up at his corpse face and started to cry, with a shattered coronary artery and blood vessels bursting all around me, I ran to my mother. Luckily my mother dies in a much less abrasive fashion, and I could tolerate her old corpse smiling at me in her sleep. Two weeks later, my grandfather died of a heart attack. Peoples corpses change all the time. One day my mom will be happy and dead in her sleep, and the next, she is placing a loaded gun in her mouth, praying for forgiveness. I suppose it shows that fates can change, and how stressed out my mom is at the time. My death has never changed, which makes me think I am doing something wrong. My lips are a deep blue with tiny white bubbles bursting from in between them. My face and hair is soaking wet, and my skin looks weathered from a extended submersion in seawater. I cant tell, but it looks as though my organs are all filled with water. I suppose I drowned, but I really cant be sure where. Was it off a boat or in a pool? I know how to swim, so it really shouldn't be too difficult to save myself. I thought if I became a really efficient swimmer my death would change, but so far its remained. 'You seem tired, and a bit nervous today." My shrinks accusation snaps me back into reality. "Im just, working on it. One step at a time." Something tells me its going to be a long meeting. Perhaps this is why he chose to take the pills. Because of people like me.

As time passed I was jealous of what it said about him. If powers are a reflection of our character as scientists believed, I came to envy what this said about his life. He was free, he was pure and he was without a care in the world. What did he know about pain? of being beaten by your father every day for imagined sins and infractions? Of having to steal your best friends allowance to wear decent clothes? of being labelled by girls as a'creep' and of your few friends pitying you? But times had changed. New Years eve, my birthday, had arrived and I smiled at my reflection. I wondered what my power would be. Super strength for my strength through the hardships? Mind reading for my ability to empathize? I was entertaining these thoughts when my phone rang. Hello? Hey it's Andrew here, you ready for the party? Sure, pick me up in ten. Hello? article: It had been such a long day. Work in itself had been bad enough. I wouldn't be surprised if the office printer had become self-aware and was currently planning my gruesome death. As much as I had abused it today, I probably deserved it. Good thing inanimate objects doesn't really care about what you do to them. Or, of course, what they do to you. I had been to preoccupied to notice the first warning; the special telltale buzz that signified my phone now being below 20 battery. It wasn't too bad, it would still last a couple of hours, at least. After work James had picked me up, but instead of going home as planned, he started gushing about the amazing sales they were having at the mall, due to the 10th anniversary of it's opening. I could clearly see what he was hinting at, and, against my better judgement, I suggested that'we go take a look'. And so we did - James dragging me to every store with big flashing yellow'sale' signs. It was first when we left the mall, sitting in the car on the way home, that I saw the 5 battery flash on my phone. My heart skipped a beat; it was fine though. As it was these days, everyone always carried around a powerbank. But alas, when I ruffled through my backpack, there was no sign of it.'Damn it', I thought. I must have left it at home. I considered asking to borrow James', but it seemed silly for him to have to dig through seven bags to find that now, and it would also be embarassing and make me seem so childish. No responsible or even remotely organized person would let their phone get this low. We were close to home, anyway. I glanced nervously at my phone. 4. I could feel the minutes ticking by as we passed the cornfield that I lived next to, and then came to a halt on my driveway. We said out goodbyes - me a bit quicker than usual. Probably James would get upset about it and call me to ask if everything was alright later. But later was fine. Another glance at my phone told me I needed to hurry. I was running out of power - and time. I could hear James departing behind me, as I shakily but hastily tried to unlock my door. When has it been this hard fitting a key into a lock? I spared another glance and my phone, which I was cluthing in my hand. 3.... Running into my bedroom as I finally managed to get through the front door, still cluthing the phone, I reached for the charger at my nightstand. Plugged it in. Phew. I took a deep breath - I had made it. That was getting way too close for comfort. But something was wrong. I looked in horror as my phone did not respond. No green light started glowing. No confirmating buzz of'yes, I am being charged'. I switched the contact on the wall on an off several times in panic; nothing. I unplugged and re-plugged my phone. Still nothing. Fuck. Adrenaline now pumping through my system like fire, I grabbed my phone and ran out in the street.'Maybe I can still catch James', I though - but when I made it out onto the street, his blue Honda was nowhere to be seen. I cursed myself - why did I live so far away from everything, again? If I ran, then maybe, just maybe, I could make it to my nearest neighbour. I broke into a sprint down the road, sweating from panic and fear. And then I felt it. My phone buzzed. I stopped and looked at it, heart sinking. It was flashing an empty battery, buzzing one last time before the screen turned black. 0.

article: (Oh, this dovetails so nicely into my world. I am so jumping in.) Now that we were no longer dodging mortars and the intermittent - and wildly off-target - missiles, I could actually get a breather. Check the camera's still there - it is. Erase the footage of me screaming like a little girl, definitely. Start over again. "Ahem. As ma stop, clear my throat again, take a drink of water from the canteen. "As many of you already know by now, the fighting out here is fast, frequent, and furious. For the past two weeks, I've been embedded with the BDM 42nd'Red Vipers', a premiere special forces team, and for the past two days we've also been joined by the BDA 2957th'Volunteers. I shoved the camera, turning it toward the bloodied and mud coated humans covering in the trench next to the Bovi. They were at most, half the size of their counterparts, and even that was a stretch. "It wasn't so long ago - just 2 years in fact - that we would be shooting at each other. But that's all changed. Now we're fighting side by side, for the same worlds." Switching the camera to autofollow, I rose and approached the two nearest humans. "Excuse me, you mind if I ask a few questions?" "Not gon na make us sound like idiots or monkeys?" Racism and prejudices against the humans were still pretty rampant. There was a preceding war, they had lost, and we had brought them under our government when their atrocities had been revealed. It was..... painful. But that wasn't my job or my concern. I wanted to tell the story of soldiers, and race didn't matter. "No. None of that horseshit. You as people. I'll be gentle too. Fair enough?" They nodded in agreement. "So," flipping the camera back on, "can you tell me why you joined up with the volunteers to start with?" The woman actually smiled a bit, pushing the worst of the mud off her body armor. "That's easy. They said'the bad guys are coming for your world, we need help.' Went straight to a recruiting station and signed up. This world's my home, figure I owe it at least that much." Nodding, I turned toward the man, who shrugged and tried to look sheepish. "She says it better than me. I was military before, though, so I knew they needed bodies. Signed up that day, haven't been home since." "I see - so how did you end up with the legendary Red Vipers, a special forces regiment." Scratching his chin and ignoring the blood, he shrugged again. "Honestly, I don't know. I told them, I'm military, I want to be near the front lines, where can I do the most help? They looked up my records and said'we want you to help with the Vipers.' I used to fight the Vipers, so I knew who he meant." "I just said put me up front," the woman offered, "put me up front and let me protect my neighbors. I won't complain about anything, just give me a shot. Next thing I know, I'm meeting this tall drink of water who tells me I better ask for help when I need it, and I better get it when I ask." Nodding, I flipped the camera to face me. "The Red Vipers have been at the front of many battles, despite being on the flanks and behind enemy lines. They were the first to respond to this new incursion just last month, even though they've been fighting for 7 years straight. Tell me, how do the Vipers you work with look?" "Scary," the woman offered calmly, "they see a target, they go for it, they make it dead, and they get everyone out. Sure, we get a few wounds, but we live." "Yeah," the man agreed, "best of the best of the best, definitely. They're tired as hell, you can see it, but they're still fighting top form. We haven't lost anyone since I got here." Inadvertently answering the question as to why he'd been embedded here. Of course, my thoughts get interrupted as a MAC90D set opens up full rate on an enemy something. Even in the trench, I can feel the wind from the launching shells and reloads. That's when it occurs to me; they said social interest. I turned toward one of the Bovi - looks like a Major. "Sir, can I ask you a few quick questions?" He grunted and nodded, using a soaked handkerchief to try and clear some of the mud from his muzzle. "You've had the volunteers here a few days now. How would you describe the relationship?" That actually made him pause, thinking about it, not necessarily in diplomatic terms. "A week ago, would've refused. Sat'em down as aides. But frankly, having seen them fight? Maybe they can't haul an AMR, maybe they can't carry a hundred kilos at a go, but damned if they don't have it where it counts." Rising to his hooves, he turned and actually saluted the two humans. "I'd take these two into hell with me - done themselves more than proud." Predictably, they both saluted back, clearly stunned. That setup always worked for the propaganda stuff. Besides, folks like that never shirked their duties. They'd fight twice as hard just to prove they were every bit as good as the other species. "Then can I ask you all.... how do you think the battle is going here?" Looks were quickly exchanged, and the Major took over again. "Official canned answer, we expect to rout the enemy any hour and completely destroy their assets. Unofficially, we've taking a pounding but they're getting it worse. Soon as we get some air support, it's mopping up time. We're in a good position, we have the best people, we'll be home for breakfast at least." "So we're winning?" "Yep. We're winning," he agreed, "just as soon as the air support gets here." There was a scream of engines approaching, and he looked up while also pointing. There was no mistaking that it was a Hog II ground attack aircraft. There was an unusual whirring as the main gun fired, the camera tracking as it moved off into the distance. And didn't turn around. "Well shit. Bingo ammo. So we wait a little longer." All I could do was turn toward the humans, who looked elated and dejected at the same time. "So what are you thinking?" The woman shrugged helplessly, but the man shook his head confidently. "Bad call, should have sent fresh planes. Gotten some of ours out of mothballs faster, maybe. But, if the Major says we can take them out? I wouldn't doubt it for a minute. We'll win. Then we'll go find another fight and win that too. Biggest mistake these idiots ever made was invading our homes. Every inch they want to take, we'll make them fight and bleed for." I couldn't have asked for a more perfect close. Flipping the camera to face me again, I put on my best smile. "And there you have it. This is Larry Sun for DFIC, signing off."
label: human

article: Not a murder but I tried In my younger years I lived a life of extravagance, I was regularly out at sea, wind and salty water splashing at me, I would wear the finest clothes, and I would indulge in the pleasures that life had to offer. However, one day, while I was out at sea, I almost died. The ship had been caught in a terrible storm, and we were tossed around like a feather in the wind. It was then that I realized that I had been living my life in a way that was selfish and wasteful. I started to reflect on what was truly important in life and vowed to change my ways. From that day forward, I made a commitment to live a life of purpose and meaning, to help others whenever I could and to live in a way that honored the beauty and miracle of life.

article: Steve sat in his chair, staring at the hanging, starred shield as he did every night since his retirement into suburbia. Most nights were calm, but some nights were rough and he found himself absorbed in thoughts about his past life as a police officer in the city. As he sat there, lost in thought, he suddenly heard a loud crash outside. He quickly got up and headed to the window, where he saw a car had crashed into a tree just outside his driveway. Steve immediately grabbed his phone and dialed 911, rushing outside to see if he could help. As he approached the car, he saw that the driver was slumped over the steering wheel, unconscious. Steve quickly assessed the situation and realized that he needed to get the driver out of the car before the engine caught fire. With the help of a passerby, he managed to pull the driver out of the car just as it burst into flames. Steve stayed with the driver until the ambulance arrived, talking to him in a calming voice to keep him conscious. As the ambulance took the driver away, Steve took a deep breath, grateful that he had been able to help in some small way. As he made his way back inside, he couldn't help but reflect on his past life as a police officer and how he still had a desire to help others in need. The next day, Steve decided to reach out to the local police department and ask if there were any volunteer opportunities available. He knew that he still had something to offer and wanted to make a difference in his community. With a renewed sense of purpose, he sat back down in his chair and looked up at the starred shield on his wall, feeling grateful for the chance to make a difference once again.

article: Scene: Walmart 1676. I recover from things easily enough; I had just left the Electronics department where an older employee with salt-and-pepper hair and a sunken mouth and BRENDA on her name tag asked me, in a muttery tone of voice, if I had any meth. I just gave her the wide stinkeye and simply turned to give her the back of my head and walked briskly away. That didn't bother me much; it was a rural Walmart and to be expected. I was coming up on the grocery section, in the large throughway aisle betwixt the shoes on the right and junior misses on my left, when I came upon a sight to behold. Picture this: A mother in a motorized wheelchair. Hair a thinning, gingerly red; complexion a cross between pizza and cottage cheese; face of a man, girth of a hippo whale, arms flabby with tired fat muscles cradling yes, cradling, to her chest and at that point my mind took in the bare shoulder with the bunched cloth of a sleeve rolled around her elbow as her shirt was pulled down to breastfeed, in public, a teeny tiny newborn baby. Her mannish face, as unpalatable as it may be to the human eye, wore a contented Virgin Mary expression that was beautiful in its own grotesque way. Accompanying her was a child who could have been anywhere from four to eight; it was difficult to tell as it was an extremely chubby, swollen specimen who was clearly her mother's daughter and on her way to needing a motorized wheelchair of her own. She was pushing a cart loaded with bagged and canned dog food, bagged and canned cat food, bags and bags of kitty litter, a smattering of batteries, mens' socks (white athletic) and underwear (white briefs), and beneath it all, one package of diapers. She was as wide as she was tall, and her sweatsuit stretched on her ample frame. Her face was slack, her mouth open and moist with unchecked saliva, flecks of its dried salt spraying out with every exhalation she took, her eyes heavily lidded as if she were about to fall asleep, yet watching the infant suckle its mother's breast with primal, reptilian intensity. Even my autopilot function was dumbstruck. I was not being subtle. This living exhibit of art must not be aware of its observance lest the illusion breaks. Shoes! I'm interested in some shoes. I veered off to the right and beelined straight to the sneakers, and I continued to observe them, albeit from behind, with my peripheral vision as I balanced a display shoe in my hands. They were making movement, and I was beginning to feel distraught at the disruption that I could have made. But no, the baby was done feeding and the mother was hoisting it up to her shoulder with great effort, her flabby arm muscles quaking and trembling from a combination of weakness, elbow joint pain, and just struggling with the unnecessary weight. Once the child was settled against her cushioned collarbone, her huge hammy hand began to whack the child's back in what she perceived to be light, tender taps. The baby's head bucked up and down in time with the thudding, its eyes widening almost comically. Its mouth worked as if it didn't know whether to cry or remain stoic, when all of a sudden BLUPH! a thin bubble of regurgitated breast milk popped out. At this point the girl reached out excitedly, her swollen fists opening and closing as she grunted through closed lips at her mother. "Mmm! Mmm? Mmmm!" Her tongue flicked out and licked her lips slowly from side to side during this communication. With yet another great, trembling effort of her tired arms, the mother lifted the baby off of her shoulder and handed her with great ceremony and gravity to her daughter. The baby was dribbling yet another stream of spit-up over its lower lip and down its chin, and the daughter took the baby beneath the elbows, brought its face close to hers, and proceeded to lick off the spit-up directly from the baby's chin and lips. It's a little difficult to describe what happened next, but it's similar to watching a live-streamed movie online when it decides to pause and buffer at a specific, horrific scene. Since it's live, it doesn't pick up from where it left off it skips ahead a few minutes and you're left confused about what you could have missed. All I could think about for that time period was the sheer audacity of the act how come the few other customers hadn't said anything? Didn't Walmart have security cameras that looked out not only for shoplifting, but child endangerment as well? Is this why their Code Adam drills are such colossal failures? These ideas came in the form of indignant abstract epiphanies that overwhelmed any narrative inner dialogue that could have led to my brain making an executive decision. When conscious thought returned to me, the family of three had disappeared into the Walmart abyss, never to be seen again. I put the shoe on a random shelf and left as quickly as I could. I was trying to unsee the image in my mind until I walked into the front door and my wife was sitting at the kitchen table. She was hunched over a bowl of macaroni and cheese. Upon hearing me come in, she turned to look at me. With her mouth still full of yellow cheesy cream, she asked me if I picked up the tupperware containers. It was a little difficult not to picture the scene of a fat little girl licking spit-up from a baby's mouth whenever we kissed after that.
label: human

article: Her breath smelled like strawberry bubblegum. That's what went through his mind as handed her a pencil. " Thanks ," she whispered, flashing her stunning teeth. She sat in front of him in Ms. Burke's business class. He had noticed her on the first day of school; he couldn't keep his eyes off of her. To him, she was a stunning flower in an otherwise dull garden. When Homecoming came he finally worked up the courage to ask her to the dance. She blushingly agreed. Teenage love, what can be more beautiful and what can be crueler? Many summer nights ended with them in each other's arms, wrapped in blankets in the bed of a rusty pickup. Where they said their " I love you " s and promised each other eternity underneath the stars. Baby names were decided, rings chosen, a lifetime planned. College applications were sent, jobs were found and new people were met. Where once was a solid stone, a crack appeared. Eyes wandered, shoes were thrown, tears were cried. Many nights were sleepless, yet on one night he came a realization. He no longer cries and with time he came to see that she was not the only flower in the garden (how did he never see the thorns!) nor was she the most beautiful. Today, he can chuckle and appreciate his strawberry bubblegum.
label: human

article: The human female Margaret Waller across from him sat quietly, puzzling over what had just been revealed to her. "A war? Today is our first real confirmation that we're not alone in the universe, and the first thing we have to do is fight a war..." Her voice trailed off and her eyes became unfocused. "I suppose that's about right. The way life works." The words had no ulterior motive behind them, yet Qard was simultaneously reassured and chilled by them. Reassured that this culture was so steeped in warfare that they believed it was the universal order of life, and chilled by the same fact. There was no doubt that humans could win this war, but there was also no doubt that they'd win many, many more after their first introduction to Fluan technology. The human's eyes snapped back to him. "I'm sorry about your plight, but we have no way to fight on the fronts you've specified. We've barely colonized our own solar system; we don't have the resources to wage an extra galactic war." "Of course not," Qard said, a note of exasperation creeping into his voice. "We don't expect you to do so yourself. The Fluans have prepared a number of vessels capable of faster than light travel. A..... fleet." He hesitated not because he didn't know the word, but because'fleet' should never have been used to describe Fluan spacecraft. The assorted ships were used chiefly for exploration, business travel, or pleasure. The thought of a Fluan diplomacy yacht spitting death nearly made Qard himself violent. "They have few weapons. Our engineers will work with you to outfit them with whatever you need or desire. Once the war is finished, whether we win or lose, the vessels will be yours to keep and study." Not the full truth. Humans could study them right up until The Council of Flua remotely detonated them. Humanity wasn't quite ready to join FTL civilizations yet. "And how about our numbers?" She asked. "Including our colonies, we number 28 billion. A fraction of that would fight for you. Is that enough?" "Your numbers are sufficient." He didn't mention that humans reproduced at an unusually high rate compared to the rest of known life forms. Their numbers weren't completely ideal, but they'd easily make up the difference. "Excellent. Last question, then. I am the Primary Elected Leader of the Terra System. I can guarantee majority support by both the High Military and High Civilian Representatives. The question is, why should I? Why should we choose a war to introduce ourselves to the universe, and why yours?" A question Qard had not been expecting. He and the Fluan Council had assumed that the novelty of a new form of fighting, and the vast resources offered by the galaxy at large, would be motivation enough. "We have the respect of a great many civilizations. If you were to help us, the trade opportunities "Then why aren't they fighting for you?" she cut in. Qards felt his antennae stiffen, the equivalent of a human narrowing their eyes. "They fear our enemy more than they respect us. Defeat the Cramoul and you'll have respect as our allies, and fear as Cramoul's vanquishers. Humans have a great capacity for violence, which is why we come to you now. We face near extinction. You will prove your place among the greater civilizations by staving off genocide. It is a guarantee that no other planet will offer as much. And we have not communicated the location of your planet. If you lose, you can vanish to your home system without a trace. Even we Fluans found you by accident." Her eyes became unfocused once more. "Yes. Yes, I think that will do." Fifteen years later, the Cramoul were pushed back to their homeworld. With victory accomplished and celebrations competed, humanity returned to Terra, and Flua betrayed them by detonating the FTL drives, as planned. Four years after that, the Fluan Council surrendered to Primary Commander Margaret Waller, of Terra.

article: "It's who we are, I suppose. Whether it be worth it in the end or not," the first said. Eyeing his alien cohort. "We will make them pay. We will rebuild. Do you think Cortorol thinks that two of us exist?" The human turned away from the early dawn, striding toward the distant tree line, "Doesn't matter now does it. For all he knows his nemesis is dead. We can let him think that anyone is alive. And when the time comes we will retrieve our partner." As the dawn slowly encroached, the two onlookers disappeared into the receding shadow. Laying low until the culmination of events led them far away, where a distant star orbited by a lonely gas giant provided a safe haven for Cortorol, became a site of another tragedy.
