article: All I could focus on was him on top of my wife, grunting away. I just stood there and watched. What else could I do? My wife of 2 years, the woman I had given my soul to. In a moment of enveloping solitude, I realize everything is over. nbsp; She finally notices me and screams, I turn around and walk out calmly, and pull the air lock detach handle on our f117 spacecraft orbiting Jupiter from the largest space station ever constructed. It was impulse really, I don't know why I pulled it, but honestly I don't regret it. The room is detached from the ship and sent into deep space. They will suffer from either dehydration, or suicide - I don't really care. Everything has changed now, in just a blink of an eye. I'm now a murderer. I watch from my window as the room flies away, getting smaller and smaller, until finally disappearing. I can imagine their screams as they drift away. Then suddenly, it's gone - like my fading marriage. I knew living with 20 thousand people on this 7 square mile station would present problems, at least it makes for an easy blame. nbsp; I walk down the long corridor of our f117 ship, walking faster and faster, until I enter into the cockpit. The smart system on board pipes in "Damien, we noticed you detached compartment 34, without authorization, we need to confirm this was an emergency not detected by onboard systems?" nbsp; "Everything I loved has been a lie, she was the only women I could ever commit too," I mumble back to the smart system. nbsp; "Space Station Jupiter law enforcement have been notified, you are in violation of code 456, 2nd degree murder" The smart system says to me. I take out my key and slam it into the dashboard, and turn, "disable smart system, auth code 454545994." I guess marrying the pilot had it's benefits, she always told me the secret stuff like auth codes, the things way above my skill level. nbsp; "Smart system disabled, manual override operational" nbsp; "Damien, this is Captain Ricks, what the fuck are you doing do....," the communication board screams. I turn off communications, this is a ride I'm taking solo, without interruption. nbsp; I enter in coordinates to find the farthest black hole from our solar system. "Let's go somewhere far," I calmly say while hitting the warp drive ignition. Our mission in f117 was to be a craft that would gather data along black holes within the Milky Way Galaxy. My job was to gather data, a boring job really, that would be used by far superior people than me to look into future time travel via event horizons. nbsp; GNd5296, sector 7 - the system displays. The system displays some information on it "formed within 700 million years after the beginning of the universe, making it the oldest and most distant galaxy ever verified." The warp drive takes 15 minutes to start, where it will bend gravity and time to cut a hole in space and travel to wherever has been requested. Using warp energy was the most expensive cost of our entire operation, and was done once every 5 years. In fact, it was more expensive than creating the space station itself. Probably due to the rarity of the elements required for it to work. I don't care. nbsp; By this time a number of station security teams have surrounded my f117 vehicle. Though, I'm sure they know it's too late. See, once warp drive ignition has been hit, the slightest field of energy around us can set off a reaction that would annihilate an area the size of, well, ironically jupiter. nbsp; I look at them through the window as they scream at me, knocking on the glass, muttering things I can't understand. I just smile and wave, for I have not a care in the world. Where I'm going is an ancient galaxy far away, from the nonsense. Far away from the hurt. Far away from her. nbsp; Slam, it's like my head is being drained of life. Everything outside the window of my craft is glittering like diamonds. I can see space bend, the stars of our galaxy swing overhead and my craft travels down a worm hole. Purple, blue, red, white, colors of our universe surround me down the wormhole. I keep trying not to pass out, hold it I scream, "Hold it Damien, you can do it. HOLD IT YOU MOTHER FUCKER!" nbsp; Slam No more worm hole, my head stops hurting. Just..... calm. I'm 1 astronomical unit from the event horizon of GNd5296. It's beautiful, it's just how I imagined it. Light flowing around a massive black body like glowing energy draining down a sink. I can feel it's presence, like some 6th sense I can't explain. I sit there for hours just staring at it, admiring it, a glooming sight to behold. nbsp; I pull the nose of the f117 craft in front of the black hole. It's dark presence beckoning me like a god in deep space. I pull out a hologram in my pocket of her, and stare at her. I don't understand love. It's out HERE that I get - astronomy. The only real thing universe. I'm crying now, I hit the manual stick into burst. I'll be traveling at 500km a second soon. Slam, my body feels the tension of our craft as it speeds forward. The black hole is calling me, ready to dissolve me into spaghetti-like strands once I hit it's event horizon. "Come on, come to me," I scream in my tiny compartment. The event horizon comes forward more and more into view. "Faster, faster, here it comes! " nbsp; "All the most powerful emotions come from chaos -fear, anger, love- especially love. Love is chaos itself. Think about it! Love makes no sense. It shakes you up and spins you around. And then, eventually, it falls apart. " , I scream. I'm expecting it to be my last moment, but suddenly..... nbsp; My aircraft hits the event horizon but doesn't move, it stays fixed. A moment of sheer shock hits me, I look out of my window and I behold a sight I can not believe. I'm trapped in the event horizon. The universe before me starts changing, stars are disappearing, galaxies are coming and going. But slowly, there becomes less and less. The clock on my system is showing me as billions of years into the future, 6 billion, 7 billion, now at 14 billion. Then suddenly there are no stars, only darkness, silence, just the feeling of emptiness. The universe has suffered a heat death, every star, everything has died out. The universe is dead. nbsp; "What have you learned," a voice asks me, surrounding me nbsp; "Are you?..." nbsp; "You found what you loved and let it kill you. You let it drain you of your all. You let it cling onto your back and weigh you down into eventual nothingness. You let it kill you and let it devour your remains. For all things will kill you, both slowly and fastly, but it's much better to be killed by a lover."

article: Jim had drawn the short straw for night shift in the engine room. He would have volunteered if he hadn't. Night shift was nice, the lights were dimmed aboard the ship in the off hours, stem to stern. Captain's orders, it allowed better regulation of circadian rhythms for the rest of the crew and let Jim avoid the dazzling brilliance that passed for "day" aboard the cruiser. He supposed it was his fault, born and raised on Sian where the noon time sun was little brighter than a full moon on Earth. The engine hummed softly as Jim performed routine maintenance. The other man on duty was Stuart, about as salty a sailor as Jim had ever seen, with hair that grew only in patches and a scar that ran from jaw to eyebrow beneath an eye patch. Jim was more than a little afraid of Stu. "Fluid'll need changing" Jim nearly leaped from his skin. Drawing a shaking breath he responded "maintenance logs shows it was changed eight hours ago." "Maintenance logs is wrong, then. Changed up the fluid but didn't clean the filter. Always clean the filter. Drain, clean the filter, fill. Not so hard is it?" "Er, no..." Jim checked the dip stick and noted the reactor cyclant was a touch discolored. "Well tell that to the day shift crew! Filter needs cleaning every time the fluid's changed. You're not like Alston, I can tell. Pompos ass, thinks'cuz he studied engineering he knows how to be an engineer. Well I say if you want clean cyclant you need a clean filter. I know this engine inside and out I do. Come here, I'll show you how to clean the filter. Always use a number two brush, number three's too stiff and if you use a number one you'll be here all shift..." Jim learned a lot as they worked, and duties finished almost two hours before the end of their shift. Stu sat down on one of the benches and drew out a flask. "You're a hard worker, Jim, and you listen what I tell you. So now let's talk about the airlocks." "Airlocks?" Jim asked, taking the proffered flask. It held rum, strong enough to make his eyes water and sweet as candy. "Aye, the airlocks. You'll use'em now and again, replace ablation plate, drive needs work on the outside, you'll make your way outside from time to time. But it's the airlocks you need to look out for." "What do you mean?" He took another swig and passed the flask back. "You're not the first lad in space, Jim, and you certainly won't be the last. There have been others out there, you know, and not all of'em make it back planetside." "You mean to watch out for mechanical failure?" "Aye. And turn the lights off when you get back in." "Lights? Why?" "There's a story, and old one. I heard it on a night like this when I was your age. You heard of the Machanna?" "Sure, heard about it in school, lost to the stars out around Tau 3, it's held up as a prime example of design failure." "Oh aye, coolant had to be jettisoned from outside, had to be done once a week or the reactor'd overheat. Did they tell you in academy why they couldn't? No, I suppose not. That's not a popular story, not sanctioned and all that. Well they gave the job to a new kid, a sort of hazing. Coolant was a gel back then, was real funny to tell the new kid he needed to clean his suit before they could let him back in. Well, they gave the kid the job, and of course he gets the coolant all over himself, no way not to. They tell him he's got ta clean his suit before they let him back in, so he starts to panic, yeah, because he's already low on air. He flails around a bit, loses most of his tools, everything but his number six scraper. The folks inside see him and tell him to stop, but he's not listenin' see, because he things he's got to clean his suit. So he starts at it with the scraper, and you can't clean a suit with a scraper, it just can't be done, and sure as shit the suit gets a puncture. "Now the boy was in a fuss before, but now he's in a panic. They're shouting over the radio to get inside the airlock, it's good enough, it was just a joke. Finally the kid gets the message, and pulls himself in. He's bleedin air fast and they dump emergency tanks to equalize the pressure inside the airlock. Kid thinks he's safe and pulls off his helmet. He's half blind, sweat in his eyes, out of breath, so he reaches up to open the door, but the airlock's faulty, the outer door blows off, vents the atmosphere in the airlock and takes the kid with it." "Holy shit." "So the crew's watchin him out there. They don't tell you in academy, but vacuum doesn't kill you like they used to think it did. It's a hard death out there, your skin swells up, your eyes get so dry they'll crack, and there's no relief until you suffocate. And suffocate they did, it was a full ten minutes before the boy quit movin. But now they've got a problem,'cuz the kid's still got his tether on. So the crew draws straws to see who'll cut the tether to let him drift free, and it's the first mate that draws the short straw. "So he suits up, and while he's doing it they lose sight of the body. So the mate, see, he goes to the other airlock, and he's just about to cycle into it when he looks through the window, and standing there's the kid. So of course there's a panic, and they vent the airlock, send the body back out into space, they fire up the engines and gun it for home, but the tether snaps and the body floats free." "But the Machanna never made it home, reactor overheated. No survivors." "Aye, there was three airlocks on the Machanna, all logged by the computer. They analyzed the black box on it, and do you know what they found? That last airlock? Cycled, from the outside. The kid's still out there, Jim, in a panic, trying to get back inside the ship. But ships run dark on the outside, aye?" "Right..... except..." "Except for the airlocks, Jim. So we turn the lights off in the airlocks so he can't find'em. Aye?" "Aye."

article: We're all that's left now. Reddit, the Golden City, The Frontpage of the Universe, The Caterer to all. It floats above the ruined landscape below, a beacon of hope and of sanctuary. Once it was the arbitrator, the crossroads between many nations, the best crop of all these kingdoms would always find it's way to The Top, a huge square at the highest peaks of the city where upvotes would be traded for whatever was on display, be it an animal of advice, a humorous performance from the Youtube or even one of Reddit's own public forums such as rAskReddit. The city was divided up into it's subreddits, every day the citizens would browse and participate in their chosen topic, even the seedier ones. We should have acted. We knew war was coming, even rOutOfTheLoop could tell you that. Our neighbouring nations, 4chan and Tumblr were constantly at each other's necks; their ideological differences were massive and neither side was willing to compromise. As it always did, conflict ensued. It started normally enough, another border skirmish. A Tumblr zealot group attacked which was met by a harsh response by 4chan the escalation continued until full scale war was inevitable. We should have acted, we should have tried to arbitrate and stopped the bloodshed before it stated. But no, we just sat back and watched. After all why would it affect us? But the battles grew and grew, the flame wars would leave nought but ash in their wake. The war looked over, Tumblr had always outnumbered the 4channers by a considerable margin, soon 4chan itself was almost overrun, forcing them to bring in their nuclear option: Youtube. No one knows how they managed to convince The Trolls to enter the fray, all that we know is that it spelled the end. Youtube's trolls were legion, a boundless horde spamming and overwhelming any force standing in their way. Tumblr never stood a chance. Only now did we act, this had gone too far. But as mighty as we may have been, nothing could stand against the Trolls. When Tumblr had fallen they turned their attention to their allies and had soon consumed them as well, their rampage finally stopping after devastating several more of the Social Media States. I remember the day when Pinterest burned. I fought on the front line, they called me a hero then, but what kind of hero waits till it's too late to save anyone. The refugees came to us for help, people all kingdoms and opinions. It was only us and our twin city Imgur that still stood in the end. Even as I speak rarchitecture is planning a refugee camp for them to stay, there's no room in the city anymore. We're putting them to good use though; battlements are being constructed, weapons forged and a wall built around the cities. We must be ready, we must be vigilant. Rumors abound of a Second Troll Host assembled and that they've turned their eyes towards the Last Sanctuary of the Internet. It was only a matter of time after all.

article: The event was thorough, ubiquitous, and devastating. In an instant every human being on the planet simultaneously found themselves stripped of every shred of civilization meticulously collected over thousands of generations of human progress. The records at the beginning are incomplete at best. Some estimates derived from anecdotal evidence put the death toll at 1 billion in the first week. Those in northern climates succumbed to exposure. Heavily populated cities choked on masses of humanity piled upon themselves. Many simply accepted their fate as being a direct edict from their god and ended their own lives. Disease was rampant, stomachs accustomed to chlorinated drinking water were assaulted by bacteria from natural water sources. Without sanitation the disease burned like wild fire though populations. Starvation soon followed. In less than a month nearly 60 of the worlds population, as estimated 4.4 billion people were dead. In many areas the bone fields are still visible today. Hundreds of acres of gnarled skeletons so white they reflect the sun and can be seen form miles away. In 24 AE Collective scientists determined that humanity had been transported nearly 10,000 years into earths past using astronomy, geology, and biological data. In the early days, this was completely unknown. The remaining population had nothing. Hundreds of years of selective breading of crops was lost and the plants of the age were meek at best and poisonous at worst. Docile domesticated animals were replaced with fierce and dangerous imitations of their once familiar selves. Every well, shelter, dammed fishery, cleared field, path, road, or otherwise human influenced geographical feature was lost. Cities that once supported millions had their carrying capacities reduced to thousands. Billions more died through the first year as tribes and religious cults formed and warred over the remaining resources. By 7 AE the human population of the earth was reduced to 625 million. Even in the early years efforts were made to preserve pre-event knowledge. Using crude bark paper and charcoal writing utensils engineers, scientists, poets, mathematicians and scholars set to work preserving their knowledge and recording post-event history. In 15 AE the Collective was formed in what once the Mississippi River Valley. It was from here that civilization was reborn. Using pre-event knowledge and developing new techniques the basis of construction and metallurgy was reestablished. By 20 AE corn and potatoes had been re-domesticated to resemble a sustainable crop. Bison were ranged off in large swaths of land near the collective and predators were killed using crude iron tools. In the year 23 AE the first sailing vessels set to sea and began the task of reunification. It would be a slow and painstaking process but in 74 AE the first transcontinental telegraph lines were completed across the former United States and Northern Africa. This magnified the available knowledge and the pace of progress increased. By 150 AE the decedents of the event were on their way of making this new world their own. Even today many question the validity of the event and question if it occurred at all. The possibility of a worldwide conspiracy aside one can only assume the truth of those who lived through this time. The current year is 1251 AE and the first silicon chip has been developed based on knowledge passed down from pre-event humans.

It was obvious he was frightened, but showing that fear to the principal was not an option. He paused for a moment before uttering one phrase, "He was a 10, Mr. Andrews."

article: "What do you mean we failed?" Ruger yelled. His face was brick red and sweating, as it usually was when he was angry. He was leaning halfway over a very large metal desk. "We found you, not the other way around! We have twice as large a fleet as you, better technology, and live twice as long. What the hell do you mean that Humanity failed your test?" The Alien across from Ruger, an insectoid-like being named Hrvvax, clacked its mandibles as it spoke into a translator. "Humanity has indeed shown their prowess and ability to grow and survive as a species. You have surpassed almost all species in various fields, from terra-forming to genetic engineering. However, Humanity has failed one vital aspect of our test, one that, if failed, fails the entire test." Ruger bared his teeth and growled, "What the hell is that?" Hrvvas clacked its mandibles and sifted through documents on the desk. After a few seconds it stopped, then turned its four stalked eyes to Ruger. "The genocide of the race known as the Apperians, conducted during the Human-Apperian war of 2311 to 2342." The human's face went from brick to porcelain. "Genocide..." "Yes, genocide. Or were most humans unaware that your war with them was so final?" Ruger sat down and rubbed his temples. "No, no not at all. We were aware, but just..... I never thought we were the only ones." "You are, at least at the moment. The extermination of another sentient species is not an act of sentience. It is an act of beasts, animals. Humanity may be intelligent, and resourceful, but you are no greater than uplifted animals." The insectoid moved the documents to the side of the desk. "Humanity will be granted similar status to Uplifted Animals, including security under the Federation, as well as access to most trade hubs. However, you are declined membership in the Federation Council, and must have all plans for further expansion approved by the Council. Is that understood, Mr. Ruger?" "So we're second class citizens?" Hrvrvax shifted, uncomfortable with the conversation. "Yes, basically." Ruger finally regained his composure. "Now, Hrrvax, I want to tell you something to bring back to whoever failed us on this test. Humanity has committed genocide, yes. We did it out of fear. Fear of our own extinction. We were attacked, and we fought back, and we won. Simple as that. If you think that after doing all of that we'll lie down and allow ourselves to be denied rights that we should have, then you're one dumb bug." He stood up and leaned across the desk again, this time almost all the way across. "Inform your superiors that, unless our grade for this test is changed, then we'll show you just how animal-like humanity can be, and I promise it's not pretty. Have a nice day." Ruger smiled and left the room.

article: My mouth tastes metallic, like blood, and my eyes peel themselves open. I'm in a crowded room and everything is shaking. People are running over to my bedside gripping my arms. I look down and see my body writhing and convulsing uncontrollablly. My arms are twitching, my body shakes and twists. "This is normal everyone. Stand back! Stand back," one of the men gripping my arms is yelling to the crowd. They don't move an inch. The other man holding down my arms shoves a hard bit of plastic between my teeth and my jaw clamps down on it, hard. I'm panicking now, I can't breathe! I gasp in huge gulps of air and the yelling man tells the other to "sip in 7 cc's animorphine, aqueous, no saline." The IV drip next to me whirs and I start to feel calmer now. I get a better look at the men. They're both doctors, and the one on my right is considerably older. He looks about 60, with serious gray eyes and a stiff body type. His hands are sinewy and experienced. The other is much younger, probably in his late 20s. He has intelligence and energy in his movements. The older doctor pulls down his surgical mask and examines me carefully as I lie panting on the hospital bed. The crowd is eerily quiet. "My name is Dr. Fillow. How are you feeling?" My mouth still tastes metallic. Young doctor takes the bit out of my mouth. "What happened? " , I ask. Dr. Fillow glances at young doctor. Then back at me. "You just had a seizure. Your brain is refiring its neurons, doing a systems check, if you will. Can you hear me okay?" I nod. "Alright, good." Young doctor pulls out a small flashlight from his breast pocket and peers into my eyes and mouth as Dr. Fillow continues to speak. "This is going to come as a shock to you, but for the past 67 days, sir, you've been dead." I blink. "It's important that you do exactly what we tell you to do. We used a very dangerous experimental technique to get you back, but the ramifications of it are..... unknown. I need you "I died!" I panic, tears welling in my eyes. "Is this a joke. Is this a joke? Why are you doing this?!" "No, this is real. Everything here is real, and it's going to be alright. This is the first human revival of this kind of all mankind. You are the the first." I feel like I want to cry. Im happy and scared, and confused and my body begins to ache. The crowd in front of me is full of reporters and cameramen, watching closely. They split down the middle and a man in a dark blue suit and red tie hurries into the room. He looks like he's in his 50s and has the smile of a politician. He grips my hand firmly and smiles. article: "Are we really going to do it, P?" "We don't have any other choice, Jazzy." Jasmine sighed and pulled her coat in closer around her. Pocahontas looked at her, face blank of any expression. I'm not going to start now." Next to her, Tiana and Moana nodded in agreement. Jasmine still looked skeptical. "I'm just wondering," Jasmine said. "If we do die out there - what would we have accomplished?" She looked around at the others. "You know? If we go down, then we don't have the chance to make a stand for anything else. Ever." "Jasmine," Pocahontas said gently. "I mean it. If you're afraid "Not afraid," Jasmine said hotly. "I'm asking a legitimate question. Do you realize the type of influence that we have over people? We're rulers. Icons. If we go down, then the people we take care of can go down as well. I'm just saying, have we all thought about that?" Everyone in the tent fell silent. For once." The women all looked around at each other in silent agreement. Pocahontas stood up. "Then let's go." article: I read once that Einstien had the opportunity to sign a letter to the president to convince him to build atomic weapons before the Germans. I doubt it would have made much difference. Mitternacht was an experimental bomb, now knowing that it worked, the Germans put everything into completing three more. It ended for them, like it ended for us. In 1945, we tested our Buddy Blue bomb in New Mexico. It was a purpose build cannon the took up an entire B-53 frame, it used 11 pounds of fissile materials in a beryllium sphere, compressed to insane pressurize with radium gas, and the shot wit the cannon. The math showed that we needed ridiculous amounts of nuclear material to get the bomb to work. We were wrong. On July 6, 1945 Buddy Blue was fired in an old airframe on top a purpose built tower. The German people, so horrified by the destruction in London and New Mexico staged a violent revolt against the Nazi party, many in the army joining, along with massive Jew populations from camps, and ended the war. article: Shadows dance on the wall as overhead lights sway to an unfelt breeze. The din of my team's work is now drowned by the mass of earth and structure between us. It is cool in this dark hall. I scrape against the wall as I push further inwards, away from the lazy lights. I shuffle on, driven. I hear something. It is faint, a gentle whisper bouncing through the passageway. It beckons me. With each step the whisper grows. It is neither urgent nor is it aloof. It simply is, and I must heed it. The sounds brush past me, against me, and into me. I hear it. Human voices. Uncountable, indistinguishable. The passage has ended. There is no light behind me, though I have only walked straight. The wall before me is as smooth as the surface of water. I brush the back of my hand against it. It clings to me, as do the whispers. My very essence trembles as I caress the wall and swim amongst the sea of hushed voices. The surface shifts, and the whispers begin to slip away into the otherworldly smoothness. As they depart my thoughts trickle back. I am afraid. I am alone. I need help. The last of the whispers sink into the surface. I press against it, overcoming my fear so that I may understand this place. Beyond the wall the hushed chorus continues its song. I push harder against the impossibly smooth wall, straining to hear a word amongst the multitude beyond it. It as if the whispers are the heart of humanity, afraid and crowded together in this deep and lonesome dark. The voices are the time-lost echoes of every utterance of man: each roar of might, every love-soaked lament, every plea. I pull away from the wall with a start. Amid the whirlwind words I heard only one. A single word made from the countless voices of humanity, the amalgam of our timeless tongues, the essence of our existence: " Help. "

article: When it happened, no one believed it could be true. We all thought we could be survivors. After all, we've watched all the movies and read all the books. It started with a virus, one that seemed harmless at first but soon turned deadly. The government tried to contain it, but it spread too quickly, too aggressively. People started dropping like flies. Stores ran out of supplies, and panic set in. People started hoarding food and necessities, making it impossible for others to get what they needed. Hospitals were overrun with patients, and soon, they were turning people away. The situation became desperate, and within a matter of weeks, our world had turned into a post-apocalyptic nightmare. The streets were empty, and the once-bustling cities were now eerie ghost towns. As a helpful assistant, I suggest that we start preparing for any unforeseen situations, whether it's stocking up on emergency supplies or learning survival skills. We never know when a disaster will strike, and it's better to be prepared than caught off guard.

Our enemies had been a race overcome by violence, an emotion that ran so deep it could not be stopped. Neither their rage nor their people themselves. Our people on the other hand were a peace loving bunch and we held the upper hand in technology, having relied on it to act in our beliefs. Every problem we faced we maintained our pacifist stance, using our science as a shield, and so we had'progressed', heaping all our troubles into the metaphorical closet and shutting the doors on them. After all it had worked on'them'. Perhaps we should have realized it earlier, or maybe we just turned a blind eye to it, but our mountain of problems would just pile up, eventually coming back to bite us. But what could we do? In the end we lacked the conviction to confront the threats we faced, to put an end to them. So as we watched the gate collapse, our enemies pour forth from the walls that failed to restrain them, we were rudely awoken, like adults who never grew up, we were forced to throw away our naivety. We knew that this was just the beginning, even if we were to survive, we could never regain what had been lost, and there was still much more we once willingly forgotten.

"What can I do to help you escape?" The figure asked. "Do you have any information on your captors? Is there anything you need that I can provide?" I finally found my voice, my words shaky and weak. "I don't know who took me or why. Please, just get me out of here." "Don't worry. I will get you out of here," the figure promised. "Just rest now and be ready when the time comes." article: Some people train for combat by going to the gym. By sparring. The fools. I know every facet of the human body. Every weak point, every organ. I can visualize your entire nervous system as if I could see right through you, and with enough force to the right spot, I can cripple you without you even knowing you were exposed. So far, I have been content to beat up on other, lesser students in a little fight club for spoiled rich kids too bored with their comfortable lives. I won a little tournament we had last weekend, and caught the attention of a scout. At least, that is what he said he was. He told me that boss runs a fight club, the real thing, not the hipster backyard wrestling we had going on. This is the kind of fight our dads would be betting on. Apparently they round up urban types who bash each other senseless for their amusement. He put me in touch with his boss, who offered me a shot at a 20,000 purse. I didn't hesitate. No one can stop me. Tonight is the big night. I didn't do anything special to prepare. I didn't need to. I expect to win the same way I always have, by rushing in and jabbing my opponent's exposed nerves, then kneeing him in the solar plexus or just pushing him over. No need to get fancy. I'm not being graded. The "arena" is an unfinished apartment structure a few stories high built like a doughnut around a large empty pool. The balconies on the apartments overlooking the pool act like private booths for the crowd, and there are hundreds of faces looking down from them. Multi-colored lights hang underneath, lighting the pool up almost like a rave. Two featherweight hispanic guys are flailing around at each other, but not hitting much. Imagine myself taking them both out in seconds and then shouting, "Are you not entertained?!" I smirk. One of them eventually goes down. The crowd roars. I see money being thrown from some of the balconies. When they drag the guy away, I notice that the pool has some dark spots. Is that blood? Maybe I can trick my opponent into slipping on it. The scout tells me I'm up. He has this huge shit-faced grin that makes me want to punch him. I guess he is proud of his new talent. Well, I'd better get this over with. I will have to fight at least 3 times tonight, so I'd better save my strength. As I walk out, the announcer really lays it on thick with my academic credentials and medical knowledge. He really plays me up as some kind of genius ninja. He's not wrong. Heh, maybe I should bring him along on job interviews? I'm pretty sure I heard him call me "Sherlock." So I hop down into the pool. It's pretty coarse and..... yeah that's a lot of blood. Alright, as long as it's not mine. Let's do this. Suddenly, the crowd erupts, and I see more money being thrown. For..... me? Wait, no. It's my challenger. He's a couple inches taller than me, but way more ripped. Also, lots of tats. They call him "the Professor," and say he dropped out of MIT on a full ride for physics, in order to do MMA. Pretty sure it's sarcasm. The guy doesn't look like he could spell MIT. Heh. We face off. I plan my attack. I will duck, sidestep, and shut down his right leg, then keep circling back to the kidneys, then hit everything exposed when he comes back at me. All that muscle won't matter when his brain can't send signals to it. Everyone here is going to just have to watch their favorite get dropped like a bitch. A chime sounds. He moves almost in slow motion, stepping forward with his right. I duck and weave, jabbing at his upper right leg. I hit exactly where I aim. I always do. This is too easy. I take a step to the lef- My head jerks back. He grabbed my hair!? How?? Shit. He lifts me completely off the ground. I kick at him. He just laughs. Alright, focus. I am going to make him regret this. I lash out with a flurry of blows at all his weak spots. No effect. Fuck this. I jab at his eyes, and promptly get my face slammed into the floor. I'm numb. Everything is a blur. Then I feel searing pain shoot through my ribs. Okay, so I guess only my face was numb. Then it gets smashed into the floor again. Maybe it wasn't quite as numb as I thought. Then I realize something. I am very smart. Well, obviously, right? But being so smart means that, right here and now, I realize a few basic things about my circumstances. First, I am obviously not in good enough shape, and lacking in pretty much all the actual fighting skills. I was good enough to beat up other kids who were even more spoiled and out of shape and inept at fighting. Second, unless a person pretty much stands still and let's you do it, trying to hit pressure points is stupid. That's why no actual fighters do it. And here I thought it was just because they were too stupid. Third, this is clearly a set up. The scout would have known how badly I'd get my ass kicked, so apparently watching a rich kid get beat up makes for some quality amusement. I'd plot my revenge but, well, I'm in the process of getting punched pretty hard in the balls. This guy is really an artist, you know. Every time I think I am too numb to feel anything more, he manages to surprise me. Then I black out. When I wake up, I'm in a hospital, my face covered in bandages. I'm pretty drugged up, but I manage to make out that I have several broken ribs, and my face is in pretty rough shape. Also lots of soft tissue damage. I'll be here for weeks. That's not even the best part, though. You know what the best part is? This old asian guy comes in and sits down next to me. He just stares at me for like an hour. After I manage to croak something unintelligible out, he tells me that one of my "victims" was his son. His son is a physics grad student at my school. I beat him up, and he bombed a big test afterward. His father holds me personally responsible for that. So he paid the promoter to set me up and put me up against a real MMA fighter to teach me a lesson. He made sure I would get beat up bad enough to miss my exams later this month. Eye for an eye.

article: I saw the old man push the swing, again. He had to be at least ninety, and as my aunt would say, "So close to death, he has the Grim Reaper on speed dial." He would sit for a while at the park where I worked as a ranger. Then, struggling to get up from the weathered, wooden bench with arthritic pain, he would rise, go over to the swing, and give it a few desultory pushes. At least, they seemed desultory to me. Each day since I started, for months: He'd sit with his cane, and stare off into nowhere. Then, get up, totter over to the swing set, and give an empty seat a few pushes. Often, that set was occupied by laughing children, challenging one another to swing higher than the rest, sure of their immortality and their ability to be just fast enough, or strong enough, to avoid mistakes the kind that, unfortunately, ended in a broken arm or twisted ankle for the ones who were not as quick, or as brave, as their peers. The old man would wait with the patience that only the elderly have, having known the passage of decades. When those children were done, he'd walk over to the chain-and-rubber child's playground toy, and give it one, two, three pushes. Sometimes four. Then, after a minute, he'd leave. ..... One day, I was overcome with curiosity. I approached him as he slowly made his way to the recently vacated swing set. "Hello?" I came up from behind him. Today he was wearing a yellow short sleeved shirt, the folds of his worn, aged skin moving shakily as he maneuvered his cane to support his frail body. He kept going. I don't think he heard me. "Hello!" I repeated, a little louder as he made it to the swing he traditionally pushed, lacking any child to enjoy it. He slowly turned and looked at me. "Pardon me?" He said with a thick accent. I would guess eastern European roots. "Hello!" "Hello, young man. How are you?" He extended a shaky hand, and I returned a soft handshake. I was approaching forty; I wouldn't say I was all that young. Compared to him, though, I was baby. I couldn't help but notice what looked like a bruise on his inner arm. Poor guy; they probably poked and prodded him for blood at his doctor's office. "Fine. How are you, sir?" I replied. "Oh, just getting along. I come here every day for wool-gathering, you know. Such a beautiful park, here." His voice sounded old, and tired. "It is, sir." "I think my brother and sister would have liked it, here." He said, eyes momentarily downcast behind his thick, Coke-bottle glasses. "Where are they?" "Dead." "I'm sorry to hear it." "Thank you, son." He looked up again, at me. "So, you have a question for me, Officer?" Heh. My uniform. Just under two years on the job, and I'm still not used to people addressing me as'Officer'. "My name is Dan." "Daniel?" "Just'Dan'." "Okay, Daniel. What's your question?" "Well, sir. I noticed you come and push the swing every day, with no children in it. May I ask why?" "You saw me do that, eh?" He smiled a little at this, like he was a child caught stealing from the cookie jar. "Yeah." "Then watch, and I'll explain." He turned to the swing, and gripped the chain with his right hand. "The soldiers took us my brother, my sister, my mother, and me when I was six years old. My father was probably at the factory; I do not know." He paused, his unsteady right hand shaking the chain, his left leaning on his cane. "The soldiers took us, and separated us. My sister and mother in one boxcar; my brother and me in another. I rode a night and a day, and when they let us out, we were herded into long houses. My brother and I stayed together. They put us children to work on machines where our little hands could get at smaller parts. Sometimes my friends' hands were crushed. My brother lost a finger..." He paused, again. "They gave me this to make sure I knew I was a number, not a person." He turned his arm, and showed me the bruise. Only, it wasn't a bruise; it was a series of numbers. Old, faded, but indelibly marked into his skin. "The Americans came and freed us, just a month too late. My mother and sister were dead from the gas chambers, and my brother died of pneumonia. I was ten when I left the camp. I was lucky, and got sent to live with my aunt here in America, where I got work in a bakery." He walked behind the swing, and steadied himself with his cane. "My brother, my sister, and me? We never had a childhood. We never played. We worked, starved, and did our best to avoid the guards' attention. So, I do this." And he pushed the swing. "One push, for my sister, Anna," The swing went out, and came back. "One push, for my brother Yosef," the swing went out, and came back again. "And one push for me, because no one ever did." And he pushed it again. ..... The silence was deafening, punctuated only by the creaking sounds of an un-greased playground swing, and a survivor's memorial to a childhood that was taken from him and his siblings.

article: I loved that picture. Truly, I did. Although at this point, I doubt that I'll ever be able to convince him otherwise. What do you even do with something like that? Something entirely sentimental? That's probably the worst part of the break up, knowing that I have no other option. That picture, that incredible, sweet, thoughtful gift, was my favorite possession. I hung it on the wall, next to the mirror I dressed in front of, so that I would see it every day before I left for home. Seeing the goofy joy on his face gave me the strength to handle the day. Life is really unfair sometimes, but knowing that in that moment someone loved me made it all seem ok. He really did love me. But it wasn't enough. Yes, he loved me, but he loved me less than her. Or maybe not. Maybe there was some other hidden reason that he put me second. Maybe it was just that she got there first. She won the race. Or maybe I really am somehow less than her. At this point it's just speculation. Now I have no beacon, no talisman to make me feel strong. Instead I'm left day dreaming about horrible things happening to her. I try to keep them ridiculous and funny so that I don't feel like a horrible person. I picture her getting punched by a monkey, or getting her arrested for racketeering. Like some girl who behaves like a defenseless child would ever be capable of running a mafia. That's the most infuriating part of losing him. Knowing that this was entirely planned by some woman as a power play. I guess that's why the Scooby Doo fantasy is so appealing. Everyone is standing around with her being held in some net when Fred pulls off her obviously cheap Halloween mask. In my mind that's the only explanation for her (obviously less attractive than mine) face. She turns to me and say's "I would have gotten away with it too, if it wasn't for that meddling woman." Of course, I'm seen as the hero, and ride off into the sunset with him. I promise I'm not some insane ex-girlfriend. I would never actually do anything to harm his relationship, because it would kill me to do anything that might make him unhappy. But it's still so hard not to feel jealous, and not to hate someone who is so manipulative. Especially when she takes something you need. That's why I packed up the picture last night. And why I'm driving to his house right now. Because as long as I have that picture, I know I'll hold onto hope that he might eventually choose me. All of the other gifts, the love tokens gathered over a period of building a life together, are fine. They serve a purpose. But the picture is only useful as a reminder of what I've lost. And the only reason I would keep it is if I held onto hope for a future where we're together. I still love him, and I believe that he still loves me, but he's made his choice. So I'm choosing to give the picture back, not because I don't love it or him, but because I love them both too much.

article: "If you asked most people about their general opinion on trees, they would probably answer, "Trees? Those things still exist?" The truth is, most people don't much of an opinion on trees. Most people born in the past few centuries haven't even seen a tree before, and have never been graced by the subtle wonders of the colorful shades of oak in the fall, or the retreat of a willow, or the brawn of the sequoia. These sorts of things only existed in photographs of old encyclopedias. "When synthetic wood was first created, most were quick to adopt. Synthetic wood possessed superior qualities, they claimed. It was not flammable, it was sturdy, it was cheap, and it looked just like wood. So we didn't need trees anymore! In fact, every reason for which a tree is useful - for shelter, for warmth, for oxygen, for wildlife habitats, for aesthetic pleasure on a nice evening walk - has been invalidated by synthetic wood and other equally absurd human inventions. "Anyone who has ever struck a match before can understand what I'm saying, because when you strike a match, it grants you a sort of control, a dominance, over something that is untamed. On the tip of the math dances a flame that disregards everything else, and only burns so long as you allow it. And seeing that wood burn away, being consumed by raw nature, is something that is lost on people these days. I read stories about great fires that could be seen from miles away, burning away hundreds of thousands of trees, leaving behind nothing but charred yet fertile ground, on which new trees would grow. A cycle that would've continued indefinitely, until humans said, "we don't need trees anymore. Trees are bothersome, ugly, and catch on fire. Let's do away with them." And so they did. "This is why it is important to plant trees. Trees give us life, they give us beauty, and they give us joy. We must not let people forget where our humanity is rooted. We must remind them of the trees!" Everyone was required to read this passage written by the founder when they were accepted into the Tree Planting Club, which was hardly a club, and more like a collection of distinct and autonomous cells operating in different cities around the country. I was introduced by a childhood friend to this club, David. David was obsessed with trees ever since childhood, and would show me pictures of all sorts of trees when we were kids. "My dad's a botanist," he would say, "but he hates trees." In all honesty, I often doubted the validity of the goal of the Tree Planting Club. Humanity has gone hundreds of years with most people not having even been influenced in some minute way by a tree. Not even food grew on trees anymore. Every food was replaced a synthetic version that (supposedly) tasted better, was cheaper to make, and didn't require constant watering and maintenance to produce. I joined the TPC soon after I found out Dad had been arrested for planting trees in public spaces. He was a writer, and one I looked up to, even though his novels never sold well. He had a spunk and determination that made him a great writer, but a terrible father. I wanted to follow in his footsteps, and if it wasn't my path to follow, so be it. I would quit TPC and get a normal job. But I'd like to think that I'm a writer too, and I wanted to write about something interesting, like trees, and how they affected people. That's how I found myself in the back of a cargo truck, sitting on the floor (if you can even call the sterile, metal base of a cargo box a floor), fiddling with the lamplight, which seemed to flicker and die every few seconds. David held a grim look on his face. After all, we were about to commit one of the greatest acts of vandalism: planting a tree. Because no one likes to admit when they are nervous, we sat in the humid box in silence, allowing the solid air to pull the hair on our necks up straight and pull the sweat from the pores on our palms. In between us lay a great maple tree. According to the books, the tree stood shorter than most, but it largest one I've seen and was apparently the largest one we could fit into the cargo box. "A minute from the plant site," Camille said from the front. We began to prepare our gear. We revved up our motorized shovel, our Chizzler, and suited up into our exoskeletons, and Camille flicked on her police signal interceptor. Planting a tree used to be easy. I read a pamphlet once that taught people how to plant trees, and it went like this: Find a soft area of dirt and dig a hole, and then drop the tree in the hole so the leaves are facing up. Then refill the gaps in the hole with dirt, pack it tight, and leave the tree. Tie ropes to support the tree of necessary. Obviously there was no dirt patches or soft soil in the middle of Times Square, where we were headed tonight to plant a tree. Luckily, we arrived when there were only a few people walking the streets, perhaps tourists who think it would be a neat experience to walk around Times Square at three in the morning. Even at this hour, you couldn't see the moon even if it were straight above. We built these buildings to look as if they were stretching out to reach for the stars, yet we blocked out the whole sky in the process. So people don't look up anymore, except to watch the endless panels of advertisements flash by faster than we can understand them. As the truck came to the stop, we slid open the backdoor of the cargo box and hopped out. We had a short window of operations, so we moved quickly. David grabbed the Chizzler and spun the motor up to a speed where it could destroy even fortified concrete. The plan was simple - drill a hold in the sidewalk, fill it with soil, roll the tree in, and cover the hole back up. Just as described in the pamphlet. As the Chizzler hit the concrete, the machinery made an awful, dull roar that probably awakened anyone within a three block radius of us. But it worked fast, and within 30 seconds, there was a tree-sized cavity in the sidewalk, filled with loose concrete and industrial dust. I used the shovel to remove all the excess rock fragments, while David lifted the tree out of the cargo box with the help of his exoskeleton. "Hurry up, people are watching, it's only time before someone calls the police!" Camille yelled from the truck. We didn't say anything, but it was clear to her that we acknowledged the urgency. We moved like clockwork, yet it still didn't feel like enough time. David was holding the tree upright as I ripped open bags of soil and began emptying them into the hole. It took nearly five or six large bags to complete fill the hole until the soil was packed tightly enough that the tree could stand upright by itself. "The police are on their way, we got ta go," Camille said. There wasn't enough time to clean up after ourselves. The Tree Planting Club had a policy of never leaving a mess when they planted, because it would reflect poorly on the organization. The TPC also had a policy of "not getting caught" because people who were truly enthusiastic enough about trees to commit great acts of vandalism were obnoxiously hard to come by. We dashed back into the cargo box, and as the truck pulled off we watched the tree become smaller and smaller through the open back door, until it was a stub in the urban landscape. "Let's hope that went well," David mumbled as he pulled the back door down, which hit the floor with a mighty bang. I fully expected the tree to be removed when I woke up. The city was usually pretty good about vandalism. However, I opted not to read the news that morning and decided to take the metro into the city and see for myself the result of our work. Would they tape off that section of the sidewalk? Would the lasting impact of our highly rehearsed tree planting just going to be a brand new section of concrete in Times Square? I sipped my coffee as I rounded the corner into the Times Square center. There was a huge congregation, with people clamoring and yelling and shoving, which was naturally the result of thousands of New Yorkers and unwitting tourists packed into one tiny block. But above all their heads, I could still see it. The brilliant radiance of burnt orange maple leaves, "the color of Autumn." The tree was taller, grander, and much more majestic than I remembered, and had apparently not been cut down. It stood gorgeously in the autumn sunlight. I later discovered that soon after we planted the tree, a group of locals, woken by the noise, took interest with the tree and surrounded it when the authorities came, to prevent the tree from being cut down. In a short period of time in the early morning, the news had spread and hundreds of people rushed to the tree's defense and created a human wall. And by noon that day, it had become national news, and everyone who enjoyed the bustle of pivotal events gathered at Times Square. They kept the tree, by the way. It was one of the only trees planted by TPC that didn't get almost immediately removed. This tree is almost twice the size, many times the awesomeness of the original tree we had planted years ago, and is maintained by the City of New York. Hopefully, now, when people visit Times Square, they'll have something to look up to that isn't those chrome edifices and their gloomy dispositions. No, I know they'll just be able to stand under the tree and look up, and they'll understand something inexplicable they hadn't before, like they'd solved a great mystery in their lives they hadn't known even existed. edit: slight edits to the story to make it more consistent

article: " Mr. President, " General Kopanski said. " We're waiting on you. " Jim Graves never imagined he would be here, the destruction of a half-billion lives commencing with his command. Not lives, he reminded himself. Not really. Around him, a select handful of cabinet members and army officers stood, waiting for him to say anything. He had been silent for the last fifteen minutes. The general was the first one to break the silence in all that time. Jim had almost forgotten they were there. Just do it, he told himself. This order will be the most significant event in human history. He dwelled on that. Human history. It was a fictional history, but somehow solid. The struggles were real. The pain was real. Simulated, fake, illusory - yet real all the same. " Let me speak to the doctor, " Jim said. The staff filed out slowly. He could see the stress, fear, and excitement on their faces. This anticipation had reached a near unbearable climax for weeks, but now that the moment for his decision had come, he found invisible walls in his way. He was so close. He had only to say the word. But he wanted to speak to the doctor just one more time. Moments later the man entered. Dr. Volgi was in his late fifties, balding, and a bit too thin. The man always seemed unhealthy. His eyes were lit up with enthusiasm, but everything else about him looked faded. His pallor was grey, his posture crooked. This man, he reminded himself, had spent his life in libraries, lost in books, in deep basement labs, at the cost of his own health and body. " Yes, Mr. President, " Volgi said. " Doctor, you once calculated the percentage that you were wrong, " Jim said. " Run through the calculations for me. " Dr. Volgi looked surprised. After all their discussions and consultations, he had turned Jim into a disciple. A true believer. He still was, but he needed a fraction more certainty. It had all made sense during those meetings and discussions. It was only here, the moment upon him, that he saw the full spectrum of possibilities. " Well, " The doctor said. " There are endless assumptions built into this, but the basic theory about our universe is about as certain as the theory of gravity. " " But gravity is another piece of your theory, " Jim said. " Our theories about it were wrong. " " Our theories about its origins were wrong. Our calculations about its effects and mechanisms are accurate. The system invents the laws, and the programs abide by them. One of them being gravity. " " How sure are you that this will actually crash the system? " Jim said. He had asked this before, but he needed to ask again for his own sake. That was the worst part - the knowledge that, even if Volgi was right, the plan might not have the intended effect of summoning the virtual gods. Volgi shrugged. " I am confident about this as well. It's clear that people are the most complex programs in this world. Even the sun is simpler. With so many... deletions at one time, I am sure it will trip up the system. It may not crash it, but the system will recognize that something has happened. " And then we'll finally get their attention. The attention of the gods. Those who crafted this realm. At the cost of a half billion people. Jim clenched and unclenched his fists. His mind spun with questions, half-articulated fears. " Alright, " he said, his confidence returning in a sudden flare. This will make you the most important man who ever lived. " Send them in. " President Graves gave the orders, and the bombs flew. Many flew to Asia, devastating the coastline, others traveling far into the Russian interior. The detonations of the bombs had all been synchronized to explode as near to the same time as possible. Jim was standing in his office when they hit. As hundreds of millions died, a flash of pinkish hue shot across the world, colors distorting and flaring. It happened everywhere all at once. Lines became less defined, the earth vibrating around them. Dr. Volgi came staggering into the room, clutching his chest. His eyes were wild. He looked at the president. " Mr. President, " the doctor said. " Your head... " Jim looked at himself in the mirror. A flashing red dot hovered over his head. He studied himself, his pulse escalating wildly. He felt two small horns on the side of his skull. They hadn't been here before. They had simply appeared. Congratulations, Jim heard in his head, a thought silently transmitted. You have reached new levels of Evil. It wasn't this thought. It was foreign. Confusion overcame him. The words were alien. "What's happening?" he asked Volgi. "I don't know," the doctor said, voice cracking and low. Sudden anger rose to the surface, like oil from a well. His body felt different. You're new level is accompanied by new powers. You'll notice you have more control over your environment now. With a thought, he lifted the Volgi off the ground. The man gurgled, clutching at his throat. "You were supposed to be sure," Jim said. "You were supposed to bring the gods here." He didn't let Volgi answer. Instead he flung him across the room where he slammed into the wall. Volgi slumped to the ground broken. His anger began to subside. New powers. So his first attempt to summon the gods had failed, but it had gained him something. It had educated him. And he still had nine billion lives left to play with. He turned and began levitating down the hall to find Kopanski. He had a war to finish.

article: The death-bells tolled for the king and continued on into the wedding song. The war had ended when the Sword of the Sun had died defending the Sun King, and the Princess had sacrificed herself and her royal name. She paid for her life with her hand in marriage. The necromancer had wasted no time in securing the kingdom. Although the peasants were unnerved by the king's attendance at his daughter's wedding, the free bread and ale quickly overcame their reluctance. It was a bit plain, but they had been hungry for a very long time. The wars didn't end, of course. Everyone knew that necromancers were inherently evil. The Land of the Sun had become Shadowfall, and brave knights and greedy kings often waged war to bring it back in the light. But the peasantry no longer sent their sons to war. They sent their fathers instead. The vast graveyards of all the previous wars opened, and the dead flooded out to protect the land. There were so many dead, in fact, that the king sent the extra skeletons to work the fields, to build roads, or perform other menial tasks. Crime also decreased. The necromancer watched his kingdom (and later his kingdoms) through the eyes of the undead. He employed Black Dogs as scouts and spies. They were terribly efficient creatures, and are only visible for a moment from the corner of the eye. Thieves, rapists and murderers often vanished before their crime could be committed. The peasants grew fat and wealthy. They devoted their time to the arts and sciences, often sending their children to the necromancer's School for Minions to teach them letters, numbers, and basic necromancy. The necromancer often toured these schools, searching for exceptional talent. On one of these trips, a bold child asked "Why are you doing nice things, if you're supposed to be evil?" The scholars and pupils waited, both expectant and fearful. "If I killed everyone, my kingdom would never grow. One must keep the living alive or there will be no more dead. So I make sure you have enough food to make many children. I have been alive for thousands of years. You only live for a hundred. I can wait." The child's eyes widened. "The Black Dogs keep the peace. Can't have you all killing each other too soon now, can we?" The child shook its head slowly. It tried to ask a question, but the question refused to force its way out. The necromancer smiled. He'd found one. "You wish to ask about the schools?" The child nodded. "Once in a great while, there is a person who is born but will never die. These schools help me find them. You, for instance." The child finally found a voice. "Then what?" It asked. "Care to find out? I'm afraid it will be a very long time until you can come back here." The necromancer extended an emaciated hand. The child took the hand and went with the necromancer. The village had a great feast in the child's honor, toasting the necromancer with their finest ales. Back at the Sun King's castle, the child was bathed, fed, and brought into the ritual room. "What now?" it asked. The necromancer grinned. "I have been so very hungry, for so very long. And we are so much more delicious when we're young." Later, the necromancer admired his form in the mirror. He now looked like a muscular, ordinary young man. Of course he took care of the people, made them happy. Rebellion was too much effort, too much risk. He was evil, not stupid. It was too bad the princess had already died. He might have put his restored form to some use.

article: I never knew I could feel love before I saw her. There she was, playing with her friends without a care in the world, and I knew my life would never be complete without her in it. At first, I tried to fight it. A young, delicate thing like her with a fat, awkward man like me? It just wasn't right. I was always one to make fun of people in love, how ridiculous they looked and sounded. At 31, for the first time in my life, I finally understood. She was the last thing on my mind before I drifted off to sleep. Waking up in the morning became a pleasant experience, because it meant I could daydream about her some more. Picturing her bright green eyes and her shiny black hair was all it took for another mediocre day at work to become another day in paradise. I imagined us cuddling on the couch, watching reruns of 90's sitcoms she most likely would not care about, her tiny little body nestled in my big arms. There was no fighting it anymore, I was madly in love. It wasn't too long before I couldn't take it anymore. I loved her and she was going to love me too, no matter what anyone else thought. I jumped in my car and drove to the place where I had first seen her playing with her friends. Surely she'd be there. On the way, I found myself second-guessing my actions. Was I really doing the right thing? What if she wanted nothing to do with me? She was so young and innocent, could I really make her love me? The moment I saw her again, even more beautiful than in my memories, I knew that feeling couldn't be ignored any longer. So, heart pounding, hands shaking, I asked: "How much for the black kitten?"

article: The conference room was lined with seven seats, one for each member of council. Behind them stood a secondary representative wearing a large headset. article: I walked through the streets of my great city toward the Senate. Caesar wasn't one who was kind to people who were late to meetings. Lately, I'd been wearing his patience thin with the questions during the night. Other senators were meeting for some reason, but I had always had work to do, the city needed attention, and I had a way to give them hope. I arrived in the Senate just as Caesar was. I didn't have a lot of time to get to my position, and I couldn't allow the man to see me. I motioned to Tullius to distract the man for me. He and I had been good friends for our time in the Senate; I figured he would cover. The men of the Senate rose as Tullius asked Ceasar to approach Climber. The two of them were moving for a greeting; there was somewhat of a power play going on right at that moment. Climber was reaching to get a better hold on Ceasar than he had on him. Ceasar wasn't the kind to stand for that; he would punish Climber. I slipped between the rows and glanced down at the waist of the man beside me. He was Cassius, a man who had long wanted Ceasar's position and rank. He had removed a dagger from his Toga. I nudged him, "You aren't supposed to bring those into the Down the stairs, Servilius pulled out a dagger of his own and stuck the leader of the Senate in the shoulder. He cried out in pain as other men moved to rush him. I stood still, awestruck at the rebellion that I was watching. The men were brutally killing him. I didn't move to stop them, they had their reasons for wanting him dead, I had mine. Ceasar drew his last breath a dozen minutes later, bleeding across the Senate. Minutes later everyone reconvened to discuss the matters of the day. Cassius, who had retaken his place beside me, approached me at the end of the day. "Sorry for the shock," he began, "we wanted to invite you to the meetings, but you were always busy." "It's all right," I replied, "just know that if anyone asks I am telling them that I put a dagger right in his neck." "His neck?" "I want to seem important to history you know."

article: The sky above the half-finished capitol is lead grey. The streets run with the muck and grime of thousands. The moneyed amble off in their carriages, ported back to their estates and their rich brownstones, ensconced in warm fires, catered to by servants. The poor and destitute are left to stumble on through the filthy streets run with mud, boots sucked off their feet with every half-hearted step. The tall man steps off his soap box, his jester's stage, and dons the worn felt hat he carries at his side. His spirits dampens him, envelops him as the overcast November sky. He walks back to his home, forgoing the coach and the men that wait on him. He takes the long way back; the meandering way by the bends of the Potomac. He sees in the distance the brick and stone fortifications. The black rimed cannons that point south. Always south. His eyes turn to the navy ships. The porters unload the corpses by the dozens, by the hundreds. There are not enough flags to cover their mutilated, diseased bodies, and they are covered by tattered tent canvas. The freezing rain starts to fall, and his mood takes a violent, bloody turn. "Damn them. Damn them!" he shouts silently into the corridors of his own mind. "Damn them I'd have them all strung up and hung. Traitors to their bones! By Gabriel and all the angels, to Hell and the Fire with them." He rips up the speech he had penned this morning; the one that spoke of the fellowship of the common man, of the concord and shared destiny of the Union. His boot sinks into a muddy, viscous puddle. He can not extricate his foot, and as a crashing wave the absurdity of the situation catches up to him. He laughs a self deprecating laugh, and his foul mood lifts. He unbuckles the boot and continues homeward. (Post Script: I consider President Lincoln to be a mentor figure of sorts; his life and his works are those from which I draw a great deal of inspiration. I hope this short piece qualifies. Thank you).

article: I love her. She loves me. I'm sure of it. Absolutely, positively, one-hundred and fifty percent sure of it. When I wake up in the morning, she's what I think about. At night, we sit together. While she reads, I just watch her. The mere sight of her is enough for me. She, on the other hand, gets so wrapped up in her book that it's like she doesn't even know I'm there. At the moment, I'm making her a book of pictures I've taken of her. For a while there, back when I still had to stay six hundred feet away from her, it was difficult to get the shots I wanted. But, hey, that's what zoom lenses are for. Now, however, that time's passed, and I can get as close as I like. Lately, however, the problem I've had is one of glare. article: They must've got the wrong one. It's okay. I have that kind of face. Or had, I guess. I can't say I have much of a face at this point. The same sentiment rings true for the face I used to have, now scattered on the floor before the body it used to define, inside-out and painted crimson with pulp of what was my frontal lobe. It looks painful. I don't know if it was. I think it was. I think it must've been. It's clearly painful for the remaining corporeal beings in the room. I'm not sure what else to expect when you put a loaded high caliber weapon to the back of another man's head and pull the trigger, but this was definitely not the result they anticipated. The only one with any semblance of composure is the dog, who just whimpers, licks the speckles of my blood from his chops, and settles on his haunches. The man holding the dog is not nearly as calm. That's understandable, considering he was the only one facing me as the bullet entered-and violently exited-my head. The handler stood at a 45 degree angle to me, holding back the dog on a considerably short chain. Prior to my execution, the two had put on a great show, each trying to out-bark the other. It might well have terrified me, in its own right, but at the time my attention was rather focused on the barrel of a gun pressed unnecessarily forcefully against the peak of my skull. In the end, the show I put on for him was significantly more effective. Though they he positioned himself what should have been a safe distance away, a good portion of me had sprayed across the handler and his dog, a bright contrast against his all black attire. Now shot, now ethereal and now somehow fixed above and throughout this scene, I watch as his eyes expand beyond the size allowed beneath the holes of his knit ski mask. His body starts convulsing, rattling rhythmically as if one reversed the resonance of a banged gong, exponentially building to his explosive "Fuck." As if waiting for this audible cue, the one in the corner vomits. It's a full-body, doubled-over-on-your-knees vomit. Whatever weapon he was holding hangs loosely on his neck as he partially spews on it with his yellow stink. Tucked away in the dark corner behind the scene, clutching an automatic rifle the size of his torso, he must have been trying so hard to look so stern. Yet I hadn't even noticed he existed until I no longer did. His stream is fully expunged before the "Fuck" even finishes bouncing off the walls. The lone woman in the room (I'm pretty sure she's a woman) is now in front of the gun-wielder, between him and the chair in which I was seated, where the body I had worn had been sitting. She pleads with gunman, beats him with her fists, screams her fucking head off at him. "What did you do?" "Were is the reset?" "Who the fuck was that?" The gunman only stands, his arm still erect, holding the gun in the same spot my head had been. A yellow pool beneath his left foot adds to the abundance of bodily fluids filling the room. Then the feed cuts off. I can't say why it was on for so long. My brain wasn't intact, and yet my thoughts were-are-intact. They're strong and unstoppable, completely unquenchable, adrift without stimulation in this soft dark nothing. For those final moments, what living tissue was left of my mind to carry me through that scene? I didn't just watch or hear or see; for the dwindling instance of my life, I became that room. And now, in this total deconstruction of time and matter, what's left of me to be abandoned in this eternal circle of thought? I wish I knew a bit more. Though, I suppose that's the great wish of the dead. For all the closure and resolution found in the films and the books and the ballads of the living, nothing prepares you for the questions never answered in the absence of your life. without even a hand to count to track the time or an eye to see it, I can't measure how long I've been left to thinking. I'll just call it an eternity. I turn these impossible observations over and over, playing them forwards and backwards as well as I can, buy all I'll ever know, for certain, never changes. I was killed by a bunch of kids who thought you could reset life.

article: I'm not rude. I can volley small talk and identify that groove in a person's self esteem where a compliment could be inserted (like your waiter might do when their rent comes looming). I place those compliments carefully, knowing exactly how the little groove got there in the first place. Even though pervasive comfort and complacency have ruined our human utopia, I still can't stomach watching a kid lose a stuffed animal. I remember how I could fit so much attachment into a terrycloth rabbit in my youth. I remember leaving the rabbit at a La Quinta outside of New Braunfels on vacation twelve summers ago and feeling every fiber of emotion being sucked through his black bead eyes back into mine through the tinted windows of a Waco-bound greyish Dodge Intrepid. I had transposed misplacing an item into abandoning a living, loving thing. To be honest, The only security I have ever known came from shirking the love I enlisted to anchor material possessions into my earthly endeavors. I recognize that most people don't feel that way, and I hurt deeply for them. It isn't a pain of pity. I believe it's fear stinging in my memory. When I see a kid losing his rabbit, some part of me drives all the way back to New Braunfels every time. That's why heading home from a party long-ended took a backseat to hearing the carefully-angled comedy of errors being orated bitterly from the bottle-strewn porch of the blue-green two-story on Chittersby. David rambled himself back into sobriety over the course of an hour or so. By the first break in his self-sympathizing soliloquizing, every other show-goer had hailed a cab excluding myself. If I head home now, I thought, my arrival will likely wake up my live-in girlfriend. Then she might want to talk to me, or touch my skin. Anything outside of the house beats that, even rabbit recovery. Arbitrary social interaction, random sex, and binge drinking kept me entertained while I waited for my Mom to die. It isn't as fucked up as it sounds, she wasn't sick or anything. Poor health maybe, but not sick. As a youngster I loved her more than any person alive. As I grew older we fought, but I still loved my memories of our relationship more than I could ever love anything else. I vowed to never hurt her. When I resolved to take my own life about a year ago I was fully aware that I'd have to wait until Mom was dead. Last month her bleakest years drew to a close without climax; she died in her sleep, at home. David sensed that his sole audience member had drifted away from his dramatic offerings into their own thoughts and experiences. I suspect that David is sensitive to these types of shifts, because his speaking voice grew loud in an attempt to re-recruit my attention and empathy and loud enough to wake up the slumbering party host behind the porch window. She came outside. Being two total strangers on her property, I took her request as reasonable and politely apologized after we were asked to leave her home. Knowing that we would likely never meet again, David reached out. On our short walk through the big crunchy yard he disclosed that he had a stockpile of pain killers and soon everyone would realize that they trampled the wrong guy. Everyone would regret not loving him. Even me, because I was just like every one else. Shallow. Insincere. I stopped him as he crossed the street. I stopped him to tell him exactly how wrong he was. To tell him that I knew exactly how if felt to have your love ripped out of someone and shot right back into yourself without so much as a good-bye or a thank you note. I needed David to know that I had lost so much love that I didn't want any more. I was ready to die with a smile, because that was my best middle finger to the absurd blink of existence known as humanity. I inhaled, preparing to take this kid's rabbit and destroy it right in front of him, right in the middle of the god damned street. In the heat of the exchange, Neither of us heard the drunk driver speeding as fast as he could away from an accident he had caused a few blocks over.
