He straightened his uniform and, with considerable restraint, said, "The next thing I hear had better a reasonable strategy of attack, you pathetic piece of shit." Sargent Sarcasm nodded calmly. "Well, as you know, it has been shown scientifically that your average Canadian has a capacity for reason that is equivalent to that of a Golden Retriever. I suggest that we put up signs and billboards throughout Toronto that say'Welcome to Buffalo.' The Canadians will believe they are in the wrong city, wander North, and succumb to hypothermia in the frozen wastelands of the Arctic." "Unless they are eaten by Polar Bears first!" yelled Captain Obvious, clapping his hands. Admiral Asshole sneered, and stormed out of the room, slamming the door behind him. "He didn't like your idea," Captain Obvious stated. Sargent Sarcasm replied, "Well, Captain, not every war is as simple as Iraq and Afghanistan."

article: At 75 he had been stubborn. At 120, irascible. But now? At 193? He was downright impossible to deal with. It's one thing to become set in one's ways. It's another thing to insist on lighting a cigarette in a booth of a small Long Island diner. It had been more than 10 years since smoking in restaurants had been banned in New York. But these small steps in cultural evolution had had little impact on Walter. Simon glanced up, then quickly away as Walter took a long, slow drag and allowed the smoke to drift lazily from between parted lips. Simon didn't dare utter a warning. He'd been down this road too often. Why draw Walther's wrath when some waitress would come along soon enough to do the deed? Only it was never Walter they chastised. Simon would bear the brunt of the scolding. " Are you crazy! " they usually began. " How can you let a child have cigarettes?! " " How can you let a child drink liquor?! " " Why is your little boy looking up that woman's dress!!! " The vices of an old man had become Simon's parenting nightmare. And here they were again - another frowning waitress hovering over them. Simon could do little more than look helpless and try to snatch the burning butt from the apparent seven year old. But Walter was quick. His " youth " gave him the advantage of speed and dexterity. He'd duck and dodge and play the spoiled brat to perfection, eyes glittering with perverse glee. He seemed to savor Simon's discomfort. It was unmistakable. " You're not my real father! " Walter shouted before scurrying under the table. Simon went beet red as he nervously looked at the waitress. " He's just joking of course..... You come out from under there right now! " Simon demanded hammering on the table, sending the salt shaker skittering sideways with every slam of his fist. A searing pain caused him to howl as the lit cigarette was pressed into his kneecap. The sound of wicked-little-boy laugher sliced icily through the greasy air of the diner. People were looking now. Too many people. Drawing attention was never good, but stunts like this were becoming downright dangerous. People assumed that Simon was Walter's father, and a terrible one at that. How long before someone called the police? They couldn't go on like this. Simon attempted a weak smile, his eyes glossy with the dew of burn-pain. The waitress scowled and turned on her heels, retreating toward the kitchen. He was pretty sure she wasn't checking on the soup of the day so he'd have to act fast. Where Walter had agility on his side, Simon had man-hands and grown-up strength. While attempting to look as casual as possible, he fished under the table until he'd cornered Walter. His fingers found purchase among the ample curls of the man-boy's hair. Sliding sideways, he gave a mighty tug and extracted Walter as he hurriedly exited the booth. His strides were long and resolute. They crossed the restaurant with such speed, he looked like a traveller trying desperately to catch a flight, suitcase flailing in tow. Once outside, Simon regained enough composure to realize it would not look well for him to be dog-walking this " child " down the street by his hair. At the first alleyway he ducked in, yanking Walter after. Now, behind a dumpster, safely out of view of the street, they squared off. " Goddammit, Walter! Do you have any idea the trouble you could have gotten us into? Gotten ME into? It's like..... " " Spare me the histrionics. " Walter interrupted peevishly. " Really, you're like a woman the way you go on. " " No! I mean it! This has got to stop! I swear with every rejuvenation you become more and more impossible. We have to be discreet! " " What discreet. You haven't figured it out? They're cattle. They're meat. We're immortal. We don't have to play their game! The world is OURS! Eternity is OURS! " " They..... are..... DANGEROUS! " Simon exclaimed. And then, as if trying to distill the seriousness of his message, he hissed through clenched teeth " And that makes your carelessness dangerous. It makes you dangerous..... to me. " " Sissy. " Walter replied flatly. Simon stared, stupefied at his longtime companion's glibness. He'd never been particularly fond of children. And since this really was no child, he took advantage of the opportunity to slap the shit out of him. No, literally he slapped him so hard a little piece of poop came out. And that was that. There was nothing left to say. The race was on. Now all that mattered was who would be first to get to the supply of elixir.

article: There is this sense of being all alone, even if you are at home. The feeling still persists and comes at you most strongly when you are all alone taking I understand how you feel. It can be challenging to deal with loneliness, especially when you're at home. If you're open to it, there are several things you could try to alleviate this feeling: 1. Connect with others virtually: With technology at our disposal, we can still connect with others through video calls, messaging, or social media platforms. Reach out to your friends or family members and schedule a call with them. 2. Engage in your hobbies or activities: Taking up activities that you enjoy can distract you from feeling lonely. Whether it's reading, watching a movie, or doing some craftwork, engaging in activities can help you feel more relaxed and content. 3. Practice mindfulness: Mindfulness can help you stay present in the moment and in touch with your emotions. Through meditation or deep breathing exercises, you can learn to appreciate the small things and find peace within yourself. 4. Seek help: There's no shame in seeking help from a professional therapist or counselor who can provide you with guidance and support. Remember that it's normal to feel lonely sometimes, but it's essential to take care of your emotional and mental wellbeing. Try to reach out to your loved ones, practice self-care, and take up activities that bring you joy.

article: "So he just boarded himself up in his trailer?" Lenox, the head producer, demanded. "No, sir," his assistant said. The young man was sweating, but it wasn't because of the mid-summer Arizona sun that pounded down on them. "He's..... he's in LA." "What?!" Lenox threw his clip board against the cracked earth of the desert. "You've got to be fucking joking! We've got 200 staff, 10 big name actors, and 16 fucking thousand extras out in this fucking desert, and this fucking prima donna skipped town over a fucking contract dispute?" Michaels, the director, walked to the edge of the hill and surveyed the thousands of men that lined the desert. Tucked under his arm was a newspaper describing the My Lai Massacre in Vietnam. Michaels's army wore Roman armor, carried a short sword by their side, and stood in perfectly formed ranks. "I mean," Lenox rambled on, "we're spending tens of thousands of dollars just to keep any of these fucking extras from dying of thirst in this heat." Michaels picked up his walkie talkie. "Tell the army to march," he said. An air horn rang out, and the men started to march westward. Despite not having any official training, they appeared to march in unison at that distance. Every one of those men believed that this role would be his big break and wanted to impress the cameras with how well he marched. "What the fuck are you doing?" Lenox demanded, running up to Michaels. "None of the cameras are running!" "Then get them running." "Jesus Christ." Lenox fumbled for his walkie talkie. "Start filming. We can at least get some shots of the army marching. Whatever you do, keep those cameras running." The army proceeded toward the setting sun, and toward the small Arizona town where they had set up shop. The hiccup of a town had been generous hosts to the film crew. Especially generous considering this movie multiplied the population of their town by ten. "Alright, Michaels," Lenox said. "They're just about on top of the town. Let's have them turn around and get them marching east. We can get a good shot with the sun at "Keep going," Michaels said into his walkie talkie. "What do you mean,'keep going? Lenox asked. "There's nowhere to go." "Have the men break down the doors of that antique shop," Michaels said. He paused as the voice on the radio replied. "Yes, I'm sure," he said. "We'll cover the damage." "Have you lost your mind?" Lenox asked. "What are you doing?" One contingent of the army charged into the town. The men threw rocks, breaking windows and began to kick down the door of the antique shop. The rest of the army, eager not to be left behind, rushed into the city as well. Before long, the carnage had spread to a diner next door and beyond. "What in the hell is wrong with you?" Lenox demanded. "Call them off!" "Go ahead and try," Michaels said. "For God sake," Lenox picked up his walkie talkie. "Perkins! Knock this bullshit off! Get everybody out of that town! Perkins!" Lenox continued to shout into his radio, but the men continued to wreak havoc in the small town. "It's amazing isn't it," Michaels said. "Men will do almost anything if you give them a uniform and a few instructions. It's like we were programmed to obey. No wonder war is hell." "This isn't war!" Lenox yelled. "It's a fucking movie!" "No it isn't," Michaels said. "We ran out of money weeks ago. And our star just fled the state. This movie is ruined. As are we." Lenox put his hands in his hair and looked at the flames that had begun to rise in the town. "Then what the hell are we going to do now?" "You said it yourself," Michaels said. "Keep the cameras running."

article: The world had been in disaray for as long as I could remember, and that had been a long time - 69 years, 11 months, and 29 days to be exact. Ever since the event infused humanity with powers, the world had fallen apart. Rampant crime and terror had overtaken the planet as villains become supervillains, and heroes became complacent. No one wanted to be an accountant when they could save the planet, nobody wanted to work at a power plant when they could travel through time as easily as the rancid air that all on the planet breathed. But in the chaos of the world, the only rule was that the power always came before the 50th birthday. Except in my case. And although the people lived forever, and fought wars forever, were sick forever, and watched their society crumble forever, immortality to all had always been seen as the blessing that came after the Event. Only I could see it as it was - the fence that kept the people in the cage that the God that had either failed them, played a cruel game on them, or been killed by the humans he raised so high that they could only fall long ago. They were all rats in a cage. All but me. And so, on my 70th Birthday, I finally gained my power. I awoke. I breathed. I saw. I breathed. I saw. And so I chose, I used my power, and I died.

article: "El! El! " , someone screams in the distance. Seems like they're calling for me. "El, can you hear me?" I turn around. It's Tim, my best - and only - friend. Should I talk to him? I'm already late for work..... but he's done so much for me. I walk up to Tim. "Hey. What's up?" "El! God bless you!" He's clearly on the edge of crying. "Tim, what's wrong? What happened?" "My boss..... My boss..... He..... He reported me." "To the Org? " , I ask in utter disbelief. This is the third time Tim got reported in a week. Nobody can be this cruel. "To the Org. I..... I'm tier 4 now. How will I pay for air? You know how much it costs for this tier, don't you? What can I do?" "You know what? I'll give you some of mine. Tier 2 price. I already get plenty of air from my boss anyway. Dunno about water and food, though, I'm sorry." "THANK YOU SO MUCH, YOU SAVED MY LIFE! " , he shouts. I've never seen anybody this relieved in the twenty-five years I've spent on this planet. "Here, have a sip. Now I must run, can't be late for work. See you soon." "See you." Just at the door of my work, a tall man stops me. He wears an Org uniform - this can't be good. "Eleanor Martinez?" "Yes." "I'm Commander Smith. Come with me." He takes me to a nearby police station. There are five others at the station. Two of them seem to be officers, the rest are probably some criminals. Am I a criminal too? I am, but how could they know? "Eleanor Alyssa Martinez, do you know this man? " , Commander Smith enquires, and promptly shows me a picture of Tim. "I do." "Bring him in," the commander orders one of the officers. "Yes, sir," he says, and opens a door I haven't even noticed until now. In steps Tim. "Timothy Adamczyk, did this woman sell you a unit of air, circumventing the government pricing and rationing system? " , the commander asks. "Yes, she did." "Ms. Martinez, do you plead guilty?" "I do," I reluctantly say. "Oh, and Tim. Fuck yourself." "I'm sorry, El! I'm sorry," he cries, but I don't want to listen. He betrayed me. It only took a couple of minutes to decide on the verdict. They will shut off my air tomorrow. Tim falls down to tier 7 as a punishment, but he'll become tier 2 again in just a month. The fucking snake just couldn't keep his mouth shut, could he? [ Remark: I feel like this is absolute rubbish, but I promised myself that I wouldn't throw out anything I write while practicing, so here it is. ]

article: It had been a good day; I'd had a nice lunch (three cattle) and was settling down for an afternoon nap. Then I heard the footprints. They always think that because I'm huge I can't notice small things, and they can sneak up on me. That one guy, dressed in black with a curved sword, did actually make it pretty far, but he had extra soft boots. And still, I heard him coming. But this was different. No clinking of armor. And the echo was clearly someone walking down the middle of the main passage, instead of sticking toward the side. And walking regularly, instead of in quick bursts, like someone sneaking from safe spot to another. Either this was the most overly-confident and foolish knight in all of existence, or he was just lost. Then he called my name. "Hello? Is this the home of Valgraud the Destroyer? I'm Turning the corner, and seeing me laying on my pile of treasure, he paused, both in his walking and his speaking. Then he continued, "Um, yes, I see that I'm in the right place. My name is Thomas, and I've brought you some gold." He threw a coin into the pile. "I have a proposition for you." This was not something I was used to. Usually they try to steal my gold. Sometimes they promise me gold if only I do something for them. I eat them. I chose not to eat this one. I fixed him with a stare: "Your money has bought you five minutes of life. Use them wisely, and you may get more." He looked nervous. That was nice; they taste better when there's some adrenaline in the blood. He said "Well, you see, you like gold, and I know a way to get you lots of gold. Not as much as you've got here, I admit. But still, you'd have more gold than you do now." I nodded at him, and said "Yes, and what's in it for you? Going to keep some of the gold, are you?" "Oh, no," he said, "I don't actually care about gold that much. I care about stories. And people care about stories. They like stories so much they'll trade gold for them. I want stories, and I want to share them with people for their money. And I'll bring the gold to you." I decided he'd get a couple more minutes. "Go on," I said. "I'm a writer. I want you to tell me your stories, stories of thousands of years of history that nobody knows anymore, and I'll write them down. You'll get full credit, of course, I'm not a plagiarist. But then I'll go and tell the stories to people from what I've written down, and collect the money, and bring the money back to you. I was hoping for maybe two or three hours' worth, and then I'll travel around for a year or so, and bring back all the money, and then we can get a few hours' more written down. I don't want the gold. I just want to tell stories." This sounded wrong, to me. "Why would a writer be satisfied working as a scribe? If you want stories, you can just make them up. There is something you're not telling me. Truth, now! " He looked terrified. Words started spilling out of him. "People hate my stories. My stories stink. I need good stories." He sat down, looking dejected. "I'm a terrible writer. I've tried to write my own stories, but I have no sense of pacing and I always get started and then can't figure out where the plot should go. And all the characters end up being versions of me." He kicked at the gold. "I lied when I said people hate my stories. They would hate my stories, if my stories were interesting enough to bother hating. Mostly they just don't pay attention at all." He sighed. "When I said I was coming here, people said I'd get killed. I tried to blow it off, but the fact is that I'd rather get eaten than go on as I was, a failure at the only thing I ever cared about." This was pathetic. I considered eating him, but "pathetic" tastes lousy. He shrugged. "So, what'll it be? I brought some paper, I can write down some stuff right now. I'll leave you alone for about a year, tell the stories as many places as I can, and bring back all the gold that I collect. If you're happy with how much it is, you can give me more stories. If you're not, I guess you can eat me." I considered his proposal. Then I ate him. Why should he get famous telling my stories?
label: human

article: Elevator to Platform B I stole another glance at my watch. The station was on Mountain Time. Of course, that far off the planet's surface, the entire concept of time was completely arbitrary. The Department could easily have had us work longer hours, and indeed it may have been more efficient to alter our schedules for work off-planet. But old habits die hard, so they instead opted to simply flood the station with artificial daylight in alternating blocks of twelve hours. And since the station was located in geosynchronous orbit far above the Utah desert, Mountain Time it was. I let my wrist fall back to my side, satisfied that the elevator was not late. Yet. Three or four dozen times I'd made this trip so far, and not once had the goddamn lift been on time. If it didn't arrive in the next ten minutes, I was ready to raise hell with the Transportation Bureau. But even as the thought crossed my mind, I saw through the transparent ceiling above my head the elevator slowly descending down the shaft like a great glass donut. The shaft itself stretched up toward the heavens, a perfectly round black cylinder tethering the station high above to the Earth. In five or six minutes, the elevator had slowed to a stop before me. I stood and gathered my things. There was a slight hiss as the doors opened and the pressure from inside equalized with the lower atmosphere. Ten or so people made their exit, all assisted by canes and walkers as their bodies readjusted to Earth's gravity. I saw each of them take several deep breaths, the first lungfuls of fresh air they'd had in who knows how long. The display above the door changed from red to green, and I stepped through the portal and into the elevator. Only one other passenger followed me, an older man, probably in his seventies. Good, I thought. He didn't look like he'd be much of a bother. I've had rides in this thing during the holidays that were absolutely dreadful. Ten hours locked in a sealed container with dozens of screaming children and their exhausted parents while I made a vain attempt to sleep my way through the trip. It was absolute hell. But with only one other passenger, it wouldn't be too bad. Hell, I could even sit on the opposite side of the shaft from him and we wouldn't even have to look at each other. Gleefully, I stowed my bags in the compartment behind a seat and strapped myself in. The man chose a seat somewhere off to my right, far enough away that I could ignore him easily. The doors slid shut again and I heard them vacuum-seal in place. There was a steady hum, and the lift slowly began to rise. We were a few miles in the air, before the elevator had begun to pick up speed, when my companion spoke. " Quite a view, ain't it? " I looked out through the glass. Vibrant red plateaus dotted the landscape in every direction, lit by a fiery orange sunset that was slowly fading to purple. I made a noncommittal grunt. To myself, I rolled my eyes. So much for my nice, quiet ride. " Never seen anything quite like it. No, sir. " " Yeah, it's fine, " I replied gruffly, hoping that he would correctly interpret my tone as an invitation to leave me alone. No such luck. " I mean, are you seeing this? " " I've seen i- Look, buddy. I work on the shuttle platform. I make this trip a dozen times a year. It's pretty and all, but I've seen it. Okay? Jesus, you're acting like you've never been in space before. " He fell silent for a moment. " Well, I haven't. " I was surprised. " You've never been to space before? Not even, like, on vacation? " He shook his head sadly, then leaned back to look up at the sky. " When I was a boy, I always wanted to go to the moon. I used to watch all those old cartoons where they'd go up there and..... Do you remember Simon and Bobo? " I stared blankly. " Ah, I guess you're too young for that. Anyway, I always wanted to go. Then they announced that they were building this thing, and that space travel would be so much cheaper, and my heart just soared. I was fifteen then. " He stopped for a moment and swallowed. " But I never got to go. I grew up on a farm, so there was always too much work to be done. Pa always said no. " The planet's surface was growing fuzzy beneath us, cloaked by the haze of the lower atmosphere. The lift was picking up speed. He continued. " Pa died, and I inherited the farm. And then I had even more work to do. So I never really got the chance to go. But I'm old now, and I can't work anymore. Got no family to speak of. So I sold the place. And now I'm going to the moon. " I nodded and said that was nice. He didn't say anything for a while after that. When we were somewhere in the middle of the thermosphere, I remembered something. " Hey, uh..... I'm sorry, I didn't catch your name. " " Kurt, " the old man replied. I nodded. " Jack. You know, the first time I was on this thing was in the middle of a meteor shower. " His eyes widened. " Really? What was that like? " " It was incredible. " I smiled. " It's way different from on the ground. You could see them blazing past just a mile or two away. They're bright. Really bright. They move so goddamn quick too, faster than you'd think. " I trailed off, lost in the memory. Thankfully, Kurt chose not to break me out of it. When I came back to reality, I saw through the transparent floor below my feet the behemoth that was the Earth. From this height, it seemed even bigger. " I'm gon na get some sleep, Kurt. This is the part where it's not real interesting for a while. " He nodded. I closed my eyes. I awoke to the sound of the lift doors opening, the familiar hiss that I'd heard so many times before. I stood and gathered my things, then I followed Kurt through the portal and into the station I'd come to know as my second home. " Do you know how to get to Platform B? " he asked me. " Yeah, that's where I work. It's this way. " I slipped behind the counter, punched his ticket, and sent him on his way, wondering whether or not I'd see him again.
label: human

article: Of all the students I've taught in my fifty years at the Jackson School for the Exceptional, only one stands out as truly unique. Her name was Angela Myers. When I first met her, I felt nothing but pity. At 14 years old, she was 4'10, and 200 pounds. While other students at our school were busy flying, teleporting, and enjoying other thrilling and exciting abilities, Angela was different. She was usually sitting alone reading, munching on some snack in a quiet, methodical way. The bag of chips was never empty, the can of soda was always perpetually full. Angela's power was free refills. Despite the urging of the other teachers to control her snacking, Angela would still eat compulsively. Sometimes I would sit by her and try to make conversation. She would mostly shrug and stay absorbed in her book, or even the floor if she was out of reading material. I got the feeling that she ate because of a deep depression, and that if she didn't break the cycle it would destroy her eventually. "You know, Angela, I think maybe the other kids would take to you more if they just got to know you. Maybe you could offer them some of your snacks sometime?" I offered cheerfully. "The other kids make fun of me because they think my power is stupid," she replied bluntly. "They think all I'm good for is being a fat laughingstock for them to mock while they have all of their fun walking through walls, or whatever." She finally looked up and made eye contact for a moment. "They definitely don't deserve free refills." "Not everyone is going to see how special you are on the inside Angela," I said, reaching for something to console her misery. "Sometimes people like you and I have to work extra hard to show people on the outside what we have inside of us." She looked at me quizzically at asked, "What do you mean people like us?" "Well, my power is seeing people's feelings. Empathy is what it's called. Believe it or not, I got picked on quite a bit at school, too," I explained as I started to clean the crumbs and other mess off the table. "I felt other people's emotions so intensely I had to wear special headgear until I was 19 years old. They called me Space Girl." Angela spit out some of her soda on her chin laughing at this. "Space Girl, really? But you're so pretty now. I'll never be pretty like you, Ms. Fitzgerald. "But don't you understand? You are pretty, Angela. I can see what's inside people, and I know that you have a good heart. If you shared it with other people sometime, you might like how it feel," I said giving her a light pat on the shoulder instead of a hug. I could tell that Angela was very picky about being touched, another one of my gifts. "Just give it some thought. That was on April 11, 2063. You might remember that day as the day the Liberation Army Super Humans attacked the school to protest in the Fertilization Act. Over 300 lives were lost that day in the attack. I was injured myself that day. While trying to protect the students, one of the attackers hit me with some kind of death ray. I was watching my skin wrinkle and wither. Blood was oozing from my orifices and my fingernails fell off. I went blind and collapsed. When I opened my eyes, Angela was there sitting over me. article: I was six when I first realized that I could see the knot in people, black and twisted and hanging there in the middle of their stomach. I didn't know what it meant or why it was there, but I knew it wasn't something that other people could see. As I grew older, the knot in people became more pronounced and hard to ignore. It seemed to be tied to their emotions - the more stressed or upset someone was, the more tightly the knot twisted and turned. I soon learned that the knot in people was a physical manifestation of their emotional pain and trauma. It was a burden that they carried with them, sometimes for years or even their entire lives. But as much as I wanted to help, I didn't know how to untie the knots or relieve the pain. It wasn't until I met a wise old woman who told me about the power of empathy and compassion that I began to understand how I could use my gift to help others. By listening to people and recognizing their pain, I could offer them comfort and support. Sometimes that was all they needed to begin to release the knots that were holding them back. Now, as a counselor and therapist, I use my unique ability to see the knots in people to guide them towards healing and self-discovery. The knots may never fully disappear, but with understanding and support, people can learn to manage them and take control of their lives once again.

article: The line was never flat. It may have stuttered before, but for the first time, green against black, the line was flat. Pauline had heard of death, but there was something so archaic about it..... it never crossed her mind, the fact that an existence could be ephemeral. This world had never known of a life ending, only humans did, and for god's sake, we aren't humans. There was always a comfort in immortality. Being born without consequences. Pauline was still young, 86. A nurse. Sickness in this world was just discomfort. No one likes a stuffy nose or a broken arm. She had seen only a fraction of what this world had to offer, yet felt as though she had seen it all. In this world so similar to what Earth once was, her days began to melt into one. Rising with the Sun, sleeping only after her children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren were fed. She jumped from cliffs, planes. Tried drugs. Like everyone did. She had made mistakes. Loved. Lost. But she always found herself new friends..... new lovers. Like everyone had. She had traveled to the shells of old civilisations, great and powerful, reduced to only dust. Being at the hospital when the first one passed, she did not sleep that evening. She wondered only one thing. Without an end, is there a beginning?

article: What do you want with it alive? That was the question he should have asked. These kinds of curiosities do no good to the dead. Only makes them restless. The knight wondered in the dark on the dry cavern floor. What was to be done with the menace, the leviathan, once it was chained? He tried to remember what the man had looked like, the man who had placed the parchment on the town's square, the man who wanted a very special bounty. He thought for a while, in the growing heat - the man wore a cloak, had mysterious shifting eyes, and spoke in a low mumbling voice. That can't be it. That couldn't be all he remembered. He wracked his brain, his brow sweating. The man's voice was always calm, confident. Not like the other kinds of men who traded bounties, the boisterous and weighty voices attached to armour and steel. He remembered the awe the man inspired - in him, in the others who he had come across. His back ached, his strength sapped by each throb in his spine. He distracted himself. The man was rich. A king from a foreign land? Or an exiled prince or some sort of regality. Someone desiring a pet? No, too simple - the men of such reverence and wealth owe more to a cause. Perhaps to study the creature? Maybe the man desired a living weapon? In which case, why, wouldn't the man who tamed such a beast be more formidable than the beast itself? As the cavern walls shook, the knight gazed around in the dim. Don't dwell. He sighed, now knowing the regret in his hubris and cockiness. Who was he to question the motives of such a man? He'd thought, perhaps he would be granted an answer when he brought the blasted thing back - perhaps then he'd deserve to know. Deserve to see. Maybe it was as simple as a man wanting to experience a fresh, exotic delicacy; or a complicated urge, both cheap and expensive, fulfilled; or even the unique honour of killing the subdued thing himself. What was his game? A thousand feet from his sword, his shield splintered and ashen, his body nearly broken and quite definitely bruised. The knight turned from behind the rock, towards the sound of approaching footsteps. One-two. One-two. Front legs, then back. Quickening. No more than a few gigantic steps away now. As he braced for the inevitable, the impact, a crash upon his body - he tried to recollect anything else about the man, anything that might have given away his intentions. There was a gust of wind and an eerie stillness. Silence. He turned once more and saw nothing before him on the cavern floor. Then, the shadow from above caught his eye. The shadow of the beast. And as it roared and fell towards the cavern floor, the knight gave up on the riddle, his mind blank as the memories faded through his consciousness. With a deafening THUD, he would never know.

article: "Tell me a secret." Yup, there it is. Everybody knows that question. A woman went free last year, the only one who had ever escaped his clutches. She told us. "He said to tell him a secret, and if he did I could go." The world asked what she told him. She answered, "He said if I told anybody else it wouldn't be a secret anymore." "Well? TELL ME A SECRET!" He has a knife and he's getting a little crazy with it. I'm tied to a chair, but armed to the teeth with exactly what will stop him. I have my secret, and it's going to tear him apart. "I know what she told you." He stops. He turns. "The little bitch talked? But that was OUR SECRET! I'll hunt her for this, I'll have her back and I'll have her guts and I'll have her head and I'll..... I'll..... AAAAAAAARRRRGH." He brutally slaughters a pillow on the couch under the window. It looks like the couch has seen his knife many times as well. I think he has some issues. "No, she didn't tell a soul. But that doesn't mean I don't know her secret." "HOW COULD YOU KNOW? It's a secret, that's how they work, EVERYBODY KNOWS THAT NOBODY KNOWS!" This guy and his fucking wordplay. It's like a middle school child writing poetry. "That's my secret." "That you know?" "How I know." "Would you tell it to spare your life?" "I'd tell it to end yours." "HA! Like I haven't heard threats!" "But you have heard secrets, and I've got one for you. Actually, I have four." I toss the handcuffs at his feet and stand up. "Secret number one: my father was a stage magician. Secret number two: I hunted you. I found out who you were and I turned myself into the perfect victim just for you, so you'd bring me here." He's looking a bit flustered now. Good. Ah, there it is - he rushes me with a yell. I sidestep, block his wild (but telegraphed) swipe with the knife, twist his wrist until he drops the knife, then drop him onto the floor where I deliver a good hard kick to the face. He recoils in pain and blood spurts over the floor - I've broken his nose. I kick the knife away from him and put myself between it and him. "Secret number three: the woman that got away was my mother. And her secret? She could tell truths, as a soothsayer does. But do you know what her DOUBLE secret was? She couldn't. She did cold reading on you - read clues about you, made inferences, wide vague statements that you reacted to that let her narrow in on the facts she needed. I learned sleight of hand and a little bit of martial arts from my father, she picked up on the psychology of it all very well. Plus, she could really pull off the'sawed in half assistant' trick." "Ad youb hebe to kiw me becaud I took you bub?" The broken nose makes it hard to understand, but I get the message. "No, she got away clean. We needed to research you, after all, and she took a calculated risk. I didn't want her to do so, but we needed to know what kind of handcuffs you used so I could get the right key. Now, secret number four: your third victim was my father." It won't bring back my father, but the look of fear in his eyes as I wrapped my hands around his throat will give me comfort until my dying day.

article: I was wearing that damn T-shirt that mum hated so much, which of course made me love it all the more. Across the front was what had always claimed was a photograph of an aborted baby, but even back then I knew it was just random red splotches with the words " FUCK YOUR LIFE " across it. It was strange seeing myself from the outside, like watching a home movie or an old photograph, but real and in 3D, right in front of me. I remembered this day from the other side as well, this office, an old man standing behind the desk, but of course this time the man would be different, this time I would be seeing myself. " Come in Peter, I'm Dr Phillips, take a seat anywhere. " I saw that immediate snarl of hostility that I had spent weeks perfecting in front of the mirror and my younger self flopped into the chair nearest the door. Interesting, I had originally chosen the chair nearest the desk as I had wanted to show the therapist I wasn't scared of him - already it seemed there were changes from the original timeline, I wondered how far they would go. My younger self was scowling and picking at the nail varnish that was flaking off. Just one of the many ways I was trying to make myself stand out, to hide from my old self. I knew the anger and resentment that the child was feeling - betrayed and sent to a therapist by a mother who din't understand, didn't seem to care what would happen to them, or what had already happened. This was the moment I had come back for, that I had chosen this moment for. Changes to the timeline were possible, but they had to be well timed, or it had a habit of mending itself, somehow finding its way back to its original configuration. The future somehow made its way along, but some changes could still ripple through and I couldn't risk not existing, that's why it had to be now and not three months ago. I moved from behind the table and walked over. " Your mother is worried about you Peter. She sees you retreating from your family and friends, growing hostile and angry. " He, I, sneered. " It's just me man, I do what want. " He looked away, not making eye contact. " Bullshit. " I smiled at the way his head snapped around. " You put this persona on as it made it easier to cope. " His mouth opened and closed a few times before he was able to weakly reply. " I... I don't know what you mean. " Now he just looked weak, like the child he was. " Peter, there is something you have to see. " He looked at me as if I was insane. " Trust me Peter, I know about what happened three months ago and I want to help. " He was unable to reply and all his bravado was gone and confused. I opened the door and he followed me, keeping enough distance between us to run. I led him out of the office, down the corridor and into a second office that I had rented, along with every other room on the floor above and below. He paused at the outer door and I moved on in and opened the inner door, flicking on the light. The walls were coated in plastic and the windows were covered to keep out any light or stop anyone seeing in. There was only a chair and strapped to the chair a figure. I heard Peter gasp and I looked back. He walked forward, looking dazed and at last looked at me. " Why do you have my step dad here? " I smiled. " You know why he's here and I know what he did to you. " I gestured into the room - he was tied securely to the chair, tape around his moth and eyes. " Do what you want Peter, but leave your anger in the room. When you're done I have a change of clothes for you. " I gestured to some clothes in the outer room. He looked again. " I don't... I don't understand. " I crouched a little to his level, it would be another six months before he put on our last few inches of height. " He will never be punished if he isn't today. I'll deal with whatever you leave in that room, this is your only chance to get even. " He looked again, seeing the knives and baseball bat leaning against the wall and slowly walked in and pushed the door shut behind him. A few moments passed and a muffled scream started that didn't stop. Slowly I began to feel a felt a sense of closure and I knew that the boy who came out would be able to live a life better than mine. He would be a better me.

article: The world has changed, and I with it. nbsp; No one knows exactly when it started, but somehow we've finally noticed it. I guess we kind of found out after several killers managed to live way past a normal person's lifespan. When you kill someone, you can get the rest of lifespan. You know how they started raising cattle in those large pens thousands at a time? It's like that, except with children. Before this got out, in the rich countries, a lot of wealthy people started adopting. At first, we all thought it was great. All these wealthy people, adopting those poor orphaned children. I guess there are some things you're better off not knowing. I'm not young anymore. I guess I'm glad I found out only after my spouse passed on. If I had known before, I probably would have joined the others, purchasing healthy little children as sacrifices. Now I'm just waiting until I can pass on into the next life. Life's too painful all alone. I remember a time when children would run up to their grandparents, eyes filled with life and joy. Since the news came out, I haven't seen any sign of my grandchildren. I don't blame my kids, I guess. Better safe then sorry. Actually, maybe the ones I should be worrying about would be my children. They wouldn't..... would they? No, I'm sure they're fine. My kids have at least been sending pictures. Children sure grow up fast. I miss those old days. Just about anyone could be a murderer these days. Who wouldn't want to live forever? The politicians and almost all of the wealthy are doing it. I remember when things were different, when children weren't just a commodity. It's legal now, to kill a child without a guardian. After so many millennia, we've finally created a world without orphans. I just wish it wasn't this way. A specific type of slavery is legal again. I kept up with new laws and bills because I expected this. The media never covered it, of course. Every country has always had sex slaves. We all knew about them, but most of us turned a blind eye. Rumor has it, that industry has been integrated into the current one. It's a way to make sure there's a steady supply of children. Childbirth takes a toll on a woman, there's a limit to how many times one would be willing to have kids, and sex sells. Two birds with one stone. I wish it was nothing but a rumor. A lot of young healthy people have just disappeared around the world. It started becoming way more common once the laws for mandatory DNA and genetic exams were passed. A lot of young talent has also appeared in their place in the governments too. There's a lot of government funded Eugenic programs, the kind that encourages selective breeding. At least, that's what their site says. But we all know it isn't just selective breeding. There's culling too. Money has always been power, I guess it's obvious in this world. How else would it be legal to raise children in big, nice-looking facilities just to buy them and slaughter them for their lifespan? Oh, the kids are well cared for, at least physically. I don't doubt that. I've toured one of those facilities. Really nice big building, refreshing and peaceful. It's filled with toys and games and places for kids to play. There's plenty of sun and grass, and the food is top class and nutritious. The health and safety standards there are ridiculously strict. The children there are lively and active. None of them have much more than a basic education. Most of them won't need it. If they show they're really talented though, they have a chance to get out and be truly adopted. Everything that enters the place is carefully evaluated before the kids can get it. The news they see is heavily regulated. Reels of children being adopted, some of them kids they knew. Professional actors or people who have been evaluated are allowed to "adopt" children. It's mandatory when purchasing from the better facilities, for them to keep the kid alive for one year and treat them nice, so the others won't catch on. Fake letters are sent back to the kids, with some candies and treats, telling them about how wonderful it is. Those kids in there were so innocent. None of them knew the truth. I had to excuse myself several times. I got some hard looks from the caretakers when I came back with slightly red swollen eyes, but I'd spent a big chunk of my savings to see this. The amount I had spent would have been enough to buy ten children, so they let me continue. I've written everything down. I wanted to publish it, but..... no one cares. The ones who have the power to change things want to live forever. The ones who want change have been suppressed by fear. The most prominent public speaker for this cause was assassinated and his reputation was thoroughly soiled with what I'm sure was false evidence. It's going to be decades before this is undone again. Maybe it'll be centuries, or millennia to come. Maybe things will stay this way forever. I remember a time, where young people could help old people with no fear. I remember when children could play on the streets and visit their grandparents. The children in the facilities live much better lives then the children now. Most kids are home-schooled now. For some, it's a way to protect their children, for others..... Abortions have gone way down now. Some people have even made it out to be a work of God. The irony is lost on them. Sacrificing babies used to be a devil worshiper thing. The economy is going strong. Young men can't have children. Their only value is genetic diversity, to help avoid too much inbreeding. Women though, post-pubescent and pre-menopausal women are valuable. They're a protected class. If a girl survives to have her first period, she's usually safe. After all it would be bad if the world's supply of children ran out. Some days I'm glad I'm old, at least I don't have much to fear. I'm old enough I only have to see this for a couple more years, and then this nightmare ends. Those young people, their lives are only beginning, and it might end any day because of someone looking to live longer. Some days I wish I was younger. I dream of the things I could do when I was young. Maybe if I had taken a different path, I'd have a power to turn things around. Either way, it's wishful thinking. I'm just an old person on my deathbed, still dreaming of a better world, a beautiful world.

article: I watched as the Malvox emperor, along with his six generals walked towards me and my alien translator. About 300 yards behind the emperor, were around a quarter of a million Malvox soldiers marching in formation. The air was tense as they stopped about ten yards away from us, and the emperor spoke with a low, rumbling voice that seemed to shake the ground beneath our feet. "Greetings, humans. I am Emperor Zelg, ruler of the Malvox empire. You have trespassed on our territory and violated our laws. Explain your purpose here, or face the consequences." I translated the emperor's words to my human companions and they looked nervous. I tried to calm them down by whispering that I had a plan. "Your highness, we come in peace. We are explorers from Earth, seeking to learn about other planets and civilizations. We apologize if we have unknowingly crossed into your territory, and we would be honored to learn more about the Malvox empire." The emperor raised an eyebrow, clearly surprised by our response. "You humans are unlike any other species we have encountered. Your boldness and willingness to speak to us with respect is appreciated. However, I am not easily convinced. What evidence do you have to support your claims?" I hesitated for a moment, then remembered the small device in my pocket. It was a gift from our alien allies, a universal language translator that could detect and translate any language in the universe. I took it out and approached the emperor, holding it out for him to see. "Your highness, this is a device that can translate any language in the universe. It was given to us by our alien allies, who have helped us explore many worlds. We hope that this device can help us communicate with you and learn about your culture and civilization." The emperor took the device and examined it closely, his eyes flashing with curiosity. After a moment, he nodded and handed it back to me. "You have piqued my interest, humans. I will allow you to stay for a brief time, under the condition that you respect our laws and customs. You will be closely monitored, and any violation of our laws will result in severe consequences. Am I understood?" We all nodded, relieved that we had not been attacked or imprisoned. The emperor signaled to his soldiers, who stood at attention as he turned and walked away. We followed, eager to see what the Malvox empire had to offer.

article: "Let's see here........ Enkenberg The Brave? How did you earn that honorific?" The old man leaned back in his chair while raising his eyes off my resume and onto me. Wizarding had changed since I first began 1000 years ago. Now every thing was about business and was handled from office buildings. When I first started we were conjuring spirits and brewing potions in log cabins! Now we have to live along in secrecy with the humans since there are so few of us in comparison. I leaned forward in my chair, my suit was bunching up. "Well in the year 1666 I worked directly under Grandmaster Pyromancer Jean-Paul the Second in England. When he attempted to turn to necromancy during the plague as you probably already know, the other apprentices and I brought him and his undead legion down. The European Wizarding Society awarded us with those honorifics." The old man leaned back in his chair even further, I didn't think that was possible. Suddenly he snapped forward and replied "Well that's very impressive Enkenberg. Really, I had no idea we had such an important wizard in our midst! However, you understand this is an entry level position as a Novice Sorcerer?" "I understand sir." I spoke bluntly. "Well then you also understand the job listing required 2000-3000 years of wizarding experience for this position? I'm sorry Enkenberg, you're just not qualified." I stood up, "but I've studied under the greatest masters for 1000 years! I've conjured countless new daemons, intricate spells and medicinal potions!" "Yes but we need actual work experience here. Even your past 1000 years don't really count. Have a nice day and thank you for coming in." I work at Starbucks now.

article: 30 Years ago, I had left the tribe I was now about to see again. Isolated in the depths of the jungle, which was becoming smaller every week, they were unique in many ways. They valued intelligence more than strength and had their own little strategy game - a mixture of go and mancala. Their heroes were the ones who could get lots of food for the tribe while barely lifting a finger. They did not value technology much - only had a shrug when I showed them a knife, explained guns to them, or such. But when I taught a few of them how to read and write, they got much more interested - though mostly in things concerning biology, chemistry, and such. They were really clever - quickly managed to produce their own soap after reading about it in one of the books I brought along with me. And after the first such successes, everyone wanted to learn to read, and everyone tried out everything in the books, often with funny, and sometimes with scary results. But they quickly learned to be careful when things became dangerous. I left the tribe once every week or so, and brought more and more books - all areas of science, at first simple books like encyclopedias and school books, in the end the most prestigious affordable scientific literature. When I went back home, I made sure they'd get the most important published papers - in full detail, as I knew they were already past the pop-stuff. For a few years, I received a letter every once in a while from one of the kids I taught how to read and write, with funny stories of their newest exploits. Later, when she married, the letters became less, and more about herself, her feelings, and her relations. She mentioned how grateful everyone was for the books and journals. Not much more. Now that I was a pensioner, I wanted to see what had become of them. So I traveled to them. I was greeted with a lot of laughter and friendliness. There were some comments how much I had changed, which sounded strange, but I couldn't really sort them in. The kids I had taught how to read and write were now grown ups - but looked more like 20-somethings than the around 40 year olds they should be. There were a lot of others I didn't recognise at first - all of them looked as if they were 20-somethings, except the kids and youth. They still despised technology to some degree - living in simple but now very big huts. They also showed me the labs each of them had. Some of them in tents inside their huts, apparently to keep them clean. I didn't know what they did in those labs - they were not fooling around and showing off like they did when I left. Nor was it a big thing for them to talk about. Only when I recognised one of the strangers did it occur to me: the woman, a mother of two of the children I taught, and who I had liked a lot back then, had not changed the slightest bit. I looked her up on my computer, where I had stored digitised copies of the photos I had made back then. I showed her the picture. I asked her whether it was her mother, not wanting to believe what I saw with my own eyes. Until I realised it was undeniably the same person. Relationships were in flux in this tribe. And so she stayed with me. But when I wanted to kiss her on the evening of the second day, she held me back. She led me to a section in a large tent in one of the larger huts which looked like an operating room. She asked me to lie down. They gave me something which made me fall asleep. The next day, when I woke up, I felt really good - full of energy, like after a really good night's rest when I was 20 years younger. I couldn't see much of a difference in my body, except that my skin seemed to be a little tighter, and some scratches and other blemishes had gotten less. I asked what had happened, and they were astonished that I was unaware. Didn't I send them all the books with all the knowledge which they applied? Over the next few days, my skin got elastic again, my eyesight and hearing went back to what they were in earlier times, and even my brain felt quicker. And then the shocking parts began: I could hear distant people talk when I paid attention, feeling my ears move a little to focus the sound into my hearing channel. I could make out leafs on trees in distant mountains when the weather was clear. I somehow knew which direction was north at any time. And when a fog came, I knew exactly which direction the sun was - because I could see the polarisation of the light. Every day, I discovered new abilities within me. It was like finding out how to move a muscle you never knew you could control. Or like seeing color for the first time. A small black dot formed on my forehead - I had barely noticed it on the darker skin of the tribe. And thought it was an ornamentation. But it enabled me to see longer electromagnetic waves - turning the milky way into a bright spectacle, making the far away cities look like fountains of light when watching them from a mountain, and making my phone glow with every call I made when I was near a cell tower - the closest of which was a day's journey from the tribe. It also gave all the humans a little glow from their heat. Then, when my body looked barely 30 years old, the skin modifications which I had seen on the tribespeople, stripes on the chest, appeared on my body, too. Everyone was happy seeing them, while I was puzzled what they would be good for. Eventually, some kids of the tribe led me to a nearby lake. They told me to dive, some of them leading the way. When I was under water, I realised I could hold my breath longer than expected. And when the oxygen level went down enough that I thought I should get up again, the stripes on my chest opened up and started filtering water! I could move my lungs, and felt that I had something like a water sack between the lungs and the ribs, filtering oxygen out of the water. Then one of them spoke. While under water. His speaking sounded different, but was understandable. It wasn't caused by air moving out of the lungs, but by a new muscle close to the voice cords, which would vibrate against the water like a speaker against the air. And I could do it, too! - after some trying. They had houses in the lake. Their tribe was at least twice as big as I thought. The lake also had a very deep cave, which apparently was a mine providing a few useful minerals. An underwater river connected the cave to another lake further up a nearby group of hills - which was also the reason why there was always enough oxygen in the lake. A feat of brilliant natural re-engineering, as I was told right then. I thought about what would happen if anyone found out about all their achievements...

article: Creak creak creak. The hinges needed oiling badly. He winced slightly at the noise as he pushed the old swing. The wind blew softly, tousling the grass and sending a shiver down his spine. He sighed, forgot his coat again. "Hey sport, you remember the first day I brought you here? " , He continued pushing as a slow smiled crossed his face. "You spent hours upon hours running up and down the hills. They hadn't installed the playground back then but you didn't care. I remember spinning you around, playing hide and seek in the bushes, one time we even brought water guns." He sniffed a little, still pushing the swing. The cold was getting to him. "Of course, once they installed the playground we spent even more time here. You played with other children then, growing up with others your own age." His hands shook. Hands that were once robust now hung weakly. The skin that was once ruddy and rough with callouses now were mottled with age. Yet he still continued to push. "You grew up so fast, but I couldn't stay. Do you remember the words I said to you in middle school? I promised you I'd be around. I told you that no matter what happened to our family, I would be there in your heart, "He looked down at his feet, "Yet I broke that promised didn't I?" Eyes that once twinkled with their own youthful sparkle watered with tears that refused to fall. "I'm sorry. I'm so sorry for disappearing out of your life." "Dad, what are you doing there without your coat? Its getting chilly." "Eh? Really?" She smiled lovingly and took his hand, "Come on, lets go home." The two walked slowly away, leaving an empty swing to swing in the evening breeze.

article: The children's faces lit up when they finally saw it. The sun danced off its crimson-brown scales, slowly revealing its full frame as it emerged from the darkness. The cave opening was etched into the side of a towering man-made granite wall, which reached all the way to the electrified wire-roof, sealing the pen. A thick layer of enforced glass separated the spectators from the creature. The children in the group pressed their faces up against the glass to try get closer view. Their excitement used to delight Ben, but not anymore. Now he couldn't help but feel for the Attraction. "Her name is Sherin," Ben announced to the spectators. "She's 133 years old." Ben knew Sherin for eleven of her years. However, she had been in the park for more than double that. He remembered the day he was hired as a dragon-keeper. He had no experience, and the education was limited, at best. But even if the education was more thorough, he wouldn't have listened. He was a different person back then: he was just a boy. He was just like these wide-eyed kids who he observed with unfair disdain every day, their sticky candy-coated fingers staining the thick enclosure glass. Just like them, he wasn't aware of this noble creature's realty. It's not their fault. They're only kids - they don't know any better. How could they? He recalled one piece of advice given in training by a senior supervisor: distance yourself. It's the one piece of advice he should've taken seriously. ' Treat this like your regular 9 to 5 '. That's what that bastard said. How could I treat this like a regular job? It's not. These creatures aren't wild turkeys. They're more human than most of my friends for god sake. And they're captives. Plain and simple. They're captives and I'm their gaoler. I try be a friendly and caring gaoler, sure. But my presence exists to control them. " Why isn't it flying mister? " one of the children shouted. " She may be tired, " Ben lied. That answer was always different. I hate lying, but I have to. Not just to save others from the truth, but because deceit in ingrained in this job. I'm not permitted to tell outsiders how she has gradually lost her ability to fly since she's been cooped up in this pen. Not that I would want to explain that. It breaks my heart. And why do I stay? Because she likes me. Don't ask me why. I'm a cog in this damn machine. But I sense her relief when I'm around, and I like being around her. If I leave, who knows who will be put in charge. I no longer trust people, not after what I've seen here. Ben walked closer to the enclosure. He took out rag cloth and glass cleaner and scrubbed the candy residue from the glass. The children were now talking amongst themselves, losing interest in the dragon who was lying still with her face almost covered by her wing. " OK, kids, " Ben said, trying to sound enthusiastic. " It's time to see Barone. The male dragon. " " Is it even bigger? " asked one of the shortest children of the bunch. " A lot bigger, " Ben replied. " And does this one like to fly? " Ben swallowed deeply. " Not today. "

article: A rainbow snow of pixels pulsed across my monitors, tone-shifting and obscuring the paper I was grading until it faded away like droplets three seconds later. For a few moments I was transfixed, as if the unfamiliar pattern the pixels rippled was more than noise. As the last fluctuations collapsed toward single pixels and off of my screen I sighed. "Chris," I shouted across the room to one of my grad students, "any idea what would cause a monitor suddenly tone-shift what I'm working on?" He looked up from the lab table he was working atop with a small pressure chamber and its connected laptop. "You too, professor? I just had something like that on this screen as well." He glanced at the monitor on my desk the only desk in the room. His pupils narrowed and surely lost focus as he looked past me and my computer in thought. "Chris?" I'd thought this had more to do with his electrical and hardware field than my materials science, but he was surprisingly unresponsive. "If you had the issue as well, it would make sense for it to be a network issue but it looked more like fingers pressing on an LCD." He turned his stool toward me with a troubled look on his face. "But it went away real fast. Maybe there was an EM pulse?" I shrugged and calmed down. Somehow I'd gotten agitated by the screen without noticing my emotion. Seeing my student troubled, my role of mentoring and providing a calm sounding board took precedence over phantom anxieties. Gently, I probed his response. "Did this look like an EMP wave?" I assumed not. "No, ma'am. I've seen electromagnetic fields cause a sort of shaky image or normal snow but this was made of moving points. At a field strength enough to have pixels magnetize into weird patterns the monitors should have lost signal." I was by now turned away from my screen and had rolled the deskchair toward the open tile to show Chris he had my full attention. "So," I began slowly, "what does that leave us?" He began to list off possibilities as he rested his tilted head into an open palm. "A virus that causes a specific pattern without other issues unlikely, if this was a pressure change in the room we would have felt it, and I can't think of something magnetic or electrical that fits. It was like an invisible swarm of bugs pressing on the screen with their footsteps." "But if it wasn't air pressure and not a magnetic wave then that leaves a network issue," I concluded. "So someone maybe hacked the campus just to play a pattern over the monitors?" He seemed content with that. "I'll check the resource use then. This sort of complex look would put at least minor strain on the CPU or GPU." "No luck." Chris turned back toward me. "Resource Monitor doesn't show any weird spikes or processes. I guess that's fine since we don't have to notify site security but it doesn't solve the puzzle." Damn. I cursed in my mind that I'd have to leave this alone. "Is your experiment still fine, by the way?" If the same thing that affected the monitors affected the apparatus then Chris could need to replace the sample. Our hope was that by stretching the alloy by reducing ambient pressure it would permanently lose some bonds and form certain patterns. The smaller the scale these patterns could be made regular, the more useful this material would be in future computer chips. It was standard Materials Science work, but any shock to the apparatus could ruin it. He was silent a long while. "Actually, no. Around when the thing happened to the monitors, there was a sensor glitch and afterwards they're contradicting." "As in the sensors need to be fixed?" I had gotten up and started walking toward Chris and the experiment. "Or the sample is doing something weird?" He looked stumped as he checked over the instruments so I took one of the thermal cameras from a cabinet. His experiment was relatively stable temperature so it hadn't needed any of the cameras, which would view hot areas as blooms of red and white against the purple and black of cool objects. I turned the camera on and it seemed to boot just fine. The objects in the room were a standard blue cloud. As soon as it was responsive I began narrowing its range of sensitivity by swapping its lens and settings. When I pointed it into the experiment, something was very wrong. The alloy pulsed with colors somewhat like my monitor had. "Chris," I tapped him on the shoulder and passed the camera over. "Your sensors are probably fine." He tilted his head into the camera rather than hold it in front of himself, probably to keep the image on the screen visible to me. "Ma'am, what the hell is this? Temperature spikes? But there should only be under a watt of electricity running through it right now." As the screen on Chris' laptop once more pulsed and sparkled with the strange snowlike patterns, I shrugged. My heart was beating fast and I knew I should be excited, but an unscientific part of my mind was wary and even afraid. At least in the room I was in, physics had begun to break down. Slowly the pulses across screens as well as the background interference that showed on our sample would become more common. Eventually these deviations from order began to form heartbeats.
label: human

article: As I walked hand-in-hand with my husband and wife team, I spotted the bottle washing ashore. "Hang on," I said to my friends. "That looks like it could be worth something." As I skipped over to the bottle, a creeping sense of unease came over me; the hairs on the back of my neck rose like they were trying to man the lifeboats. Pulling out the cork of the bottle, I noticed the year imprint on the bottom of the bottle: 1914. The letter popped out with no help when I tipped the bottle. Breaking the seal on the letter, I unrolled it, reading the letter. Dear Hanna, If you are reading this, then I have failed. We are cursed, and soon it will pass to you. It is matrilineal, meaning it is passed on through the females of the line. Soon, you will be able to see things no other person will see. You will know when some things will come to pass. I wanted to save you in particular because of the pain this journey will cause. Leave your lovers, Karis and Alberto. Go west, to Waikiki and stay there for three years. If you do not, you will end up in a sanatorium, broken and meandering, when the world needs you. I will do my best to prepare you. In the attic of your mother's home, you will find an old trunk. Once you have left your lovers, you MUST retrive this and go. Supplies will be included, although you will need to go to a pawnbrokers first. May God and Lucifer have mercy on your soul, Angelou Maria de Cervantes, Cursed Contessa On the thirteenth day of the fifth month in the year of our Lord 1914. Heart pounding, I picked the bottle up and walked back to my lovers. I showed them the letter, but I saw..... something. A shadow rising beyond them, in the form of a slim man with greying hair at his temples, glasses and a pinstripe suit.

article: Old age caught up on Jimmy Santry like an Olympic runner. He always felt he was unstoppable. His health, he thought would give him immortality. He strode towards his well lit bathroom mirror. The rumble in his lungs was forming. It never amazed Jimmy that spiders, long legged daddy's, and ants would creep around his sanctuary of cleanliness. Often enough, he would flick them off his face, shoulder or naked chest. Jimmy loved company. On closer inspection of his wrinkling face, he spotted pussy spots. A man of his age reimagining puberty, 60 years on. Popping puss never felt so gratifying. The yellow, infused with red wine blood struck the reflective mirror. A wipe of his finger always did the trick. Tasty too. The rumble was raging more viciously now. He erupted a fit of phlegm and blood into the sink. Old Jimmy never let his bodily fluids go to waste. It was feeding time.

article: I didn't think twice when the newbie asked me. "Single workaholic with a sleep disorder? I mean, this has to be a mistake!" I sighed, more loudly than necessary. I was actually mildly annoyed. I would take no pleasure in leaving my current post - a pair of uncommonly gentle 4-year old twins. Every morning I chose a different Disney classic and they crowed in delight so genuine that I couldn't help but mourn their coming loss of innocence. Adult humans can't help but let their narcissism suck all the joy out of waking. For the most part though, I relished my role as the veteran. The most experienced and accomplished among us and yet I hadn't been put out to pasture like so many before me. They called me in when the rookies, with all their internet-age bells and whistles, got scared off by an actual challenge. Do you know what it's like to wake someone up who's on Ambien? How about a sleepwalker? When the fancy, Sharper Image clocks burned out, I came to the rescue. And I didn't leave until the job was done. There was no client whose sleep habits I couldn't stabilize. So when the infant with 25 different varieties of ocean sounds whined to me, I knew what my answer was. But that didn't mean I wouldn't make him sweat. "How do you expect us to compete with smart phones if you can not wake up one 37-year-old insomniac? I can send you back to bootcamp anytime..." Every wire within me stiffens as I hear her groan from down the hall. She's in a bad mood. Thud...... thud..... THUD..... I feel weak. The orange light from my digital display starts to flicker. Damn it, man - nut up! If she thinks for a second that there's a reason too, she'll take pleasure in snapping me in half before she tosses me in the dumpster. In three months I have gone from the best in my fleet to near-defector. Duty. It used to define me. Now I'm terrified that it will chain me to this lunatic just long enough to kill me. Creak. The door swings open. She's wasted. I flee to a higher plane of consciousness, focus on staying entirely still. But I can't help but watch. She's a reedy woman and her spindly legs stab at the ground awkwardly as she struggles to remove her underwear. As she collapses to the ground, the hardwood vibrates. She pulls a flip cell phone from a balled-up pair of corduroys, then digs deeper and retrieves half of a cigarette. One shaky hand struggles with a lighter as the other snaps the phone open. She sucks in deeply on the lit cigarette and her eyes widen. Shit. It must be the ex. A sinewy arm rockets up and out. The phone shatters against the wall but all I can hear is an all-consuming shriek that expands until it fills the room. The last time that her ex came over, I didn't know better than to take pity on her. I lulled her to sleep with melancholic classics then filled her dreams with soulful heroines who belted their vengeance. Aretha. Beyonce. Somehow I still believed that with a few well-chosen anthems I could re-wire her sense of self. But halfway through my favorite Ella Fitzgerald she woke up in a rage. She battered me until I knew I must be gone, circuits smashed and dying out. But then, a sound. The final notes of the song that I used to love, warbling through my half-crushed speaker. Something died within me that night. I still do the dance every night, switching between soft orchestral movements, meandering smooth jazz, shitty poprock. I do whatever I can to keep her asleep and relatively calm. In the morning I wake her gently. Try to read her every whim. But 8 out of 10 days, I have barely lulled her from sleep when she assaults me into a half-conscious silence. - She's in bed now and a waft of cigarette smoke invades every crevice in my plastic shell. She turns a glassy glare at my display. She's angrily stabbing at the buttons on either side of me. There's no need, the default alarm is set, but, even in an alcoholic stupor, her neuroses know with certainty that I'm not fit for duty. I used to be insulted. Now I can't seem to care about anything but survival. She's shifting my dials somewhere new, her stubby fingers roughly gripping me as I struggle to keep the sound quality clear. Suddenly she stops. Wait, why are we in AM? She never listens to AM..... "Ruuuuushh...." the first word that I can make out is elongated in an obnoxious tone that can only mean one thing - shitty talk radio. Oh no. This is too much. I'm a union man. If there's one thing worse than being tortured by your worst enemy, it's being forced to listen to that worst enemy affirm Rush Limbaugh's rantings while she does it. Any dedication to duty evaporates in that instant. I focus all my attention on holding in every ounce of energy for one second, then two, until 10 seconds have passed and she notices Rush's cackle fading away. "Piece of shit!!!!" She lunges, her glass of gin spilling from her hands, and in that instant I unleash every electron in a vengeful spark that flares up wider than I'd dreamed possible. In one beautiful flash I see her eyes widen in horror as her body seizes in electrical shock. I'm fading fast now, barely aware, but not until she collapses do I give in. Blissfully, the final sparks that fly across my circuits summon this realization - I did my duty. It just wasn't what they said it would be.
label: human

article: It was wet. Everything around her was wet; it wasn't just water it was denser, heavier. She was stuck in a giant sugar-free jello all because she wanted to flee her sorority. This was hour fifteen and her diabetes was starting to make her nauseus. They'd thrown all kinds of things at her- insulted every action she has ever taken. It would all be worth it though- Alpha Gamma Row girls always got their man and their job. Six of the last seven presidents went on to lead a hospital department, make millions and marry a man either running a city or a hedge fund. She would own a portion of the world, if she could just last a little longer. Massie, the president this year, came tumbling down the stairs, "what's up Sugar, how ya doing? Oh, sorry I probably shouldn't mention that word to a diabetic." "I'm good. Four more hours and I'll be good." "We've decided to extend that a bit actually..... and you need to recite a sonnet every hour- see the tv over there? It'll be flashing through a few for you to choose from." She managed it. Somehow she fought through the next six hours without passing out and memorizing the sonnets. She would never enjoy Shakespeare or Jello again but she was a queen in training now. Until the pinning. She still hadn't slept. Jello was unsurprisingly difficult to sleep in. Memorizing the sonnets had taken the last of her soul and when they pinned her, the pick pierced her skin, causing a droplet of blood to soak her dress and take the last bit of sugar with it. Her head smashed into Massie. The hospital room was bright white. Doctors were inspecting every inch of her and an iv was placed in her right arm. "uh..." she moaned. "Ma'am, you..... you're body is completely out of sugar. A normal person would have passed out hours ago but a diabetic..... they should have died. You can't ever dip below 50 on your blood sugar again. Ever. You need to hide away in the desert and simply drink apple juice and eat snickers bar until you recover." She frowned. This wasn't going as planned," the sorority is being sued- the entire sorority. The judge is probably going to rule in your favor," a nice pants suit wearing lady said to her. "You'll be a multi-millionaire if that's any consolation." Smirking, she realized she'd won faster than any other president, she was too good for their sonnets and jello anyway. [ end ]

article: At last the Exile had arrived at his destination, and at once he knew what had beckoned him. Long ago this forsaken ground had been a graveyard for nobles, lords and highborn. It was their guardians. Hunched over the husks of twice-plundered crypts, crouched at the plinths of great headstones time had long since withered down to rubble, the gargoyles possessed a horrific beauty that only a master's talent could make possible. Yes, the bones of monarchs passed lay beneath them in mass, but it was the artisans' souls that were truly entombed here - not within the opulent sepulchers of their thankless patrons but inside the angelic monstrosities these craftsmen had carved with all their hearts' true toil. That toil had preserved them unnaturally through out the ages and it was the same labor of love that now made them so responsive to the Exile's binding touch. Eagerly they sprung to life: shedding petrified skin of stone for leathery sinew and long-passed oaths for duty anew. In stasis they had been beautiful..... alive they were otherworldly. His newly sworn legion swirling around him, the Exile set out on the path from whence he came. A return journey to the enclave that had dared to banish him. article: Dear Amira, It has been a long time since we've talked. Well atleast while I was sober. What has it been 6 years? That time went by so fast and I hardly remember most of it.
