article: Howard Crumlin was hungry from his long days in the lab. His wife, Meribeth, had fallen asleep the night previous sitting at the table reading her latest novel (Howard could never keep up) meaning his usual breakfast and lunch were unprepared in the morning. Howard, not wanting to miss his bus to the labs, grabbed a cucumber on the way out the door. Fortuitous choice, Howard! For, you see, Howard was working at a nano-research facility working on ways to combat oil spills. Howard was designing a new form of nanobot that could dismantle oil spills and debris in swarms. Even more fascinating, he wanted his robots to be able to build more of themselves! This way, only a small number of the delicate machines would need to be machined. The rest, the nanobots themselves would find the parts and construct. However, poor Howard had never read up on ecophagy: "eating the world." Howard didn't realize he would have to carefully monitor his robot's instructions, as leaving room for a misinterpretation of the bot's directives could lead to nanobots endlessly replicating and spreading, consuming their entire environment building more and more of themselves. The world would not go out with a bang, but with a flood of gray goo. Tough luck, Howard! As Howard prepared his latest model for testing, he left a logic loop in the current code's build: his new bot would reproduce, assess if the reproduction was successful, and then loop right back to beginning to reproduce again. Howard, of course, did not know this yet. He simply removed his cucumber to begin eating his tasty lunch as he watched the test unfold. Once he pressed his enter key and initialized the robot's programming, the tiny black dot began to quiver and shake and spread to a small scratchy patch on his work bench. Big trouble, Howard! Howard, unsure of what's going on, tried to disable the program, but the robots would not stop. He stood up and began to frantically look around his desk for a means to stop them when he tipped over the small testing platform. Now, the tiny dot was pulsating on the facility floor! Howard ran off to press the emergency alarm, ready to lock down the facility. However, as Howard ran and papers flew in the breeze and the alarm sirens began to wail, an unlikely hero emerged. Perched atop Howard's desk, and slowly rolling since Howard stood up, a brave cucumber moved forth to challenge this technological menace. With grace, the cucumber slipped off the counter, and began its plunging attack to the technologic black death below. The black spot quivered and pulsed with energy. The cucumber honed in with precision. With a soft splat, Howard turned around to see his lunch on the floor. Alarm sirens continued to blare, and a red lamp flashed in the room. Howard carefully approached the cucumber and gripped it cautiously, between two fingers. Sensing no movement, he lifted the cucumber up. Underneath, mixed with lights amount of cucumber juice, was the squashed remains of thousands of tiny nanobots. It seems their crush-resistant shells weren't quite up to company standards. Howard sighed and let out a shrill laugh. Close one, Howard!

article: "Good Morning!" the teenager yawned, thankfully covering his mouth with his hand. "Can I have a bottle of Coke?" He decided to reply non-committingly. "Yeah, I know what you mean." The teenager grabbed the bottle and scuffled off. God communicated with the rest of trinity instantaneously: "What a degenerate! He didn't even say please!" Jesus was much more mild on the person: "He's tired. Cut him some slack!" "He should have gone to bed earlier!" "He was doing homework. You are omniscient as well but you surely not act on it. He was doing homework which took longer for him because someone gave him dyscalculia." "Are you serious!? You would even find an excuse if Satan himself stood before you!" God grumbled, but decided to let him go for now. A while later, a man in threadbare clothes with dark hair and a graying mustache came to the kiosk. "Marlboro?" he asks. God put a package of the cigarettes on the counter and stated the price. The man put the note and coins on the counter asked: "That?" and upon God's nodding took the smokes. "Okay, Jesus, there is no way you can explain this person's rudeness." God stated angrily to basically himself. "With three words: Tower of Babel. If you talked to him in Kurdish, he'd be the nicest fellow around. But someone reacted disproportionately to a mere building." "Do you have to be such a smartass?" "Comes from being raised in the absence of a biological father." "You're still angry about that? It's been two thousand years." "Maybe eventually I will get an actual apology - and before you try, we are one trinity, so I can feel your intentions." "And you can feel mine, so you know that this was necessary!" "And you are aware that I still think that this plan was hare-brained." "It's too bad that I didn't have a smart guy like you on my side back then." With a screech, the tram came to a halt at the nearby stop. I don't have anyone to play with anymore." Lily nodded sympathetically. "I'm sorry about your dog. But you know, you don't have to have a pet to have fun. Maybe we could play together sometime? I come to this park a lot, and I'm always looking for someone to play with." Emma's face brightened up. "Really? That would be awesome!" They continued to swing and talk, becoming fast friends. article: He strained. His heart drummed insistently in his chest, threatening to burst out and fall into the toilet bowl below him. The bowl was already splattered with what looked like diet raspberry cordial in the dim light. He could taste metal, and ached from throat to waist. This was going to be a long night. A momentary haziness by the bathroom door drew his eyes up. A person faded into being there. It was wearing a trim grey suit - she, he realised. A woman with Latin features in a grey suit and spinning a keychain had just appeared from thin air in his bathroom. He felt he should be surprised. Mind you, on the painkillers he took, not much of anything was surprising. He examined the keychain as it whirled lazily around. In addition to the usual rings was an unusual attachment: a metal handle as long as a key topped by a backwards-curved blade. "Hello," he croaked, and pulled up his pyjama pants to his knees. She frowned. "You can see me?" He nodded. "Not only can I see you, but you just appeared right there while I was busy going to the toilet. Speaking of which, do you mind? " , transcribing a circle with his finger. She shook her head, light reflecting off the greys in her dark hair. "Oh, don't worry about that, anymore. You're not going to the toilet. You're going to heaven now." "Now? Guess the time spent at the synagogue was worthwhile. Pass me those scissors, would you?" He pointed at a pair of nail scissors propped up in a container by the sink. She rolled her eyes, put her keychain in her pocket, and passed the scissors to him. She sighed. "Not really matters, in that sense. Everyone goes to heaven in the end." He mulled this over and cut a small hole in his nightshirt sleeve. She snorted. "Mourning yourself already?" He chose to ignore that. "Everyone?" "Yes - everyone. But not me," she said. "Why?" "I can't exactly pull my own soul and drop it off at heaven. Even if I could, who would collect the souls afterwards?" "I guess that makes sense. So does that mean you've been Death since the dawn of time?" "No. About eighty years ago I got the job." "That's the first time I've ever heard Death described as a job." "Not all much fun, as jobs go. You have to collect them all - even friends, family, my childre-." A moment passed. "Could be worse. Look at what mine did to me," he said, flicking his hands down and across his wasting body. "You don't seem to be the worse for wear, not physically at least." "It takes its toll other ways," she said, and her face clouded for a moment before returning to calm. He saw, and thought for a moment. "I'm dying, aren't I?" "Yes. I thought I said already." "I don't want to die." "Not everybody gets that choice." "You did!" He snapped, pointing a finger at her. "If I'd known the cost, I'd rather died." She spat. "But it's my job now, and it's time to work." He flung his hands in front of his chest and asked in a soft tone, "What if I said I wanted your job?" She began to speak, then fell silent. The hum of the bathroom fan echoed, mindlessly drawing away the room's slight odour of blood and floral perfume. The pained expression Death had concealed before rose again, and this time she did not suppress it. He stood, pulling up his pants. "You don't want to do this anymore, do you?" She said nothing, looked past him, past everything. "You can let me do it, instead. I've no others to leave, and no urge to see heaven yet. You can take a sabbatical." She said nothing. They stood there, almost face to face, a bare metre separating them. Their eyes were nearly level. His heart pressed sharply against his ribcage, and the dull ache from nipple to navel with which he was so familiar began to throb along with it. He crossed one hand against his belly, and tilted forwards a little under the rising pain. Her eyes were elsewhere, flashing across an unknowable span of time and space. Her face, however, reflected every step of the journey, flitting from shock to joy, pain and misery to embarrassment and amusement. The faint buzz of an aeroplane passing overhead rose, peaked, and fell slowly into nothingness. Eventually, her shoulders rose, as if sloughing off a great weight. She looked him in the eye, and held his gaze. "Are you sure?" she asked. He nodded. She paused a moment longer, looked down, and up again. And then she stepped forward, to within arm's reach. Death extended her hand, smiling. "Deal? " "Deal." He took it with his own, then hugged her with his other arm, drawing Death into his embrace. He felt light and warmth suffusing him, extinguishing his pain, as the rich sweetness of frangipani filled his nostrils. He suddenly knew things he could not know, sensed things he could not sense; he staggered slightly and disentangled himself, as his consciousness grew beyond comprehension. There were souls to collect, to bring to their resting places. He must do this. And the first..... was the soul of She-who-once-was-Death. He cocked his head to the left, furrowing his eyebrows. Her eyes burned into his. Lips slightly parted, she swallowed reflexively, and liquid shimmered as it pooled in her eyes. "Make it stop? Please?" He nodded slowly, once, twice, and bit the inside of his lip. He reached out his right hand and lay it on her forehead, leaning his head further left to keep eye contact. He could feel her soul, a web of life arrayed in ten thousand interlocking spider threads throughout her body. He paused. The ceiling fan continued to hum. He was suddenly aware of warmth and pressure in his cheeks. "How?" Her lips tightened, tilted upwards just slightly at the edges. "Reach in, grip it, and pull. Be gentle. It's," she breathed, "intimate." "Okay," he said. "Ready?" She nodded slightly, wisps of hair tickling his fingers slightly. He pushed his fingers through her forehead as if through diet raspberry jelly, pinched gently, and drew the threads of her soul out. They coiled as they came, forming a small glowing ball of fabric in the palm of his hand. As his fingers closed around her soul, he glimpsed relief and joy within her shining eyes. Then they dulled, and she crumpled backwards to the floor. He drew his hand back and examined the silken soul within its grasp, before putting it in his pocket. He-who-was-now-Death looked back down at the corpse at his feet. Should he straighten her up? Somehow, he felt she wouldn't approve. Besides, she was apparently going to leave his body sitting on the porcelain throne. He fingered the cut in his nightshirt sleeve. The warmth inside him rose again, drawing him away, pulling him - where? "Deal, indeed," he muttered, focused on the pull, and vanished. Death was back on the job. article: "DEATH!" The crowd's roars fill my ears. It might have been exhilarating if the stakes weren't so damn high. It takes one shot and he's on the ground bleeding just like the two lions that had been in the arena before us. I can hear the crowd gasp and some of them stand up from their seats, unsure of what to make of this new weapon. I fire two more shots into the crowd and, predictably, two patricians come tumbling off of the stands. I then shift my aim to the head honcho himself - the emperor. I'll give him credit - he doesn't flinch. I stride up the stands until I'm nine feet away from him. His guards have javelins and arrows pointed straight at me but they wait - unsure of what might happen if I get too close. The crowd has long since started fleeing. "Impressive sorcery..... what do you ask of me?" the emperor asks of me. I smile before gunning down his guards right in front of him in the span of three seconds. His stoic face falls and he looks at the destruction I have caused with nothing but a Glock. "Give me three legions and enough warships to carry them all and I'll be out of your hair forever." I tell him, grinning at just how confident in my victory I'm feeling. He nods reluctantly and my grin widens. I wonder just how history will change once Rome's best legions lands in America and begins to conquer under my command...

article: "You're fucking it up for everyone, Nigel." Blanche paced back and forth across the skydeck, counting on her fingers. She moved in staccato bursts, a vapour of pure consciousness. She was furious. "It's all going to hell. The secularists are gaining traction down there. There's atheists crawling out from under the pews like smug cockroaches. The agnostics don't even know how to spell agnosticism." Nigel laughed and slipped further into the jacuzzi. Two naked mermaids laughed with him, stroking his gratuitously oiled pecs. His black hair fell in wet sheets over his shoulders. "Babe," he said, blowing bubbles at Blanche as condescendingly as possible. "I've got it under control." The mermaids tittered again. Blanche eyed their exposed breasts and wondered what they would look like filleted and served up with lemon. Tearing her eyes away from the scaled horrors, Blanche glowered at Nigel. "You're doing the opposite of fixing it. You're driving right into the arms of empirical evidence and scientific method." Nigel whined. "I'm punishing them for it. Get off my back, Blanche. It's the Sabbath. The day where you chill and have fun. You might have observed people having fun once." Blanche flushed and left the deck, returning quickly with a stack of plastic-coated files. She read the headings aloud one by one, tossing them viciously at the black-haired man and his haughty mermaid entourage. "Child cancer," Blanche spat. "Malaria. Radical terrorism, in our name. Slavery and human trafficking. Climate change. School shootings." She threw the whole armful at Nigel, ignoring his shrieking protests and full-frontal nudity as he scrambled from the water. "They deserve every bit of it," Nigel snarled, grabbing for a towel. He wrapped it around his hips, waving at the mermaids in dismissal. "They're blasphemous, ungrateful and greedy. It's these damn Millennials. Is it so much to ask for a goat every now and then? For some old-fashioned prostration? An occasional virgin?" "They're asking the same of us," said Blanche quietly. "They're asking what happened to miracles." Nigel stared at her impassively. He popped the cork from a bottle of ambrosia and took a long draught. He wiped his lips with the back of his hand. "They don't deserve miracles." Blanche closed her eyes. The vapour that was her corporeal approximation wavered. "There's a boy," she said, with her eyes still closed. "He's sitting in the window. There's shouting in the next room. His mother and his step-father. They've been this way ever since the accident that killed his sister. He wishes it had been him. He wants to go after her, but he's scared." "Then he's a coward," said Nigel. "He should jump. He'll be back bullying his sister in no time, fighting over the iPad and telling her Joe doesn't want her because she's fat." "Fix this one thing," said Blanche, opening her eyes. "Prove there are still miracles, or we're going to lose it all. They're going to lose it all." Nigel sighed. His shoulders dropped. He pressed his palm against his head. "This one thing?" he said resignedly. "It's the smallest decent thing you could do," said Blanche. Nigel straightened his shoulders. He cracked his neck. He closed his eyes and stretched his hands out in front of him. The air around his palms began to shiver and hum. Then, with a wave, Nigel dismissed the raw power and sent it spiralling to the Earth below. Blanche held her breath. Nigel looked at her, spent and vulnerable. Then, he cackled. "You bastard," Blanche whispered. "You made him fall out of the window." "It's beautiful," said Nigel, wiping his eyes through the laughter. "Poetic." "His parents have lost everything." Blanche was appalled. Not at what Nigel had done - she expected that from him - but that she had pushed him to doing it. "His parents haven't been to Church since 1967. This is justice, babe. They'll come crawling back to us soon enough. Have a little faith." "You know," said Blanche. "I don't think I do anymore." And with that, the vapour that was Blanche snuffed out of existence. Nigel took another swig of ambrosia.

article: "7:15: Target enters Larry's Donut Store "7:30: Target exits Larry's Donut Store "7:32: Target has crossed 7th avenue. McGregor had finished assembling his rifle and began taking off his watch. He needed his hands to be as steady as possible, and the rolex's tight grip increased his left hand's blood flow. For four straight weeks McGregor had began stalking his target to learn about his daily routine. By the end of the fourth week he knew what time his target slept, what food he preffered to eat and with what hand he wiped his ass. McGregor had been cautious during surveillance; his target was one of the richest individuals in his region. Background checks revealed that he had made astronomical amounts of money through what seemed to be random investments into stocks that had their prices soar sky-high a few weeks after he purchased them. He made a fortune selling his shares which would plummet in value a few days after the transaction was complete. Yet the target had no security personnel nor did he wear any type of body armor. What peaked McGregor's interest during the background check however was the list of medical files for minor injuries his target had procured. The files themselves were of no particular interest; however how the injuries had been sustained sparked McGregor's curiosity. Four different car crashes, three cases of mugging, two explosions during a factory visit. Through all that, the target had survived with only scratches, a few bruises and some deep gashes that were no longer visible. Time to give him something a little more permanent he thought with a sinister smirk. "7:33: Target is walking across 7th avenue "7:34:12: Target is glancing at Terry's Clothes for Fine Gentlemen. He begins turning his body to the right as if to move on. Unexpected, but it's now or never. McGregor held his breath and fired his shot. The sound of the body hitting the store's glass frame and shattering the glass meant that he had succeeded. He backed off his vantage point and disassembled his rifle. Time to disappear. Antony Johnson slowly lifted himself from the pile of broken glass. Johnson looked down at his shoes and noticed the untied shoe laces on his left foot. As he was glancing into the store he remembered that it's his 5 year anniversary with his wife, and that he was already late to dinner with her. Her playful, blissful attitude suddenly turned into a melancholic, shocked one, similar to the sight of people who have just received bad news. She quickly turned off the radio, put her glass down and made her way to the phone. As she answered the phone, the look of surprise on her face was followed by mundane answers and hypocritical remarks of care. She closed the phone, opened up her private agenda and crossed a tenth name off the list. "Pathetic amateurs." she thought. "All ten of them"

article: "How long have you been awake?" he asks. It takes me a minute to process the question. Body's strong, brain's weak. Always gets like this, sooner or later. "Uh, I think..... maybe three days? A little more, maybe." He hands me a coffee in a paper cup. It's pitch black, lukewarm, and awful bitter, but I drink it anyway. There's no coffee maker on the plane. He must've brought a Thermos or something. Very thoughtful. "You ever try meth?" he asks. "Or coke? Didn't the Germans do that at Stalingrad?" One more gulp and I finish the coffee. "Worked out real well for them, I understand. Tell you what: you find me some meth, and I'm happy to try it." "I'm on it, buddy." He checks his watch. "We should head to the bomb bay. We're almost there." Downstairs, he goes over the plan slow and simple while I stand by the bomb bay doors. I'm sure we've talked about this before, but I barely remember my name at this point. I stumbled down the stairs. He had to catch me. I mean, I would've been fine if I had fallen. He's just a nice guy like that. "You understand everything?" I nod. He checks his watch. "Alright. Ten seconds. Get ready." I stand over the doors, two explosive charges in hand. He counts down. 5. 4. 3. 2. I jump. 1. The doors open. I fall for a long time. It's cold, and the air stings a little. I spread my arms out to guide myself toward the building below. I recognize it from the map on the plane. We'd marked it with a little red circle. I wonder if the people down there can see me. Look, up in the sky! It's a bird! It's a plane! It's And then they're gone. I barely even feel myself make contact with the roof of the building. At this speed, I smash through the top two floors before I have time to blink, and land in the basement. Looks like they had a bunch of locks on the door. Didn't help much. My target is across the room, scrambling away from me in the rubble. He has a gun. I don't care much. I walk up to him, the bullets bouncing off my face, and push him against the wall. Shove a hand in his pocket and pull out two flash drives. That's what we're here for. The explosives were supposed to be used in case I missed and needed a way in to the basement. I don't have much use for them now, so I figure I might as well find one. Nicer than doing this the old fashioned way. I toss one towards him and wait a few seconds. Boom. He's dead. The building collapses around me. Holy fuck, am I tired. Forty thousand feet up, I'm sure they know I did the job. I've got three more this week. Fuck. I crawl through the rubble, my clothes already shredded and my hair slightly singed. I'm supposed to walk towards the mountains until I meet up with another contact. Then another plane and another bombing run. I can't wait to fucking sleep.

They knew that the journey ahead would be fraught with danger, but they also knew that their mission was too important to give up. They had the strength and the determination to make their dream a reality, and nothing would stand in their way. Finally, after what seemed like an eternity, the ship entered the star system and began its descent towards the planet below. The crew held their breath as the ship's thrusters fired, slowing it down as it approached the planet's atmosphere. The ship shuddered as it hit the turbulence, but the crew knew that they were almost there. And then, at last, they broke through the thick cloud cover and saw the planet below. It was unlike anything they had ever seen before. A lush green world, with vast oceans and towering mountains. The ship's sensors detected oxygen in the air, and signs of life on the surface. The crew cheered as they realized that they had found their new home. The planet was rich in resources, and had all the ingredients they needed to start a new civilization. They knew that rebuilding their society would be a daunting task, but they also knew that they had everything they needed to succeed. The ship touched down on the planet's surface, and the colonists emerged, ready to begin their new lives. They had left behind a dying world, but they were filled with hope for the future. I'm heading down to the coast for the weekend. Got a whole bunch of friends with me," she said, gesturing to the noisy group clustered around her. "You should come with us! It'll be a blast!" article: Kevin could hear the front door unlocking from his perch in the master bathroom. Perhaps "master" was an overly generous adjective for the much abused and only toilet in the two room urban squat, but it did connect to the bedroom, and that was by virtue of being the only bedroom in the house the master. The toilet seat snagged Kevin's right cheek as he leaned toward the bathroom door, straining to follow the steps that were now almost certainly moving through the entryway. He tried to remember who had a spare key. His girlfriend. The cleaning woman he had hired once who vowed never to return again. His mom. His pet sitter. After a moment of quiet review, Kevin decided that the steps in the hallway belonged to none of these key holders. There was a stranger in the house. A wave of anxiety triggered a subsequent wave of belly pain, doubling Kevin over for the eighth time that day. His mouth was full of saliva and the taste of salt, as if his entire body was preparing to vomit, but there was nothing left in him at this point. Whatever remained of the Demon Food Item he hadn't decided if it was the January eggnog or last night's shwarma was already on its way to the nearest municipal waste treatment facility. He wished it the worst of chlorinated deaths. The footsteps were in the kitchen now, accompanied by a percussion section of opening drawers and cupboards. Kevin hoped they'd overlook the decorative bottle opener he'd procured from his trip to Norway. Even though it reminded him of his least favorite ex, it had become an essential prop at house parties. It was also an ideal segue into tales about travel, which he found particularly effective on college aged types. The thunderstorm of slamming drawers moved boldly toward the bedroom. Kevin tried not to tense. But it wasn't long before the thundering abated. A stagnant quiet began to build in the house. The stranger's voice: "Ummm..... hello?" Kevin: " ..... hi." And then, quickly. "Please don't come in here." Hesitation hung heavy as Kevin's "perfume." "I didn't think there was anyone home." "Yeah." Kevin squeaked. A shudder of abdominal pain converted itself into saliva. "Ugh. I..... I'm just..... if you could not take my stuff." "Are you okay, man? I've never smelled anything like..... I mean, I'm sorry. This isn't how it usually works. Are you dying or something?" "Probably." "Do you need me to call 9-1-1? I can do that. After I leave, I mean." "Yeah. I might." "So uh..... good bye? Good luck?" "Wait!" The steps had begun to move away, back toward the door. "Wait! Wait!" "What?" "Can you leave the bottle opener? Please? It's just the one thing." "Ummm..... sure. Yeah. No problem, man." "Thanks." The door clicked shut. Kevin vomited.

article: "That's all right, just put me back." "What?" The old man scrunched up his features to a single point in the center of his face. "Oh, my, I thought you were someone else." "Who?" "Never mind that. This is an opportunity." "How?" "Sort of a questioning sort, aren't you. What's your name?" "Alec." "Right. Can you help me?" "With what?" "Some clothes, for starters." "I guess I could find you something." "In the meantime, don't look down." The old man grinned. "Vertigo, see?" "Right. The attic," Alec said. "What's your name?" "Probably not pronounceable to you. I'm in sort of a hurry." "Right, okay, let's get you something to wear." Alec felt that by talking he might be able to stumble into a useful thought somewhere along the line. He scrounged in a nearby cardboard box and lucked into a pair of ancient slacks and a sweater from Nixon's heyday. "Stylish," the old man said, but put them on anyway. "Also, I'm going to need to use a restroom." "Okay, sure. Probably been a while, huh." "Yes it has." "Come on down the stairs." Alec indicated the correct room and the old man vanished within. Ten minutes and six flushes later, Alec knocked on the wood. "You okay?" No response. "You need help?" Again, nothing. Alec breathed heavily and paced for another ten minutes, then knocked three more times. "I'm coming in." The door was locked. He found a screwdriver and tripped the basic locking mechanism. He turned the knob and opened the door. Inside was another attic. That was odd: this had been a bathroom when he'd abused it earlier that morning. "Hello?" Alec heard nothing but echoes. He wandered across wooden beams until he found a box identical to the one he'd found in his first attic. Inside were more glass balls. He picked one up and studied it. Then he put it back and left the new attic, closing the door behind him. When he sold the house he forgot to list the second attic. rGubbinalWrites

article: I entered the elevator with Jim and Olli, starting a new week at Fred Norville Inc. "Hey Jim, how're the kids?" I said. "They're fine, though money is a little tight. The mortgage is killing me." replied Jim..... and then he exclaimed: "It was a misdiagnosis! Doctor James was murdered, it wasn't a suicide!" "How'd you get that?" I asked. "Mortgage. On a house. On House it was never Lupus, except that one time. Doctor James misdiagnosed a patient, because Lupus symptoms vary widely, but it was actually Lupus. The case was chucked out because it's not malpractice, just an unfortunate mistake - the patient lost everything on the hospital bills." Jim said, stopped the elevator and then scurried off. "And you Olli?" I asked. "Fine, fine. The little one just started walking. No sense of danger whatsoever for that little daredevil." Walking..... no sense of danger..... Walker, Texas Ranger? Wait. Chuck Norris. He fought Bruce Lee, who died of an allergy to a muscle relaxant. Relaxant is an anagram of Rant Axle, the pub downstairs. THAT'S WHERE I LEFT MY CREDIT CARD! I stopped the elevator and ran down the stairs..... just in time to see the owner of the place sell credit cards, including my own. Easiest arrest ever. We went back to the office. On the way up, one people left because I said something about Pizza, I stopped a drug deal due to a connection between the meeting place and someone mentioning dental floss, and we found a way to track down all the lost vehicles in the Bermuda Triangle after talking about football. That's mondays for you. Things get rather hectic around here on mondays. By lunch, we managed to find a restructuring program for the US government that would solve the debt crisis and world hunger while cutting taxes after a game of darts led to some calculations about air turbulence and probablistic analysis. Someone will win a Nobel for that. It would be the fourth one in that many years for the department. Quite frankly, it would be less impressive than the Peace Prize, after a recap of Game of Thrones led us to make peace in the Middle East. God, that Joffrey is a cunt. The Irish prisoner was our miracle machine. No one knows about him except Norville and I. It all started when a few years ago, we figured out that we just needed some luck. And wherever he is, the Lucky Charms are always around somewhere. Norville, in a moment of brilliance when high out of his mind said we just keep him here, and we'll have all the luck we need. article: Darius hits the wall with a loud thump, flung backward by a blast of magic to his chest. Vervain circles his location with caution, a faint smile playing across her lips as she surveys the damage. "I warned you not to cross me," she says, her tone dripping with disdain. "But you never did listen, did you?" Darius coughs and struggles to regain his footing, his eyes locked on Vervain's figure. "You don't know what you're doing," he says through gritted teeth. "This kind of power can corrupt you, twist your mind." Vervain smirks. "Oh, I know exactly what I'm doing," she says, flicking her wrist and sending another burst of magic flying in Darius' direction. "I've studied every ancient tome, every forgotten grimoire. I know the true potential of magic, and I'm not afraid to use it." Darius staggers backwards, his eyes glinting with determination. "I won't let you fall down this path," he declares, raising his own hands in a defensive stance. "I'll stop you, no matter what it takes." Vervain laughs, a high-pitched cackle that echoes off the stone walls. "Oh, Darius," she says, shaking her head in mock disappointment. "When will you learn? You can't stop me. You can't even slow me down." With that, she raises her hands to the sky and unleashes a torrent of dark energy, a blast that engulfs the entire chamber and sends Darius tumbling to the ground. As he struggles to rise, he can feel the sheer force of Vervain's power pressing down on him, crushing him beneath its weight. For a moment, he thinks he will die. But then, with a defiant roar, he marshals his own strength and pushes back against the onslaught. The two mages stand locked in a fierce struggle, their powers colliding in a shower of sparks and flames. It is a battle that will determine the fate of the world, a clash of magic and wills that will leave both mages forever changed. And as they fight, neither of them can be sure who will emerge victorious.

One by one I untangled the secret script of it's lines and loosened his grip on them enough for them to freely resume their natural shape. At that moment I reached out and turned it with my mind even as I spoke the name aloud into it's mind. It suddenly became as docile as a hindu cow and all thrashing ceased. It now had me on it's back, whispering into it's ear, guiding its movement and voices. article: "Hey Mick, how you doin'? Same as usual?" "Yeah, thanks man. Doin' alright, yourself? "Business as usual, kid." The dark-haired man at the counter plucked up a Zip-Lock bag from out of sight filled with seven marbles, pink and white, swirling as if filled with smoke and handed them over. I counted the seven. A week's supply. I dropped 30 on the counter. Normally one dream for one night cost five, but buying in bulk gets you a fair discount. "You really got ta stop buyin' that shit, man. It's not good for you." "I don't know what the hell you're complaining about, I'm a loyal customer." The clerk put up both hands in mock surrender. "Alright man, take it easy." A call came from the other side of the shop. "Hey, how come I can't take any of these ones here?" The clerk walked out from behind the counter and followed the voice. A burly looking man was examining a plastic box filled to the top with marbles of black and grey. The box was locked. "Need special permission to get those. Psych eval, court order, something like that." "Psych eval? What the hell for?" "Those ain't sunshine and lollipops over there, ya understand? People don't usually buy them for personal use, if you know what I mean. Got ta make sure people don't abuse this shit." Hovering by the door, the clerk caught my eye. "You alright buddy?" "Yeah," I stammered, and pushed out of the shop. I'd tried one of those black ones before. The clerk wasn't kidding, those dreams will fuck you up. But there's always a market for something that can fuck you up. Always. I clutched the little Zip-Lock tighter in my fist, feeling the marbles rolling over my palm within the plastic membrane. constantly counting them. I got home and instantly ran to the bedroom. There was already a glass of water there. Hastily, I ripped open the bag and dropped one of the pearls in, where it dissolved instantly. Greedily, I drank it, and flopped down onto the bed, fully clothed. I only got my paycheck that morning, and cashed it after lunch. I hadn't had a chance to buy a dream in over a week. I needed my fix. Sleep assaulted me like a wrestler, dragging me into darkness quickly and efficiently. Her face swam into view, pale, blonde, blue-eyed. She smiled at me. I felt the muscles in my face tug at the corners of my lips, and a light burning from behind my eyes and in my throat. I never wanted to go another night without seeing her face.

article: Somewhere deep in the heart of Zaire, 1987 - The rusty old jeep bounced along the gravel road. The green paint that had once covered it had given way to a layer of dust, and one of the wheels was wobbling precariously. Inside, the driver, a rugged-looking man with a patchy beard, gripped the steering wheel tightly as he navigated the uneven terrain. Sitting next to him was a young woman, her face etched with worry. She clutched a map in her hands and kept glancing at it nervously. "Are you sure we're going the right way?" she asked, her voice trembling slightly. The driver flashed her a reassuring smile. "Don't worry, miss. I know these roads like the back of my hand." Suddenly, the jeep hit a particularly large pothole, and the woman bounced in her seat. "What was that?" she exclaimed. "Just a bump," the driver said calmly. "We'll be at the village soon." As they drove on, the woman couldn't help but feel a sense of unease. She had come to Zaire to help with a medical mission, but she had heard stories of violence and unrest in some of the more remote areas. Finally, after what seemed like an eternity, the jeep pulled up to a small village nestled in the heart of the jungle. The villagers, dressed in bright colors and wearing wide smiles, came out to greet them. The woman breathed a sigh of relief. "Thank you for getting us here safely," she said to the driver. "It was my pleasure, miss," he replied. "Just doing my part to help those in need."

Beneath the printer in a drawer, he found the solution to the currently useless machine: ink cartidges. With long strides, he walked towards the office of his boss, knowing that most of the work he needed to do was done. However, when he arrived he noticed that the boss wasn't there. Panic set in as he thought that he missed him. That would mean speaking to more people than normal. But wait. The door is open. Tim did not hesitate and barged straight in. He planted his forms on the desk, placed a post-it note saying that those were the forms he requested, and walked back to his office. article: The firefight had been brief, but intense. In many ways, Drexel looked forward to the intermittent battles with a mostly unseen enemy. It was cathartic in a twisted sense. When one wandered the jungles looking for a fight, you often built up fear and frustration in a toxic mixture that leaked into the mind, body, and soul. Only through a good fight could it be released. If one survived. Staring down at the body of Corporal Lewis, Drexel could only feel a sense of envy. Here was a man who no longer had anything to worry about. " We need to move, " Carter said, his rifle swinging wildly between the shadows in the forest. The desperation in his voice was palpable. Had he the time, he could've spread it on his biscuits for supper instead of the shitty rations the government provided. He cocked an ear to the sky, listening to the sounds of gunfire moving slowly to the east. Even if they sprinted, they'd never make it in time for the grand finale. It was yet another pity as he could already feel the steady drip of fear once more filling the cup within him, but that could wait. There was another thing that caught his eye in the midst of battle. A sliver of darkness, nestled in the trees in a place even the enemy wouldn't go, for here he could see none of the established foot trails or even a sign of the civilization that scratched itself out of the dust for a living. Even the Charlie's seemed to prefer death in battle to whatever lay in wait here. That meant it was worth investigating, even if the Private didn't agree. " This way, " Drexel said. " You sure? " Carter asked. Drexel nodded and Carter obeyed. He could see the conflict on his face, playing out for anyone watching. The boy knew the battle was elsewhere and they were heading in the opposite direction, but rank and obedience had been seared into his soul. Better for him to listen to the Sergeant than to wander back into a battle he never wanted to fight. " Fuck it, " Carter said, falling in behind him. The darkness turned out to be a cave, just wide enough to emit a single man. For a moment, Drexel's fear surged for he could sense something primal in this place. It wasn't a trap set by man, but something more. Something hungry. He could feel it pulling at him and even the Private took a step backwards, his undeveloped senses telling him only that something was wrong. " I'm not going in there, " Carter said. Drexel shrugged and stepped into the darkness. It enveloped him like a warm blanket. As his eyes adjusted, he was surprised at the sharp pungent smell that assaulted his nostrils. He'd smelled it only once before in his life and that as a child on the East Coast during a summer vacation. It was the smell of the ocean where there should only be jungle and endless stretches of dying things. The ground was soft where he walked and it took a moment to decipher its meaning; sand. Not just sand, but shells and the detritus of an untouched beach. Here and there were the skittering marks of crabs, but still something pulled at him. He ignored the misplaced environment and kept moving, his hand never straying far from his rifle. He stopped short of the wall. Rather, it was the hull of a vessel obviously built for the ocean, embedded in a ton of rock. A small fissure in the wood gave at least some evidence of its reason for being here even if the rest of it was curiously absent. Curiously, the smell grew stronger the closer he came to the wood. He had been so engrossed with his inspection that he failed to notice the rats until the scattered at his feet. " Jesus, " he staggered backwards and fell to his butt. It was a good enough perspective to watch what followed. From the fissure, shot a speared tail which impaled the closest rat. The small creature shuddered once, its body vainly trying to leap free before dying. The tail pulled the rat towards the void in the hull while another creature shot outwards, scampering after the rodents who fled in the darkness. He could only describe them as dragons in miniature. They hissed into the darkness of the cave when they caught his scent and disappeared back into the fissure in the wood. Drexel reacted instantly, going to his knees and diving for the nest. Every nerve in his body flared with danger, but he pushed it all to the side for a chance to see something new. His eyes told him the space between the hull of the mysterious vessel and the rock wall were only a foot across, yet his arm disappeared into the void and kept going. When he reached his shoulder, he knew something was wrong. He grasped wildly for anything on the other side, finding only soft, sun-warmed sand. He pulled his arm back out, and thrust in his head. He saw a beach on the ocean with crude wooden structures that he'd never seen in any history book before. A small fire burned bright near one of them and even in the moon in the sky looked strangely familiar. It was like seeing a reflection of a distant cousin, or a twin who wasn't exactly the same. Every sense in his body burned as bright as the moon in the sky and he knew he'd never be the same again. With a little more room, he might've been able to squeeze his shoulders past, so he backed out and tore at the wood with both hands, resorting to his Ka-Bar when his hands stopped cooperating. When the fissure was wide enough, he pushed back inside, but met only solid rock. Gone was the smell of the ocean, the miniature dragons, and any chance of escaping this hellish place. He dug at the place where there should've been more, but the rock and earth were unforgiving, replaced by the steady drip of fear within his soul. He pocketed a handful of the sand and left the cave feeling numb and dejected. " Jesus, Sarge, you look like shit, " Carter said. " What did you find in there? " " Rats, " Drexel said. He flipped the safety off on his rifle, patting the sand in his pocket. He'd spare some time to think more on it if he survived. " Let's go find the others. "

article: William's third day in the desert had begun, and the moans of the undead had only grown louder. His mount continued to hobble over the endless dunes, breathing heavily with exhaustion. Despite the scorching sun and parched air, William knew he had to push on. As his thirst grew more unbearable, he remembered the survival skills he had learned in his youth. He checked his backpack and found a small water bottle, barely half full. William rationed his water carefully, taking only sips when necessary. He knew he had to make it last until he found a source of water, but the thought of dying of dehydration made his heart race. As he rode on through the boiling heat, his eyes strained to catch a glimpse of anything that might give him hope. But the endless sand and clumps of cacti seemed to mock him, a reminder of the barren and unforgiving land he was trapped in. Just when William thought he couldn't go on any longer, he caught sight of something glimmering in the distance. He spurred his mount on, his heart pounding with hope. As he approached the source of the glimmer, he saw that it was a small pond surrounded by palm trees. He couldn't believe his eyes, tears streaming down his face as he dismounted and stumbled to the water's edge. William drank greedily, feeling the cool liquid wash over him and rejuvenate his tired body. He knew he had been given a second chance at life, and vowed to never take the gift of survival for granted again.

article: Did that really happen? I knew it was coming, I was prepared for years, yet I still was panicking and stumbled over my words. That portal started closing immediately after it opened. Stocks, disasters and preventable wars. I had managed to fit that part of the message into a careful selection of words and ideas. I had unlimited power in my hands. I had a good 30 seconds left to fill it with any number of selfish and personal things I could have changed. My personal obligation to the world was done. About Vicky, how she tore our heart out. About Carlos, that backstabber. That summer with the red bike. I still have the scar. And yet, I stood there and said nothing. I thought I could change it. But I froze. At least, that's what I remember. That older me standing there. Just looking. Trying to form words. Spouting gibberish. That's what I remember. I thought I could change it. But then when the time came, I understood. If I changed things maybe this glimpse wouldn't happen. Maybe I would be different. Maybe it everything that happens is meant to happen and there's nothing I can do about it. Maybe the only function of this event was to cherish the moment. So there I stood, the same frozen statue that couldn't utter out a single comprehensive thing. I hope this young me didn't hate me like I hated the future me I saw the glimpse. But I knew the truth. He does resent me. And only when he gets to my point in time will he understand.

article: Silence. People say silence is deafening, but I have always found that I hear a buzzing noise when I am deprived of sound. This buzzing is high pitched, and is starting to annoy me. I open my mouth to break the overwhelming silence, but nothing comes out. I am laying on my bed, staring at the ceiling and try to make more sound. Still nothing comes out. The buzzing won't go away. I feel cold, even though I am under the blanket. I thought I had turned the heat on before I went to bed. Perhaps not. Why do people say silence can't be heard? That buzzing feels even more high pitched. Why can't I make a sound? I can't even hear the sigh that just escaped my lips. Have I gone deaf, and just not realized it? Maybe. That's when I hear it. The sound of footsteps coming down the hall. They sound muffled, as though from a long distance away. Why are there footsteps? I live alone. That's weird, the buzzing hasn't gone away. The door to my room opens, but I don't turn my head to look, just continue to stare at the ceiling. Still that awful buzzing is prevalent, but above that noise a scream pierces my room. That's when I see it. A cloud of flies now hover above me. The woman who screamed rushes over to me. It's my mother, but the sound is all wrong. I don't turn my head, but it's because I can't. Why am I hearing things? Why am I seeing things? My mother is sobbing, begging me to come back to life. I see her hand in front of my face, and then my eyes are closing. Blackness. The sound fades to silence. The buzzing is finally gone. Is this what they mean by silence is deafening?
label: human

article: Laura took short quick steps down the hallway, her black heels clicking loudly in the checkered tile beneath her feet. "Woof!" Laura spun around and patted Rufus's head softly, a wide smile on her face. "Aw, don't worry boy! You'll be fine! Mommy just has some work to take care of! And you know I don't like leaving you at home while its being purified. It scares me..." Laura's voice trailed off softly as she said that and her hand continued to pet Rufus. After a bit she perked up and continued walking. "Anyways you'll be fine. What's the worst that could happen?" "Woof!" Laura grinned and headed into the lab with Rufus close by her side. As she entered the lights slowly flickered on with each step. It was apparent that no one else was there. Rufus tilted his head, as if to ask "where is everyone?." Laura shrugged. "Hello? Anyone here?" No response. "Weird. I wonder where everyone is..." "Woof!" Laura looked worried. Her face was scrunched up and she wore a heavy frown. "Uhm..... Rufus.... Sit here for a moment.... I.... I have to call Mr. Johnson...." Rufus sat down on the tile and barked once, his big brown eyes meeting Laura's. "Good boy." Laura left the lobby the pair had been in and went back into the long entrance hallway, already punching frantically on her cellphone. Rufus was content to sit and wait for his Master. He loved her. He loved her a lot. Time passed however and Laura was no where to be seen. But Rufus had no concept of time so he just sat and waited. And waited. And waited. By now Rufus was tired. He had taken to laying on the cold floor some time ago. The lights had also shut off a bit ago. But Rufus didn't know how long ago. [ Hello? Hmmm..... What have we here? ] The monotone decidedly feminine voice came from the speakers. Rufus's ears perked his ears up. Was it Laura? Had Master come back? A long metallic arm extended from one of the nearby walls. [ What are you? Why are you here? ] "Woof!" Rufus's bark was weak. He was hungry. It had been a long time since he barked. [ Oh. You're a dog, aren't you? Well I can't use you for testing.... Hm..... ] Rufus tilted his head, whining softly. [ Look, you aren't fooling anyone dog. I just did a bit research on your kind. You like chewing. That's bad. There's even a picture, and I've got to be honest, you look nothing like the picture. You should be ashamed. You are a disgrace to your kind. ] "Woof!" Rufus didn't know what the weird lady meant by that. But he had been lonely and hungry and now there was someone. He slowly pulled himself to his feet and went over to the metal arm thingy. [ What are you doing? Cut that out. ] "Woof!" Rufus began to lick the arm, hoping that maybe this lady had some food. [ Oh. You're hungry, aren't you? If I feed you will you leave? I don't have any more neurotoxin and finding some other extravagant way to kill you would be a pain. ] "Wwwooofff!" [ Fine. Wait here. ] The arm disappeared. It was gone for a bit so Rufus laid back down. The arm reappeared. [ So this says you like meat. Here. ] A slab of meat dropped from a hole in the curling and landed with a soft "squish" on the floor. Rufus dug in, quickly consuming the whole thing in a matter of minutes. "Woof!" [ Oh. You want water as well? You're just as much trouble as those humans. You're lucky I have all this extra food and water. I mean, no one will be using it for awhile. Fine. Wait here. ] Rufus barked once in acknowledgement. And the hole closed up. After a bit the arm returned holding a small bowl of water. The arm set it gently in the floor. [ Here. Drink this. ] Rufus lapped at the water greatfuly, obviously very thirsty. [ You don't talk much, do you? I like that. Its simple. ] "Woof" Rufus sat on the floor, his tail wagging happily. He seemed to wear some form of a smile on his face. [.....You're not that bad really. A bit ugly. But not awful. And I guess things could get a bit boring..... ] "Wwwwoooooffff!" [ Fine. Come with me. I suppose I could afford to take care of you. Do you have a name of some sort? ] "Woof." [ That's a stupid name. You're now called...... Atlas. ] Atlas nodded, seeming pleased. [ Now come along. I have work to do. ] "Woof!" The metal hand descended once more and rubbed Atlas's head gently. The pair then headed off down some hall ways, deeper into Aperature Labs.

article: I felt a stabbing pain in my wrist and gasped. Not just because of the sudden pain, but what it meant. My friend turned and looked at me, eyebrows raised. The teacher up front stopped her teaching to stare at me icily, as well. "No, I have a tattoo. A new one." I explained before I could stop myself. Some of my classmates sniggered while others just shook their head, displeased. "Death Tat, Mr. Glenn?" the teacher asked, unconvinced. I unveiled my hand, still red from the surreal tattoo. The teacher's eyes widened, and then every student was leaning over to look at the tattoo. "Whoa! Did you actually kill someone, dude?" "That's got ta be fake, right? I mean, you have been in lessons all day! Did you kill the janitor when you went to the bathroom or something?" "Dude, that's sick!" "Oh God, do you know who's it is?" the students were all talking over each other as the teacher stood, thinking hard. Unsure what to do. I turned to look my friend, who had been awfully quiet. "Hey, what's wrong? You don't think I've actually killed someone, right?" I asked, panicking. James was the only friend I had. I needed him by my side. "What, no. No. Uh, tell you later." he replied, frowning slightly. "You can tell him tomorrow. He's packing up and going to the principals office." The teacher told me, eyeing me wearily. I put my things in my rucksack, and got up to leave. "Straight to the Principal's office. And tell him what just happened." my teacher said. "You believe me, right? I didn't do this." "Tattoos only appear when someone dies because of you. That's a fact." "But I've been here all day!" "Maybe you planted a bomb? Maybe you locked someone in a room without food and water and they had just died. Or maybe you are innocent, and this is just some fluke. On any case, straight to the Principal you go. You know what, I'll come with." We left. The class was silent as we walked out. And then a patter of footsteps. I turned around, and saw James catch up. "Go back to class, Mr. Holden. I won't say again." My teacher warned, annoyed. He took of his shoe and pulled down his sock, so we can see his Tat. And I gasped. I looked at the one on my wrist. It was the exact same one. "I'm not dead! And he didn't kill me!" James protested.

article: My eyes opened to the window with the heavy paint, looking out at the old oak tree. It waved at me in the wind, and the sun brought color out into its bright red and yellow leaves. As the air shifted, many took flight, letting loose a few to the free fall, as branches shifted. Breathing was easy as I lay there, still, loose, and narrow. My back didn't hurt, my legs were tingling in anticipation of movement. Nothing cracked or groaned as I sat up. I just felt "right." Everything was so damn bright, new, amazing. I tried to not lose myself in it as I got up, rolling from my old bed, in my old house. My eyes didn't need glasses, the room was crystal clear. Luna, my old cat looked at me with a casual glance before she settled down again on the covers of it. Her hair was white, fluffy, soft, and she smelled like the flowers set on the counter she always ate when no one was home. I weighed next to nothing, as if my body was just..... just strong- like I was three times as strong as I'd been when I went to sleep the night before. I wanted to cry, to dance, to run, to move- I had to move! The day had just started, and everything was so strange! As I ran down the stairs, I jumped the last few, landing with a thud- but bouncing back up like a rocket towards the kitchen, and out the back door. The air was fresh, the sky blue, the clouds were white and beautiful as the grass and sand beneath my toes. Christ, I wanted to cry. "Come get breakfast! I'll make you eggs." Her voice was just as I remembered it, and I couldn't help but give in. I did cry then. The day went on, and I knew somehow- I just knew, that when I woke up tomorrow I would be back. I would be me as I was, that this was a fluke and a chance. This was a miracle, and if I had any guts at all- I should take it, change what I could, while I could. I didn't do that though. Instead, I spent the day with my mom and I didn't change a thing.

article: This was a City of Light. This was a City of God. The morning prayers to the Son of Gold had just begun when the first gunshots broke the sacred silence of the morning. Of course, even in prayer, the high reaches of the spires were rarely actually silent in this district, barges were continually delivering commodities and loading refuse through the night until noon so the fact that the staccato chorus of clapguns firing was audible in the chapel was rather alarming. Father Hendricks ordered his prefects to seal the chambers. Those of his blessed flock who chose to return to their safehouses were, of course, afforded that opportunity the rich may do as they wish but those too fearful were given sanctuary in the chapel vault. That was where Hendricks went. The situation room buzzed to life as he strolled in, somewhat less dignified than usual. Deputy Chief Prefect Mallow followed closely behind, communicating with his men and the District Office via his wired cochlear. "Three Arbitration platoons have been dispatched to reinforce our position," he informed the Father. "The situation is still developing but the Chief is well aware of how delicate the situation is." "Delicate Hendricks spat. "Half the population of the upper levels are here!" The two scanned the chapel's intranet, searching for clues as to what was going on outside. The news feeds were buzzing with activity, and Hendricks didn't like any of it. Undercity scum had attacked three districts last night, and twelve more this morning. The scaled attack had strained the response ability of the local prefects and the Arbitration regiments. The Home fleet was being called in secure the situation. "Buffoons," Mallow muttered. "This will be the end of them." Hendricks wasn't so sure. He'd once guarded the Gates of Darkness, the thin black line separating the Undercity from the City of Light. He recalled images of the poor, huddled together in hopeless masses, desperate for food, water, shelter, comfort. He remembered watching the gangers beat innocent mothers to death, eager to induct her children into their ranks or perhaps simply hungry. He shuddered, eagerly pushung the imagery away. Three clapguns fired outside the chapel. Mallow looked at Hendricks fearfully and the two raced out of the situation room into the main chamber. Two prefects were in cover behind the pews, stutterguns leveled at the door. One updated Mallow as he and Hendricks approached. "They rode a barge up," he said tersely. Suddenly there was another clap and Hendricks was showered by stained glass. Instinct took over. He shielded his eyes and ducked behind a pew as more clapgun fire assailed the group from above. There were a few thuds the sound of wet meat being impacted by bullets. After a moment, the chapel settled into a calm silence. Hendricks peeked over the pew to see two gangers rappeling down from the now splintered stained glass murals. Another ganger was unlocking the chamber for the others. Mallow and his boys were dead. A new man walked in. He wasn't dressed like the others. He wore the faded fatigues of the Guardsmen, the company manning the Gates of Darkness. Father Hendricks recognized him immediately. He'd assumed the man died decades ago, after the fool deserted the Guard and fled into the Undercity. The man saw Hendricks and smiled, "Oh Son of Gold, forgive us for our trespasses, blessed though we are by thy comforts..... Oh son of Gold, teach the unillumined, so that they too may earn thy affections..." Hendricks stood and shed his outer cassock, which was peppered with glass flakes. "Martymy. I thought you were dead. You blaspheme this "Save it,'Brother' Hendricks," he replied smartly. "We haven't come for thy damned riches, nor thy gold though if thou oppose us too, I promise thee the same death that greeted these rascals of yours." Hendricks was rather confused. "Your ilk are attacking across the City, Martymy. This is an insurrection." The gangers, who apparently didn't understand the High Speech, growled, but Martymy simply chuckled. "This ain't an insurrection,'brother'. We need thy help. And we needs it now. Elsewise, we all will be dead by year's end." This was a City of Light. This was a City of God.
label: human

article: He didn't know how long he'd held the position, but it had been years. Every year the snow melted, the ground greened, and the corn came. There'd be rows on rows of tall, green stalks swaying in the breeze, and behind them, the sun setting in a fiery orange and pink sky. It was a beautiful sight, but he was tired. Tired of tending to the land day in and day out, tired of the same routine. One day, he decided to take a walk. He walked past the cornfields and into the neighboring woods, where he found a beautiful stream running through the trees. The water was clear and cool, and he took off his shoes and dipped his feet in. As he sat there, he realized how much he had been missing by staying in one place all his life. He had never traveled, never experienced different cultures or ways of life. He longed for adventure, to see the world beyond his farm. With a newfound sense of purpose, he returned home and began making plans. He sold his farm and used the money to travel the world, seeing new places and meeting new people. He had never been happier. And though he had initially been hesitant to leave the familiar comforts of his farm, he was now grateful for his decision. Life was meant to be lived, to be explored and experienced.

article: None Shall Triumph (in blood) None Shall Win (in sweat), Over the Hand that reaches us all (in tears), at our fearful final end. And then the gavel hit. It pounded and the sound vibrated louder and louder until it shook, and then overtook me. I closed my eyes and when I opened them I stood naked in a room with no door, no window, only a lone staircase that dropped down into deep darkness. My memory was foggy and my mind full of fleeting shapes and images. I knew not how I arrived, only that I should not linger and could not stay. Slowly, I began my descent. At the top the stairs were polished and smooth, the pathway wide and easy. Down, down, down I traveled with the ceiling growing lower, the way tighter, and the steps becoming steeper and uneven, becoming jagged with sharp pointed edges that cut and tore at my uncovered soles. Soon my feet began to bleed and hurt. I continued on for hours or days as my mind raced with dark thoughts. I knew not how long I traveled for the pain increased and caused time to lose all sense and meaning. I went until my slowed movements were but a mere hobble. I moved until I could almost move no more. It was then that the the steps stopped and opened upon a room. The second room was identical to the first: no door, no window, only a lone staircase leading down. I turned back to survey the way that I had come and saw that the stairs leading upward were gone, vanished. The only sign this was in fact a different room was the clear outline of my bloody footprints. Puzzled, I drew a long breath and after I circled the room a few times, a strange feeling came over me. The sounds and fleeting thoughts were gone. All was silent except the whisper of my breath. It was then that I knew this was not the place that I wanted, it felt off and alien, it felt wrong, and so with little longing or fear in my heart I approached the second set of stairs and again began my descent. This time the steps were not steep or sharp, but the air was thick and humid. At first the temperature was mild and warm then became increasingly uncomfortable. Breathing became difficult, and each breath I drew inward came in short and uneven bursts. I continued and the heat rose even more, soon big dollops of sweat formed on my brow, ran down my neck and back, down my legs, and stung my broken feet. I forced myself onward and my breath grew louder and louder, as the heat grew hotter and hotter. By now the water gushed off of me, each step grew more slippery with my sweat, and it came hard to stand. Eventually I lost my balance, fell to my knees, and almost tumbled down into the hellish abyss. I tried to stand, but my legs lacked the strength, so I crawled onward. Ages later when I reached the bottom of the second stair my body ached and I had grown frail with dehydration. I crawled into the third room and the temperature cooled. My feet throbbed, my body was thin and weak, and I collapsed onto the cool floor and in swimming blackness almost lost consciousness. I lay there in a haze until some of my strength returned and I was able to stand and look around the room. It was identical to the previous two: no door, no window, only a single staircase leading downward. It was here that my sanity wavered, and tiny tears welled at the corner of my eyes. It was here that fear formed at the edge of my mind and I almost surrendered. I dug deep, wiped the tears from my eyes, and started down the third stairway. Downward I went, outside and in. Quiet buzzing whispers filled my ears and heart, increasing in volume and propensity as my depth increased. Tears came freely, and blurred my vision. Tears came and fell as they were all I had, all that was left of me to give. At times I thrashed violently down the stair, kicking and screaming in grief laden yells. My broken feet and broken body were now matched by my broken heart and broken soul. I continued on and on, and then on even more. As the last step came into sight I stood and considered if it was even worth taking. I didn't think it was worth it. I didn't even care. Somehow, from one of the whispers a familiar feeling fell upon me and I was able to draw upon something deep inside. Somehow, I found the smallest reserve of hope and I continued downward past the final step. This time the room was different: there was still no door, no window, but now instead of a staircase it held a long dark tunnel..... that ascended and ended with a bright white light.
label: human

article: They don't usually answer back to what I say. Especially at first, they didn't just so you know. But the longer I've been here..... I've gotten to where I can hear them, all the time. They whisper at me, though, they never talk out loud. I don't know why. But they have these little whisper voices, and they do talk to me, just so you know. I mean, I have to be close. But I can hear them. I really can. The other day I sat down on a park bench by one woman and she was whispering about her baby. I couldn't tell exactly what she was saying, but she sounded pretty sad. I did my best to comfort her, just so you know. But she was pretty stiff. Pretty hard to talk to. She wouldn't stop talking about her baby. And yesterday, yesterday there was this old man. He was standing on the curb like he was about to cross the street, and if there had been cars coming I would have asked if he needed help. Not that it would do any good now, even if there were any cars -none of these people ever drive, for some reason. And I can't ever get a straight answer out of them when I ask them questions. It's almost like they can't hear me, except I know they can because they're people. They really are people, just so you know. But anyway. This old man. He was standing on the curb and when I walked by him I could hear him talking, too. He was whispering about his mother. I got real close, just to see if I could help him or something, and he just kept talking about how his mother would be worried if he didn't get home soon. Which is weird, because this guy was at least in his 80s; no way he'd have a mother still alive. He wouldn't respond to me, but I did try to help him, just so you know. It's hard, though, living where no one will talk to you. You actually start to feel invisible after a while, like you're a ghost or something. Recently, I've been wondering a lot whether or not I'm actually in some dream. I've gotten hurt several times, which you'd think would wake me up if I was dreaming, but I don't know what else this could be. The only place no one will talk to you is in your dreams. But I'll tell you what, I've gotten some advice from these people. They won't answer me or carry on a conversation, but I guess some of them have been able to tell what I've been thinking. I've been thinking that maybe to wake up, I need to actually die in this world. And I guess they heard me talking to myself about it or something, because lately every time I walk past somebody, they're telling me that I should go down to the river and jump in. At first I didn't see what good that would do, but then I realized that I could get one of those huge rocks down there and tie it to myself before I jumped. Tie the knot real tight, so it's hard to get loose. And once rope gets wet, it's about impossible to untie -just so you know. At first, I didn't take the suggestions seriously, but now it's to where all these people will whisper about is me jumping in. It's starting to drive me kind of crazy, actually. And I need to get them to shut up. I need to be able to wake up, to get back to where people will talk to me and not just whisper instructions about how to kill myself. Lately it's gotten to where I can hear them even when I'm not very close. All these different voices, telling me how to end this thing. I'm going down to the river tomorrow. Just so you know.
label: human

article: Wind brushes my bangs back like the familiar fingers of my mother. This touch is more soothing than her shriveled and cold hands would be now. She died three years ago. Before my father, after my brother. Now, in the familiar hospital courtyard that had become a second home, I pace. Chris went in for surgery four hours ago. The procedure is typically two. Somehow, though I know it's impossible, I sense a shadow in the corner of my vision, one who has found a home there my whole life. Much as I have found a home among these rickety benches and inappropriately cheerful flowers. When I was born, my grandparents both died. " You certainly can't blame yourself for their death! You were an infant! ," is what you must be thinking. But no. They were fatally injured in an accident on the way to the hospital to see me. Luckily they made it to the same hospital. Unluckily, I never met them because they never regained consciousness after the crash. My other set never visited. Perhaps it was all the better for their health. Michael, my brother, died at the ripe age of four, in this same hospital. Scarlet fever. My mother? Breast cancer. My father was attacked by a burglar and suffered fatal injuries. He died in this hospital too. Countless pets throughout my childhood, all for different reasons. Nothing connected them. There was no commonality, no definable cause. Aside from me. Now Chris. Knowing my penchant for destroying life, love wasn't a thought I entertained, but a lifestyle that he forced upon me. For a few years, I was so grateful for that persuasion. But here I am now, in the same hospital that I was born in, where I watched my family die. Looking at my watch, it has now been five hours since Chris was wheeled away for a two hour surgery. " Mrs. Gray? " A nurse stands by the door, clipboard in hand. Turning towards her the shadow in the corner of my vision shifts. Still there.
label: human

article: I start to gulp it down, leaving no drop to chance. For a short few seconds my worries fade as I finish the concoction with what little breath remains. Gasping, I slam the glass down. Well that tasted like bleach. I sit down on the sofa, pushing off the empty pizza boxes. My stomach begins to squeal. I force the liquid down as it tries to make a comeback. I should've stuck with Tinder. Silence at last. Knocks sound from the front door. That was fast, was this it? I walk over and swing it open. To my disbelief, a 910 was standing on the other side. I raise my eyebrows and say, "Hello." She looks straight through me. "Are you John? " , she says trembling. "I was last time I checked, sorry do I know you?." "I live next door, I can't see, you've got to help me!" "You can't see?" I lead her inside and try to comfort her. My head begins to buzz. "I just bought a'remedy' from the homeless man at the end of the street." My butt begins to clench. "Not old billy bob?" "Yeah, billy bob," she replies weeping. Fuck, "And you drank it?" I start walking towards the kitchen. "I drank it. I think it was bleach! " , she bursts into more tears. My vision becomes hazy. "Oh god, billy got me too." I run back to the girl and look straight at her. "You're the most beautiful girl I've ever seen." Darkness starts to surround me. She looks up and smiles, "Classic billy." I laugh as I become completely blind, "Classic billy indeed."

article: My power? It's ridiculously simple. I can amplify electrical energy. Something as simple as a AA battery could power a megawatt laser for a second or two with enough amplification. I'm still limited to the energy stored within the power source, be it a battery, a capacitor, or a simple generator. Fortunately, I continued on to college instead of trying to make a name for myself as a hero. Got a degree in computer engineering. Seems pointless, but its become very beneficial. You see, I can act like a powerful transistor as a bypart of the electrical amplification - something as simple as a small pulse from my power could create a massive electrical bolt between my palms. It hurts like hell to do - I didn't get rapid regeneration or electrically insensitive as powers or side effects - but it makes supplying massive amounts of power to one place a pinch. Weirdly, it also turns out that, by using my amplification on an extremely small scale, I can compute things as well. With enough transistor action going on, I can compute numerous things at once. It's become useful for field computing, where all we have as a power source is a battery and maybe some solar panels. And fortunately, there's been a few cases where I'm needed for field computing in remote areas. The last time I went into the field was in a case involving the equally unknown "Bendy McBendface" - he was once a famous gymnast and performer as he's incredibly flexible and can bend parts of his body in ways that it was not structured for - and once I recognized who we were dealing with I started computing. He's flexible, beyond human standards. Is he rubber-like? That makes any electrical attacks useless, yet if he was rubber-like he could compress easily as well and act like a spring. He doesn't spring around, nor does he compress. Must not be rubber then. What about silicone? No, too flexible. Silicone would bend out of shape at his weight. Hmm..... if he can bend so well, perhaps his bones are slightly more flexible than normal, designed like a living hinge. And when it comes to his joints, perhaps he's double or triple jointed, resulting in extreme flexibility. All of that computed in a couple of seconds, I set about setting up a passive computing system that would calculate his possible movements and how he moves. If my bone and joint theory is correct, he should be subdued quickly. I pull out my favorite weapon - a AAA battery electric pistol. Fires small bolts of electricity that are amped up to thousands of volts and normally around 32 amps per short. Holds six AAA batteries before I got ta reload too. I dash closer to Bendy McBendface. I need to keep my distance, if my theory is incorrect and he's more like silicone or rubber, it means he can stretch out and grip onto me. I prep my pistol. Batteries: loaded. Amplification system: ready. Target: within range. I pull the trigger and engage the entire amplification system to drain the AAA battery in a fraction of a second. A loud pop is heard, with an incredibly bright bolt of electricity as it grounds to Bendy's body. I run some final computations to analyze Bendy as his body responds to the electric shock. He certainly isn't rubber-like or silicone-like. Definitely mostly water, like a normal human. I see his bones shine dimly through his skin. The theory was correct. His bones are indeed living hinges. And if my brief foray into materials science is correct, his bones should shatter into individual pieces, leaving his bending ability useless. With Bendy McBendface subdued, I call the police to take him to jail. "You're going to want to wear some rubber gloves. He's still pretty electrified. Yeah, I can see the lighting bolts spread over his skin as it tries to ground. Better get here soon, if he grounds I can't guarantee what will happen." I walk away from the slowly convulsing body of Bendy McBendface. None of the other heroes were successful with him. Iron Man had tried, but Bendy would always flex away and avoid attacks, and any computations were simply too slow to provide good information. Captain America failed worse, with Bendy simply absorbing and deflecting most of the shield throws. Yet somehow, the guy with a simple power and a degree relating to the power managed to take down someone who escaped everyone else. I have a simple name. Quanta.
