article: " I HATE YOU! " I screamed into the night. My eyes, stinging from the hot tears streaming down my face, fell silently onto the frost-tipped grass at my feet. Shivering, I took another swig from the bottle of poison in my hand. John tried to take the bottle from me in a slow, friendly gesture. " Save some for me, man " he offered, much to my dismay. " Fuck off, John. Just... " I trailed off, my eyes fixated on the pitiful sight before us. The dilapidated house that sat before us was not even worth a second glance. In fact, this entire neighborhood was one trainwreck after another. This truly was where sad souls curled up to die, a reminder that there exists a whole segment of the population that simply survives until they get old enough to expire. My phone buzzed angrily in my pocket, but obviously I couldn't get it out of my pocket right now. Instead, I lazily absorbed the unkept yard and the peeling paint in blurred images between long, slow blinks. The porch swing rocked ever so slightly on its rusted chains in the cool night breeze. As if anyone would ever sit on that thing, anyways. Against my will, my feet began the trek towards this small house. It really was small, so small. So insignificantly small. Like you could squash it in the palm of- Before I realized it, I was already at the door. Uncomfortably close to the door. Too close. My nose pressed against the wood, the smell of faded paint again reminding me of how shitty this house truly was. I felt the familiar tug of John's guiding hand on my shoulder. " Hey man, it's been a long day. Let's just head back, yeah? " I squared up to him, attempting to impersonate weighing my options carefully. " Yeah..... Uh, actually I was thinking..... " With that, I reared back and hurled the glass bottle at the door, roaring " NO! " as loud as I could muster. John quickly recoiled as shards and booze covered the both of us. " The hell, man? " He stood motionless, apparently at a loss for how to react to my outburst. I locked my eyes with his, and reached for the door. Unlocked, of course. I bet there was nothing of value in the this house, anyways. He remained motionless at the door as I walked through the door, paralyzed by my sudden violence. Alone, I stepped into the house. Barely furnished, the place looked like it was probably another drug den in the neighborhood. Emboldened by my easy entrance, I yelled into the void, " Hello? Anyone home? " I laughed, nearly hysterically, and swung around expecting to see John reluctantly following me into the house. Except he didn't. I could barely make out his shoulders, hunched forward, making his way back towards the street. The sudden realization that I was alone in the darkness brought me quickly back to reality. In reality, I knew this house. I remembered everything. Specifically, exactly where I was standing, I could remember at least a half dozen times I had been mercilessly beaten with his belt. Sometimes it was recompense for some made-up sin, and sometimes just because I was in the wrong place at the wrong time. I remembered the scars that would run up and down my left arm, a long-forgotten memory buried deep somewhere. And then the tears came again. The hatred mixed with sorrow. The seething hatred that he could be so goddamn selfish. To leave without so much as a goodbye, to be so distant for so long. His capacity for inflicting physical pain was matched only by his ability to cripple me emotionally. To make me feel less than worthless, to actively avoid my life. My God, the effort that it takes to go on like that for years. I went to reach for the scars on my left arm, to come up empty handed, again. A recurring motion - ingrained since childhood - that I hadn't yet learn to abandon. He missed everything. Teaching me to drive, giving me tips on girls, celebrating my high school graduation, joining the Army, graduating Basic. He missed everything. But I hated him most when I came back home and he wasn't there. I came back a shell of my former self. After the blast, my whole life changed. In the mirror, I looked back at a cripple. A former high school athlete, a goddamn Soldier, now nothing more than a one-armed fuck. I hated myself. But I hated him more than I hated myself. He knew - he knew because I saw him once - but he was too scared. Scared of coming back. Scared of becoming the man he should've been for me all along. How long had I been staring at the floor? A minute? An hour? A day? I stood in the pitch-black living room, tears dripping onto the dusty floor beneath me. Lost, without purpose, I began to wander into the hallway. At the end, foreboding, stood a single white door. As I approached the door in the darkness, I noticed how utterly silent the house was around me. It seemed to be especially cold and devoid of life. His face was cold and devoid of life. Hours ago, in his casket, he looked as emotionless as I remembered him as a child. Stern, unforgiving. But here, dead, he seemed to have proven that he really could not give two shits about me. That he could go this long and, even in his dying days, still ignore his son. His son. Me. I opened the door. Time stopped. I saw the bedsheets of a dead man. The awkward way they fell halfway off the bed, unmade during his final day in this world. His dresser had a single drawer open, probably missing the last set of clothes he wore. But what caught my eye was the closet. A sense of dread rushed over me, a primal fear of the unknown. The light in the closet was on. I crept towards the closet, fearful of... Of what? My right hand grasped the handle, and I gently eased the door open. The yellow light softly bathed his closet. The first thing I noticed was that he didn't have anything hanging in his closet. And then I saw it. Sitting neatly against the back of the closet was a single end table, about two feet tall. In the center was a framed picture of my high school portrait. I could feel the lump in my throat growing. To the left of my portrait was my Purple Heart that I had thrown in his face when he dared to visit me years ago. To the right of my portrait was a single, faded Polaroid of us both smiling as he pushed me on my first bike. And that was it. Those three items, sitting lonely on the end table in the closet. I dropped to my knees, my chest shuddering with every breath. " I hate you, " I muttered under my breath, less convincingly this time.

article: We present a new learning-based method for multi-frame depth estimation from a color video, which is a fundamental problem in scene understanding, robot navigation or handheld 3D reconstruction. While recent learning-based methods estimate depth at high accuracy, 3D point clouds exported from their depth maps often fail to preserve important geometric feature (e.g., corners, edges, planes) of man-made scenes. Widely-used pixel-wise depth errors do not specifically penalize inconsistency on these features. These inaccuracies are particularly severe when subsequent depth reconstructions are accumulated in an attempt to scan a full environment with man-made objects with this kind of features. Our depth estimation algorithm therefore introduces a Combined Normal Map (CNM) constraint, which is designed to better preserve high-curvature features and global planar regions. In order to further improve the depth estimation accuracy, we introduce a new occlusion-aware strategy that aggregates initial depth predictions from multiple adjacent views into one final depth map and one occlusion probability map for the current reference view. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of depth estimation accuracy, and preserves essential geometric features of man-made indoor scenes much better than other algorithms.

article: In this paper, we develop an online active mapping system to enable a quadruped robot to autonomously survey large physical structures. We describe the perception, planning and control modules needed to scan and reconstruct an object of interest, without requiring a prior model. The system builds a voxel representation of the object, and iteratively determines the Next-Best-View (NBV) to extend the representation, according to both the reconstruction itself and to avoid collisions with the environment. By computing the expected information gain of a set of candidate scan locations sampled on the as-sensed terrain map, as well as the cost of reaching these candidates, the robot decides the NBV for further exploration. The robot plans an optimal path towards the NBV, avoiding obstacles and un-traversable terrain. Experimental results on both simulated and real-world environments show the capability and efficiency of our system. Finally we present a full system demonstration on the real robot, the ANYbotics ANYmal, autonomously reconstructing a building facade and an industrial structure.

article: We propose the PeerRank method for peer assessment. This constructs a grade for an agent based on the grades proposed by the agents evaluating the agent. Since the grade of an agent is a measure of their ability to grade correctly, the PeerRank method weights grades by the grades of the grading agent. The PeerRank method also provides an incentive for agents to grade correctly. As the grades of an agent depend on the grades of the grading agents, and as these grades themselves depend on the grades of other agents, we define the PeerRank method by a fixed point equation similar to the PageRank method for ranking web-pages. We identify some formal properties of the PeerRank method (for example, it satisfies axioms of unanimity, no dummy, no discrimination and symmetry), discuss some examples, compare with related work and evaluate the performance on some synthetic data. Our results show considerable promise, reducing the error in grade predictions by a factor of 2 or more in many cases over the natural baseline of averaging peer grades.

article: "No, seriously, we do love our humans..... we just..... don't want to come off clingy." The kitten scratched itself a bit. "That's what mama taught me, anyway. Keep your distance but always make it clear you love them. S'kinda hard." "Okay..... then how do you explain the glasses?" I said, stretching a bit. "Glasses?" She tilted her head. I stumbled for an explanation that didn't go in circles, until she reacted. "The floating liquids! We just want a drink but they keep on leaping off the edge rather than be drank!" "Oh..... that explains a lot..." I tried to think of other things. "What else can you tell me about other animals?" "The less'cuddly' something is like a reptile, the more they LOVE affection. We all do, but you know how it is." She groomed herself between comments. "There are as many DOGS who look down on their humans as you think us cats do. Birds that can speak your language know WAY more than they let on. And those tiny scrawny purse-carried dogs really do think they're much bigger..... until you scratch some sense into them." Did I just catch her trying to smirk? "Oh, and you know how you can tell how good someone is by how we respond to them? We judge other animals by how good they are to humans. Especially kids. Your cubs are the ultimate test of character to us. Anyone who can't keep their cool around a curious human-cub is generally no one we want to associate with." I leaned back in my chair. "Wow..... the things I never thought about." "You should. We're not all that different, socially." She curled up. "Naptime..... plus the vet's coming." I panicked a bit and grabbed my textbook just in time for the door to open. "You sure you're going to be okay on night watch, Jake? It can get awful boring, and you'll be locked in, save for emergencies." The head veterinarian, here to check on me before she left. "Oh I'll be fine! I have my textbooks, some music, a game or two..... I can make it the night!" I said, looking down at my book to hide a smirk. "Besides..... I have a lot to learn tonight..."

article: Formalizing self reproduction in dynamical hierarchies is one of the important problems in Artificial Life (AL) studies. We study, in this paper, an inductively defined algebraic framework for self reproduction on macroscopic organizational levels under dynamical system setting for simulated AL models and explore some existential results. Starting with defining self reproduction for atomic entities we define self reproduction with possible mutations on higher organizational levels in terms of hierarchical sets and the corresponding inductively defined 'meta' - reactions. We introduce constraints to distinguish a collection of entities from genuine cases of emergent organizational structures.

article: "It is not with great enthusiasm by which I draw the sword upon you, my lord. It is simply obligation in response to a premonition that has been growing its seed throughout the land. The will of the people, if you will. The common people you have so overtly chosen to forego in your desire to champion this city's quest for glory." The man sat against the castle wall, helpless, the sharp blade tip of the man's sword hovering around his face. He was adorned from head to toe in clothing and jewelry crafted from countless hours of hard work and sweat, and yet he wore these testaments to his great power and influence without appreciation. Sweat bore down his red face and he stared into the eyes of what would be his killer with simultaneous fear and rage, too proud to look away. He responded, "You say this as though I am betrothed to these people. They are mongrels, thieves," Speaking up louder with a stronger hint of misanthropy he added, " .... Rats. I owe no allegiance to them, and the mere fact that they've paid you to kill me only shows stupidity on their behalf. When I am gone, another will simply take over and they will lose even more of their freedom. Of course, how foolish of me that I should expect these savage peasants to know this." The sword tip drew closer, the cold steel side of the weapon rubbing against his neck, causing him to breathe heavier and his eyes to grow wider. The attacker, dressed in ragged cloth and with dirt on his face and unkempt long hair replied, "You know nothing of these people. We will die before the empire has reign over us. The sweetest feeling in the world is fighting for something you believe in and showing no mercy to your enemies, and death is a small price to pay for something so grand as that.." He pushed the sword through the man's neck, smiling in near laughter as he briefly writhed in pain and then lost consciousnesses with blood spilling down onto his finely constructed garments.

article: Laura slammed her hand on the table, her face growing hot with anger. " Damn it, Jim. We can't just give up. " Jim shrugged, taking another large gulp from his glass. He reeked of whisky, as if he bathed in it. It wouldn't be too surprising considering the myriad of brown stains on his lab coat. " What do you want me to do? " he asked, his words slurred. " We've done all that I could. It's a losing battle. " " But it's not. As long as we keep working, we can figure something, right guys? " Laura looked to the others in the room but they averted their gazes. They all looked exhausted, many working until they fell asleep. And once they woke up, they stretched and continued from where they left off. " Dr. Jeger has a point, " the assistant girl with mousy brown hair said. She hardly spoke but sounded more convinced than ever before. " All we've been able to learn about this mysterious disease is that it replicates fast and is deadly. However, that doesn't explain why it reanimates corpses. It just doesn't make sense. " The others mumbled in agreement, bobbing their heads like buoys riding gentle waves. Laura frowned. She was alone on this one. " But we have a responsibility as CDC workers to analyze this disease. Otherwise, we may as well kiss civilization goodbye. " " Kiss it goodbye? " Jim said, chuckling. " It's been dead since the outbreak started. You may think we still have humanity in us but as soon as our food supply gets low, you'll see what people do when they want to survive. I wouldn't be surprised if you all will be at each other's throats by the end of the week. " Again, the mumbles rose in volume. This time, shifty glances were exchanged, the tension in the air palpable. It didn't take much to anger someone as of late. A lack of food and little rest was the perfect recipe for disaster. " And what about the refugees? " Laura asked. " We're sheltering hundreds of people here who think we have a solution to their problems. If we don't figure something out, they may revolt. " An older scientist stood forward, his eyes hidden by the light reflecting off his glasses. He must have been from a hospital or other research facility. Laura didn't recognize his face. " They are already revolting. Someone got their throat slit just earlier this morning over some stupid game. It's a madhouse down there. Without any rules, they're like a bunch of animals. " " Which is exactly what I wanted to speak about, " Jim said, draining the last of the alcohol in his cup. Laura narrowed her eyes, already skeptical. " And what is that? " " We're running out of supplies - fast. Either we try to squeeze by with what we have and hope the government comes to the rescue or we... reevaluate our system here. " " I'm afraid I don't understand what you mean, " Laura said, folding her arms. Jim scoffed, slamming his cup down harder than needed. Most jumped at the sound of it. " You can be so stupid for such a brilliant scientist, Laura. But if you need me to spell it out for you, I will. Without us, a cure can't be found. Thus, we need the supplies far more than the freeloaders down there. I propose we should cut the dead weight and save what little we have for us. We could easily stretch it for a few months if we're smart about it. That should be enough time to at least find a temporary solution " At first, there was a deafening silence. Then, whispers turned into full conversations. In practically no time, everyone agreed with the plan. That was, expect for Laura. " And how do you plan to get rid of all the people we took in? " Jim stared at her, uncomfortably long. Something in his eyes was different, almost dead. " We open the doors at dawn. All the refugees will have to find somewhere else to live. Those who make it out survive. Those who don't become lunch for those monsters. It's fucked up but that's what this world is like now. " " Dawn? " Laura parroted, dumbstruck. " But that's only a few hours away. How do you plan on letting them know in time so they can prepare? " Jim flashed her a grin, so unsettling that it sent chills up her spine. " Unfortunately, that is problematic, " he said. " I won't have time to explain all this to them. "

article: So first off, I should probably disclose that I'm a science journalist who writes about molecular biology. I finished up my BA in biology last year, and since then I've been freelancing and blogging about the biomedical community in Boston. I spend pretty much all day, every day, either reading, writing, or interviewing scientists about science, and if I'm not doing one of those things, I'm probably sitting in on a lecture about cell biology at MIT or Harvard. I'm not a scientist, but I have a much stronger biology background than the average person on the street, and if you're going to argue with the scientific aspects of my view, you're gonna need sources. For the purposes of this CMV, I'm defining "eugenics" as "limiting who can reproduce with who on the basis of their phenotypes because people who have undesirable phenotypes must have bad genes." I'm not here to debate the ethics of eugenics; my view is that with the exception of genetic disorders that have been traced to point mutations (mutations in a single DNA base pair, like progeria) or specific chromosomal abnormalities (like Down Syndrome), eugenics flat-out isn't going to work. Because genes are NOT destiny. They are not even close to being destiny, and anyone who says they are or advocates reproductive policy based on the assumption that genes are destiny doesn't understand what genes do. Here's a quick breakdown of the "Central Dogma of Genetics": The DNA is in the nucleus. It is a blue print, but it doesn't actively influence a trait until... A polymerase (an enzyme complex that builds DNA RNA) comes along and makes a messenger RNA for a particular gene, but it's still not a phenotypic trait until... The mRNA goes to the ribosome. There a protein-assembly complex reads the base pairs on the RNA strand and based on the codons on that strand (a codon is a set of three nucleotide base pairs that tells the protein-assembly complex either "start making an amino acid chain," "add amino acid [X]," or "stop building the an amino acid chain, the protein-assembler adds amino acids to the chain until it hits a stop codon... Then the amino acid chain gets folded up into a protein... Then said protein will start floating around (or get added to an existing cell structure) and based on what other proteins it bumps intointeracts with, that's how you get a trait. Not the genes at the beginning of the process; the proteins at the end. Here are a few examples (and by no means comprehensive list) of purely biological things that can go wrong between the DNA and the final trait: Before the polymerase can copy the gene, it has to land on a DNA region called the "promoter region," which is located just before the protein-coding region (e.g. the "actual gene. If the promoter region isn't accessible to the polymerase (They can get wrapped around things called histones or get stuck to the walls of the cell nucleus), then the gene won't get transcribed, and the protein won't get made. You might get a "bad" phenotype. The polymerase can make a mistake, so there's a mutation in the mRNA even though the DNA is "correct." Sometimes even thought the DNA and mRNA base pairs are error-free, a cell can end up making way too many copies (or way to few of a particular protein), which leads to a bad phenotype. The mRNA can get waylaid, lost, or destroyed on the way to the ribosome. The protein-assembly complex can make a mistake. Sometimes even when the DNA, the mRNA, and the amino acid chain are "correct," the protein gets "misfolded" or "spliced" in the wrong place, so it ends up being the wrong shape. If it's the wrong shape, it can't do its job, leading to a bad phenotype. Different cell types are supposed to produce different quantities of different proteins. That's why your eye cells are different from your muscle cells, even though they have the same DNA.This variation is called gene expression. And it can be messed with through all kinds of things- stress, environmental exposure to pollutants, diet, being on meds all the time, radiation- everything. The reason I'm throwing all this science at this thread is, because most people I've encountered who empathize andor sympathize with eugenic ideas seem to have no idea what gene expression is. That really bothers me, because we're going into an era when gene-sequencing is going to be more and more readily available. Don't get me wrong: you can tell a lot about what conditions a person is predisposed to based on DNA sequences, but there are many medical disorders and conditions where you really can't tell for sure. If people don't want to have kids because they don't want to pass on genes that might predispose their kids to certain cancers or psychiatric disorders, that's a completely valid and reasonable personal decision. But I take issue with people who pass judgement on parents by saying, "Well, heshe's an asshole, bc if heshe knew there was a history of autism in the family, they shouldn't have had kids. They're bringing society down." Because frankly, even if they had gene sequences, that wouldn't have been enough information to predict the severity of the kid's impairments or how much distress the kid would feel as a result of their condition. I think people who favor eugenics are severely underestimating the complexity of our biology, and that attempts to control traits at the population level are going to backfire. (Heterozygosity- having two different alleles for the same trait- actually helps to prevent disease in many cases, and saying that people who are carriers for certain traits shouldn't reproduce might actually negatively impact heterozygosity and genetic diversity). I also think that it's important for people to recognize that we're not going to find one single treatment that "cures" all cancers or all mental illnesses. Denying the complexity of how genes influence our traits actually does a disservice to the scientists who are trying to find medication targets and to the people who need those medications to get well. Believing that ailments can be prevented through eugenics is an extreme manifestation of denial about how biologically complex we are. CMV. Edit: formatting Hello, users of CMV! article: Genuinely looking for a good reason why some people are so caught up in the purity of their dog's blood line, cause I'm just not getting it. The way I see it, while developing specific breeds at one point made sense because dogs served different functions, at this point it's doing more harm (in the form of inbreeding and creating a market for irresponsible overbreeding) than good and doesn't need to be practiced any more. Wanting a dog with a specific personality need a specific breed for a specific job Disposition and manners are going to have a lot more to do with upbringing, imo, than species. Obviously that's a generalization, as something like energy level cannot be trained out of a dog. But it's pretty easy to gauge things like that in a dog whose bloodline you don't know by just hanging out with them a little- terriershepherd looking dogs that are bouncing off the walls are probably going to be high energy. That doesn't require a pedigree to determine. Similarly, I can't think of a reason why a service dog would need to be 100 of a specific breed. Looking for a general type of dog makes sense, but why you would need a purebred lab and couldn't make do with a lab-x from a shelter is beyond me. Mutts are intelligent and trainable and possess the physical attributes required of any dog job. Not all of them, obviously, but not all purebred dogs are cut out to be police service drug dogs either. The training and weeding out process is in place regardless, there's no reason a mutt couldn't go through it and I'd be willing to bet just as many would come out on the other side as the pure dogs. Purebreed for the purpose of keeping a breed in existence breeding for show These are not wild animals which humans have been killing off via habitat loss and poaching. Specific breeds were created by man, and it's cruel and unnecessary to inbreed them to the point of mental and physical illness for the purpose of maintaining some man-made breed standard. Dog shows seems superficial and meaningless to me and nobody's ever been able to articulate a reason why they aren't. I get liking a particular look. My family has two little mutts and I love them to bits but fantasize about getting a Great Dane when I'm out of university. However, I really can't conceive of a reason why I'd need to ensure that a dog I'd adopt was 100 Dane to satisfy that desire. I'll visit a bunch of pounds and find a Dane-ish looking dog, or go to a Dane rescue, and be ecstatic with whatever doggy I find. Please change my view so I can be more empathetic when people tell me they got their dog from a purebred breeder and I won't secretly judge them anymore! edit: formatting EDIT: My view's been changed! article: "GOD HAS COME TO REAP THE SINNERS, FOR NO GODLY MAN WALKS THE EARTH!" That was the declaration that echoed across the face of the world. The skies shook. The oceans boiled. Animals cowered in terror as beings of light and fire descended upon the their homes, searching for injustice to avenge. But they found none. The Heavens had opened too late, for while eternity stretched before their eyes and they prepared to sound the final horn, the end of the world and come and gone without note. Not with fanfare or shock or gnashing of teeth, but with a simple change of address. it was true, indeed, that no godly man, woman, or child had walked the earth in many years. However, it would be more accurate to note that no man, woman, or child had walked the earth in many years. When the lights of Heaven's vigil began to die across the globe, the angels feared a crisis of faith. When the last went out before the appointed day with no notice or reason, their fear turned to anger at a world assuredly more warped and corrupt than any since the time of Noah. God and his hosts descended upon this bleak world, expecting to find a den of devils and blasphemers to be wiped clean and begun anew with extreme prejudice. They remain there to this day, booming out warnings and lessons that no one will hear, and searching for sins that no one will commit. Their audience lies far away, a divide of both stars and knowledge, separate as oil and water. There, on the dead worlds and discarded rocks of creations past, flourishing with new life and purpose. Earth is but a fading memory here, and its forgotten gods grow even dimmer. No eyes turn to see the flickering lights across the surface of their ancestral home. No ears tune in to hear the words and warnings that held Adam's brood enraptured for thousands of years. Their attention faces forward, onward into the unknown depths that they are only just beginning to cultivate. The Heavenly Hosts waited too long to make their presence known. Now they are but ghosts, wailing in a ruin.

article: The increasing adoption of Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices present new challenges to digital forensic investigators and law enforcement agencies when investigation into cybercrime on these new platforms are required. However, there has been no formal study to document actual challenges faced by investigators and whether existing tools help them in their work. Prior issues such as the correlation and consistency problem in digital forensic evidence have also become a pressing concern in light of numerous evidence sources from IoT devices. Motivated by these observations, we conduct a user study with 39 digital forensic investigators from both public and private sectors to document the challenges they faced in traditional and IoT digital forensics. We also created a tool, Stitcher , that addresses the technical challenges faced by investigators when handling IoT digital forensics investigation. We simulated an IoT crime that mimics sophisticated cybercriminals and invited our user study participants to utilize Stitcher to investigate the crime. The efficacy of Stitcher is confirmed by our study results where 96.2 of users indicated that Stitcher assisted them in handling the crime, and 61.5 of users who used Stitcher with its full features solved the crime completely.

article: Somewhere below, a trickster god is laughing when he isn't howling. That's what Morden's heard since he arrived, still reeling from the death blow to his chest, all his ribs tingling and intact. The trickster god, the wolf mother, Odin son. Everyone around here has so many titles. "If I ever see the great prick below, I'm going to break something of his," Morden says. There's twenty metal pieces in his hands, some from the copper age, some from his age. Rusted green copper meshing with silky blue plastic alloy. It works as well as he expected it to; they'd fired the cannon once before everything broke again. "Not his fault we're using something from the revolution," Gaggle says, muffled around the hammer between his teeth. There's five of them gathered around the cannon. There's a hole in barrel, a weird dip in the outer rim that makes cannon balls plop ten feet out. They're trying to patchwork it with whatever they found nearby. Again. Imperious, their new Roman recruit, asks which revolution, then swears when broken iron shears through his hand. "Get that looked at," Morden says, not looking at it. If they had a thermal heater, a blow torch, a damned lighter, maybe they could fit the pieces in right. Their regiment is down to seven, was down to forty when Morden had joined. Seven plus the cannon is a cramping number in trenches. Mud slicks down their shoes and elbows bump. If they went up, they would be shot by bullets or arrows, and dying to such primitive weapons is an insult to Morden. Course, chances were, their trench would fill with poison when the big snake got upset again. "Maybe we should ditch the cannon?" Obbol asks, knee deep in muck. She keeps scratching her chin, until it turns red. The death itch, the tingle-prickle Morden can't get out of his ribs. "I think we missed a giant, last time. What good is it if we can't hit a giant?" "Well," Gaggle shouts, over the noise of his hammer. "Giants are tricky to hit anyways. I've seen some of them phase out, like mirages, and appear somewhere else. Hard to hit a thing like that." "You drank mead," Morden says. "That stuffs made for gods, who at the least are twenty feet taller than you." Around their little group are screams and bangs, the firecracker whoosh of small missiles, and the chitter-thunk of missed arrows. "You could barely handle Imperious's wine, so I'm impressed you didn't vomit something important." There's laughter, and Imperious groaning over his wine. It's more than the battle noises around them. Obbol slows her pacing, and Gabby finally pulls his nails from his mouth. Stabilize, calm, prepare; it was a mantra in Morden's training. He'd discovered, on his own, that laughter did the first two. The cannon's ready, and they tug it up the trench lip. Straight up into a muzzle made of dark coffee black, two eyes like harvest moons. Gaggle whispers, "Fenrir, ah shit," and Obbol clamps hard onto the cannon to aim it straight between those eyes. The wolf focuses on them, and suddenly it is bigger, a monolith and monster, towering over them, blocking out the alien stars of this world. Breath rancid between the wet yellow teeth it bares. No one can move. No one can fight. Morden is a rabbit in the corner, worn out, ragged from the chase. He can feel the teeth around his neck, in his neck. The killing bite spilling his blood. This is death part two, more permanent, for there is no battlefield afterlife in a second failure. There is no heaven in the wolf's eyes. Then Fenrir turns, sniffs, howls, and darts off. Morden leans against the cannon, breathing slow and hard. "What's Cujo after?" Gabby asks. They turn to look. It is the first time Morden sees a god. He is tall enough to match the wolf, one eye beneath his cloak, with ravens fluttering over his shoulders. He meets the wolf's charge, swings his staff, and dies in a quick snap of neck bone. "Ah shit," Gaggle says. The wolf stands beside the god's corpse. It is waiting. And all the battlefield dims to silence, waiting too. "Time's up," Gaggle continues, in a drained laughing voice. "We had our little play fight, but the gods have run out of delaying time." There is a trickster god below, but he will be free now. There is a snake beneath the ground, and it will die soon. There is a prophecy writ in stone and hanged man's blood; it demands every god die, and the world burn with them. "Yeah, time's up," Morden says, and slaps Gaggle's head. "Get this cannon moving. We're all done for, but first, we're going to shoot a god with this thing."

article: Unmanned Aerial vehicles (UAV) are a promising technology for smart farming related applications. Aerial monitoring of agriculture farms with UAV enables key decision-making pertaining to crop monitoring. Advancements in deep learning techniques have further enhanced the precision and reliability of aerial imagery based analysis. The capabilities to mount various kinds of sensors (RGB, spectral cameras) on UAV allows remote crop analysis applications such as vegetation classification and segmentation, crop counting, yield monitoring and prediction, crop mapping, weed detection, disease and nutrient deficiency detection and others. A significant amount of studies are found in the literature that explores UAV for smart farming applications. In this paper, a review of studies applying deep learning on UAV imagery for smart farming is presented. Based on the application, we have classified these studies into five major groups including: vegetation identification, classification and segmentation, crop counting and yield predictions, crop mapping, weed detection and crop disease and nutrient deficiency detection. An in depth critical analysis of each study is provided.

article: Any electric arc discharge is extremely hot, even the static pop you get from the doorknob. The key is that the heat is extremely localized too. Only a miniscule volume of air is actually heated to that temperature and it rapidly dissipates. For small shocks it's not even enough to elevate the temperature of your hand, much less burn. For "god hates you" level shocks from above, it'll definitely do some damage. Electricity prefers to travel across surfaces instead of through the center so even in a lightning strike scenario a lot of the burn is superficial. Extremely painful, but often not deep enough to destroy organs.

article: Sparse polynomial chaos expansions are a popular surrogate modelling method that takes advantage of the properties of polynomial chaos expansions (PCE), the sparsity-of-effects principle, and powerful sparse regression solvers to approximate computer models with many input parameters, relying on only few model evaluations. Within the last decade, a large number of algorithms for the computation of sparse PCE have been published in the applied math and engineering literature. We present an extensive review of the existing methods and develop a framework to classify the algorithms. Furthermore, we conduct a benchmark on a selection of methods to identify which methods work best in practical applications. Comparing their accuracy on several benchmark models of varying dimension and complexity, we find that the choice of sparse regression solver and sampling scheme for the computation of a sparse PCE surrogate can make a significant difference, of up to several orders of magnitude in the resulting mean-square error. Different methods seem to be superior in different regimes of model dimensionality and experimental design size.

article: I probably should clarify before I get a thousand replies from ratheism users. I'm an atheist, I believe in evolution and all that jazz. However, I don't believe in science's ability to provide capital-T definite Truths, only small-t truths (or what I consider to be tentative truths), which are marred by social influences, human blindness and methodological flaws. I believe there is, to some degree, a scientism to be wary of when considering questions of what we know, and do not accept anything just because it is stated to be "science," but based on a pragmatic assessment of the work's epistemological value (which I recognize, of course, to be built upon my own premises, as I am not a perfect arbiter of truth either, and ultimately requires a lot of research in order to fully understand what is being presented to me) in order to determine on a personal basis how believable the evidence is, though, of course, it is never perfect. The reason I do this is because I think that taking science as authority in itself is a flawed premise to come from, and that the questioning of science is more in line with scientific principle than not. Firstly due to the fact that science relies on a succession of paradigms (in the Kuhnian sense), but also because too often I see people purport scientific claims that are ill-founded and based on unreasonable grounds. Further, I see a danger in entrusting science without due consideration, scientists being within a social frame, to make accurate determinations without bias necessarily, be it political in nature (such as the old scientific racism or modern day neurosexism) or just by chasing the random whims of their mind's eye (I see string theory like this often, if only because it doesn't even meet Popperian requirements of falsification, at least not yet). However, often I run into people who bawk at the questioning of a reified Science in any capacity, and am confused for the sort of person who may be a climate change denialist or an intelligent design advocate. An aside: do not confuse this for blind acceptance of non-scientific things. I'm not going to replace astronomy with astrology any time soon. Anyway, I hope for some good attempts at changing my view!

article: We study the theoretical performance of a combined approach to demodulation and decoding of binary continuous-phase modulated signals under repetition-like codes. This technique is motivated by a need to transmit packetized or framed data bursts in high noise regimes where many powerful, short-length codes are ineffective. In channels with strong noise, we mathematically study the asymptotic bit error rates of this combined approach and quantify the performance improvement over performing demodulation and decoding separately as the code rate increases. In this context, we also discuss a simple variant of repetition coding involving pseudorandom code words, based on direct-sequence spread spectrum methods, that preserves the spectral density of the encoded signal in order to maintain resistance to narrowband interference. We describe numerical simulations that demonstrate the advantages of this approach as an inner code which can be used underneath modern coding schemes in high noise environments.

article: I woke up as the sun reflected onto my face from the building across the street. As I blink the sleep from my eyes, Master comes into my room. He used to wake up before the sun, but not anymore. I yawn, look up at Master's face - older, harder than it used to be. I stand up and shake off the stiffness of night and, like always, wait by the door while Master covers himself. As he fastens my restraints, he rubs a hand along the side of my face, and tells me that I am a Good Girl. I like being a Good Girl. We come home and sit together, I put my head in his lap, and he puts his hand on my side. Master's companion joins us, and we all sit on the couch. I can feel Master's heartbeat on my ribs, and the steady rhythm makes me tired. " I guess I'll make us some dinner. " I heard Master's companion say. He's a good Companion for Master. He cares for Master like Master cares for me. " I'm not hungry. " Master replied. " You need to eat something. You've got to build up your strength. " After dinner, we sit together again, and this time I fall asleep. I wake up and darkness has begun to fill the outside. Master says that we can go Outside. Like he does each time, he rubs a hand along the side of my face, and tells me that I am a Good Girl. I like being a Good Girl. At the park, we see all of my friends. Master and his companion sit at a bench nearby as I play. We live in a city now, and I hear the howling cars all the time. This time was different though. This time the whining car came for my Master. I look over for my Master and he is lying on the ground, with his Companion next to him holding his hand. People run from the howling car towards Master. I run to him, and I see something new in his wide eyes, as he draws short breaths, grasping for anyone who will hold on. For the first time I saw that Master was afraid. I nudge my head under his hand and lick his arm to let him know that I am there. He holds me firmly behind my head and I nuzzle his side. I feel fear in his grasp, and I feel his heartbeat again, but this time more faint. The people from the whining car come and take Master away. Confused and afraid, I stay close to Master's Companion. We go home, but this time it is different. Master's Companion puts me inside, and quickly turns to leave again. The door slams shut, and the pressing silence means that I am alone now. I have never liked being alone. It has been many years since we have come to this new home, and lots of things are different than they used to be. Our walks are slower. Our play is shorter. I thought that meant different was a bad thing. But our bond is stronger. So different must be a good thing. I'll be different for my Master. I'll walk slower. I'll play shorter. Different will make me a Good Girl! I like being a Good Girl. A long time has passed now, the darkness has begun to lift from Outside. Master's Companion finally comes home and we go Outside. " We have to go somewhere special today, Mallory. " I did not understand, but I knew that Master's Companion needed me now. As we walked through the city, I smelled for familiar things, but found none. We approached a building, and my Master's Companion spoke with a woman. " I know that dogs aren't allowed in the hospital, but maybe we could bring him outside for a bit? " As he approached, I smelled him. Only it wasn't the warm smell I was used to, the smell that meant I was home. It was cold and harsh. " There's nothing we can do but ease the pain now. " Said the woman. " We will make him as comfortable as possible. " I put my front paws onto his knees, and licked the tears from his face. He smiled, and lifted a weak hand, rubbed along the side of my face, and told me I was a Good Girl. I liked being a Good Girl.

article: Inspired by [this AdviceAnimals thread] . I'm at an age where a few of my peers (people I went to school with, co-workers, etc.) are single parents. Well, single mothers, mostly, I guess. Either they're divorced, or they had a child out of wedlock and the other parent didn't stick around. They're otherwise good people, and I'm sure they're good parents as well. But I usually find out about this part of their lives when they say something to the effect of...that the other parent wasn't ready to be a parent, or was abusive, or abandoned them, or was a bad person in some way. At that point, I find myself almost reflexively thinking less of the single parent. I guess I feel like they made a bad decision to have a child with this other person, and having a child is a really important decision. These are people who I interact with in my day-to-day life, and I don't want to be a jerk by looking down on them. Some notes on where I'm coming from, to narrow things down: I think my problem isn't with splitting up with a bad SO, it's with choosing to have a kid with a bad co-parent in the first place (or being unable to see that they wouldn't be a good co-parent). I don't think my view is based on religious beliefs. I don't have any problem with a modern, empowered woman choosing from the outset to be single parent, using a sperm donor or whatever, if she has the resources and maturity to handle that. I know that in some cases there were unavoidable circumstances, like if the other parent died or something. In the abstract, I don't support politics or public policy which treats single parents harshly. For this post, I'm more interested in single parents whom I know personally. Fellow Redditors, I want to change my view. Help me do it.

article: They are a calculation, like taking a square root. "Square rooting" (not an actual verb) is not a constant, obviously; so you could argue that it's a procedure. SineCosineTangent are the same way. They are actual mathematical functions, though, not something made up for calculators. Explaining exactly what they dp is a bit complicated though... Imagine a circle, centered on a graph, with a radius of 1. Now imagine you take any angle x, that starts along the x-axis, pointing right. So if the angle is 0, it just points right, if it's 90 degrees, it points straight up, etc. Take any angle x, draw a line to the edge of the circle. sin (x) will give you the y-coordinate of that point. cos (x) will give you the x-coordinate. So, you could write the coordinates of that point as (cos (x), sin (x. tan (x) is just sin (x) divided by cos (x). They have many more important and useful purposes in mathematics, this is just the easiest way I know to understand it. EDIT: Someone else mentioned the angles in a triangle. I think that's more boring so I have a harder time remembering that one.', "sin, cos, tan, etc. are a way to measure the ratios of side lengths in a right triangle. Right triangles follow very specific rules, so the ratio of one side to another will always be constant for a given angle. Sin will take the side opposite the angle (the side that isn't directly involved in forming the angle) over the hypotenuse (the side opposite the 90 degree angle), cos takes the ratio of the side closer to it over the hypotenuse, and tan takes the ratio of the opposite side over the closer side.

article: At the 2017 Artificial and Computational Intelligence in Games meeting at Dagstuhl, Julian Togelius asked how to make spaces where every way of filling in the details yielded a good game. This study examines the possibility of enriching search spaces so that they contain very high rates of interesting objects, specifically game elements. While we do not answer the full challenge of finding good games throughout the space, this study highlights a number of potential avenues. These include naturally rich spaces, a simple technique for modifying a representation to search only rich parts of a larger search space, and representations that are highly expressive and so exhibit highly restricted and consequently enriched search spaces.

article: My legs finally give out as I approach the peak of the black mountain, gasping for breath I could hear the screams of the zombie horde as it inevitably got closer. I don't know why I even bothered to continue struggling at this point. The horde ambushed me earlier in the day and while I was able to avoid becoming a full meal, one of them certainly made a decent breakfast out of my left arm. Perhaps it's just the human condition to confine struggling even though every fiber of your being has given up hope, it had been years since I even spoke to another person or experienced the comforts of what had once been every day life. Exhausted and too dehydrated to even cry in my final moments, I closed my to the auburn sunset and accepted my fate. "Are you okay!?" Hands shook me awake from what should of been my eternal slumber. My eyes were having trouble adjusting to the darkness but there was no mistaking that voice. Had I finally found another person? "Oh look at the poor dear," Chimed a more feminine voice. "It's a good thing we finally found him, shriveled thing would have gotten lost." "Too true, bastard led us on quite the chase though." The one standing over me reached out his hand. "Up you go lad, well get you by a good meal and cold beer before you know it." I grabbed his icy cold hand and stood level with the man who had saved me. Strangely enough, I no longer felt fatigued and the winter air didn't seem to bother me as it had earlier. I finally made out the decomposing face that stood before me and jumped back in horror. The creature let out a barking laugh, "oh it's been awhile since I've gotten to pop someone's cherry like that, almost forgot how much fun it is. No need to be tense. After all, your one of us now." Two weeks later I found myself on Bourbon Street in New Orleans. Here the party never stops as zombies have no need of sleep. While we can get drunk, hangovers appear to only be experienced by the living. We need to feed but I was the last living human to be found in sometime. Our kind mostly live off of the animals and for whatever reason, the raw flesh of an animal tastes better than any gourmet meal I've ever had. Once a week you need to put in time at the farms or breweries but otherwise your free to party, read those books you never got around to finishing while alive or simply Netflix and chill. If there is a heaven, tell St. Peter I'd rather spend my eternity here.

article: It depends on your college and your bank. Your college is more likely to use multiple online systems which don't really communicate with each other, so even if it's the same usernamepassword you may need to enter it much more frequently. Similarly they may have very specific password requirements, because that's what will be required for one particular part of their systems. Your bank on the other hand only has one system you'll ever interact with, and it will usually be isolated from the rest of their systems (knowing your details can't give an attacker access to their mail servers for example). Once into the system banks are more likely to require extra security before you can do things like transfer money to a new account, for example requiring a code delivered to you by SMS. There are other factors too. For example bank logons are usually random numbers which are known only to you, whereas a college logon will be an email address or student number which can be connected to you; this makes it easier for people who know you to make an educated guess at your password or security questions. Beyond all that, banks are much more likely to keep an eye on security. If you suddenly try logging on from overseas, or have a lot of wrong password attempts your bank will be more likely to lock the account and contact you than your college will be.," "Because I would bet money that the procedures your college uses aren't actually effective, I.E., requiring passwords to have X letters (Y of which must be capitalized), X numbers, and X non-alphabetical and non-numberical characters. It's just busywork that looks superficially effective to a layman and justifies not actually increasing the security to a board.,Professional web developer here. I can't really comment on whether you bank is insecure, or your school is unnecessarily secure, without further details. However: There's probably loads of behind-the scenes security for your bank, that you're completely unaware of. Anti-fraud monitoring systems, IP address tracking, multi-stage password reset systems (e.g. involving SMS), more secure logon details (not just your public email address), and so on. Since your college website does NOT have someall of these features, and was probably created on a much lower budget, the web developers have tried to compensate in other, easier to implement, ways - e.g. password strength. Often, these features are actually ill-thought out, and have the opposite effect of weakening security. This might be because the developer sucks at his job, or (more likely) because he's following orders from a manager who shouldn't be responsible for such decisions. For example, if you require everyone to have a stupidly complex password, with a bunch of arbitrary rules (e.g. "Must contain 10 characters, including upper and lower case letters, a digit, a symbol, no spaces, no repeats of 3 characters in a row, no 3 consecutive digits, no mention of blacklisted words like "password" or "letmein,.... then people will end up simply writing their pasword on a piece of paper.','Really? All my online banks are far more secured. Aside from the standard usernamepw, I also have to answer a security question everytime I login. My college login is just a simple usernamepw. What does your required?', "Honestly.... probably because they are not as secure as a bank. The school doesn't want to have personal responsibility or liability for your information being stolen (like your credit card when you make a payment). Therefore, they refuse to save it for your convenience. This puts the load of the responsibility on your shoulders instead of theirs. Also, they have no reason to provide any element of convenience. You've committed yourself to their school (probably for a lot of reasons that aren't related to convenience or systems like these). They don't see elements like this as a risk factor of losing a'customer'. Other commercial systems - Amazon, Playstation, etc - are rewarded by increased convenience because it will not only attract customers, but encourage existing customers to make more impulse purchases. (I speak from experience!) You're not really doing a lot of purchasing in their systems. And lastly, secure andor convenient systems cost money. This encourages a school to put in the minimum amount as necessary, or the biggest'bang for the buck' as they say. This also accounts for the things like not saving your credit card information, or specific password requirements, or restricting certain browsers, etc.,Its random. They might have to follow regulations which may or may not add security. But the regulations might be outdated and only add hassle to the process while not improving anything. Also if you call the university you can usually social engineer all the information out of the people without identifying yourself properly anyways. Your bank is horrible as well. Perceived security is not real security. Its all random. I could create a site where you provide a username, password and ten captchas and if I do it wrong it will be more annoying for you, but still not add any security to the thing. Welcome to the wonderful world of software in large corporations and governments. Welcome to hell. Source: Software developer, University graduate. Last time I called my university I was able to make a transaction without providing anything.

article: The stable matching problem is one of the central problems of algorithmic game theory. If participants are allowed to have ties, the problem of finding a stable matching of maximum cardinality is an N P -hard problem, even when the ties are of size two. Moreover, in this setting it is UGC-hard to provide an approximation with a constant factor smaller than 4 3 . In this paper, we give a tight analysis of an approximation algorithm given by Huang and Kavitha for the maximum cardinality stable matching problem with ties of size two, demonstrating an improved 4 3 -approximation factor.

article: I loved the smell of Pa after a long day in the field, a salty beef odor distinctly his, mixed with the lemon scented soap Ma used to wash our clothes. He always smiled in those days, a satisfied exhausted grin stretched from ear to ear, a contented happiness that I would miss in the years to come. I always used to wait for him to come in from the fields, excited when I heard the thud of his boots on the porch. I would sit beside him as he washed for dinner, watch as he rinsed clean of the moist grey soil whistling tunelessly between his front teeth. Every day when he finished he would tussle my hair and hoist me up into his arms where I would rest my head on his shoulder and breathe in that smell. The scent of those happy easy times. I can still remember when the worry started in Pa's face. I was playing just off the porch, plucking at those pretty white crooked flowers that Ma always loved. Piling them up in the multi-hued grey of the dirt ready to be strung into chains to be hung around my neck. Pa was working on his squeaky old truck, arms and face smudged with black oil as he fiddled under the hood. I had watched with gaping mouth when the Smith's truck had come down the winding dirt lane to our farm. The whole Smith clan peering out from around their piled up possessions, stacked high to the pale sky. Seemed like everything they owned was on that truck, chair and table and dresser and drawer tied together into a jumbled maze of wicker and wood. Pa and Mr Smith had spoken for a while, heads bowed close together in solemn congress, hushed and stern dispute. Pa shook his head several times, disagreeing or refusing with Mr Smith and his quiet calm implorations. After a time they stopped and shook hands with a rough tight grip, fiercely squeezing at each other's work scarred hand. Finally with a clap on Pa's shoulder Mr Smith had climbed back in his truck and then wheeled it around heading away from our farm. Pa stood there for a while, watching them rattle down our rutted road fading off into the distant grey. I woke that night to Ma and Pa in muttered argument, hissed words just loud enough to disturb my sleep. I had lay in my bed, rough blanket pulled to my chin bathed in the silver of the moon peeking through my window. Lay and listened as Ma begged at Pa in a pleading tone. Pa had finally spoke loud in the still quiet of the night, Enough. After that I heard no more, finally drifting off into uneasy sleep. It was weeks before we saw the first roiling cloud. A dark angry looking puff of black streaked with glints of silvery light. It dragged itself over the horizon and loomed there almost snarling at us as it tossed and turned unsteadily in the hot wind. Pa spent the day sealing the windows and packing everything away under tied down tarps. Frenetically moving from task to task, one eye on what he was doing the other fixed firmly on that crouched demon looming above us, stirring fitfully in the wind. Ma kept me on the porch that day and watched lest I wander off. I was scared at the look in her eyes, a fearful wateriness I had never seen before. In the late afternoon the beast pounced. It came rolling down off the hills with a mournful howl. Clawing itself across the ground, squeezing its dirty fingers into every nook and cranny forcing us to retreat into the farm house, hiding from its stinging gritty sleet. Pa tried to make a game of it that night. All of us camped together in the parlor, huddled together under a makeshift tent of bed sheets as the wind howled and scratched at the timber of our cozy home. Ma sang me off to sleep, rocking me to her chest as she sang lullabies in her quiet soothing voice. We woke the next morning to an outlandish sight. The familiar lines of the barn huddled under a mountain built of fine dust, the ground and everything I could see hidden beneath that same dull shroud. Pa had looked so gloomy that day, his mask of ash colored dust tracked with streaks of slow running tears as he looked out at the torn battered remnants of the fields. The days that followed ran together into a shapeless grey scene. Each day Pa struggling to push back at that ever inching barrage of earth, come to swallow the whole damned place. A creeping uncaring succubus draining and sapping him till his skin was a pale pallor, dyed by worry and his unceasing toil. Each night Ma and Pa debated in hushed vicious tones, each night Ma getting louder and Pa fading as he slowly lost his unceasing war. I woke one morn to a different man. Bowed beneath the weight of the world as he tied each treasured possession to a towering pile strapped to the truck with dust covered rope. That bright grin and shining eyes shuttered beneath a lampshade of his disappointment and misery. His shoulders bent over in mute defeat as we turned our backs to the farm and drove away, unable to battle any longer. Two long years we lived in the camps. Days I spent running through the powdery grey dust, chasing and playing with the other filthy urchins set loose by our parent's indifferent attention, focused instead on their own daily struggle. Two years with the taste of dust on everything, coating the back of my throat and dying my skin into a filthy mottled hue. Two years of Pa sat in that same wooden chair only stirring to refill his glass from the ever present bottle at his elbow. Slowly sinking smaller and deeper into his chair as he watched his world crumble around him, his familiar smell now the stink the dust and his sour whisky. Two years of Ma working from dawn till dusk, begging and scrounging for any job that would put a crust on the table and whisky in Pa's glass. It ended as suddenly as it began, the clouds of dust stilled and the sun smiled again from pale sky, warm on our skin after its long absence. It felt like the camp held its collective breath at first, everyone scared that it was just a brief reprieve in this never-ending storm. Finally people began to pack and leave. Tying belongings back on to long-suffering vehicles, rattling off for yearned for homes. Ma had finally stirred Pa, setting him to packing our home back to the top of our rusted old truck, finally pushing him to carry us home. I almost didn't recognise the farm when we returned, covered as it was with a thick rug of that familiar choking grit, mounded high in a pall over my beloved home. I had wandered out into the desolate fields and stood staring out across that same dull grey feeling numb at our farms indifferent greeting. As I stood there a rumble of thunder stirred the air and with a weary fear that I looked at the sky, ready to see those same familiar dusty clouds. Instead the sky was filled with puffs of fluffy white, rolling through the sky with playful glee. Drifting in the sky with their bright happy form, occasionally burping with burbling thunder. The air felt cool on my skin as I stood and gazed up at that tumbling sky watching clouds that didn't loom in ominous warning, clouds not filled with choking grit. Fat drops of rain had begun to fall, pattering and dimpling the coating of my dust choked realm. My eye was caught by a flash of unfamiliar pigment, a flower peeked from beneath the dark carpet on the ground, small fragile petals washed clean by the fresh purifying rain. I had never seen a flower like this, inked in a hue that stood out brightly from familiar dull shades. A bold and unique color, sketched in warm tones that set my heart pounding in my chest. The rain washed more of the dust away, revealing a carpet of bright happy petals peaking from beneath the featureless plane. I knelt on the ground as the rain fell about me and cupped one of the bright cheerful blossoms in my streaked pale hands. It came away easily as I tugged and sat smiling up at me from my curled sheltering palm.
label: human

article: With the recent success of visual features from deep convolutional neural networks (DCNN) in visual robot self-localization, it has become important and practical to address more general self-localization scenarios. In this paper, we address the scenario of self-localization from images with small overlap. We explicitly introduce a localization difficulty index as a decreasing function of view overlap between query and relevant database images and investigate performance versus difficulty for challenging cross-view self-localization tasks. We then reformulate the self-localization as a scalable bag-of-visual-features (BoVF) scene retrieval and present an efficient solution called PCA-NBNN, aiming to facilitate fast and yet discriminative correspondence between partially overlapping images. The proposed approach adopts recent findings in discriminativity preserving encoding of DCNN features using principal component analysis (PCA) and cross-domain scene matching using naive Bayes nearest neighbor distance metric (NBNN). We experimentally demonstrate that the proposed PCA-NBNN framework frequently achieves comparable results to previous DCNN features and that the BoVF model is significantly more efficient. We further address an important alternative scenario of "self-localization from images with NO overlap" and report the result.
label: human

article: "No, no, swing it'round the front." Beepers said. "He'll have to see it before he sees you, trust me." Bibsy adjusted the strap so that the exceedingly large canister hung in front of him. He felt uncomfortable with the whole idea, but he couldn't quite put his finger on the reason why. It wasn't that it was dishonest well, it was dishonest, that was true, but that wasn't what bothered him about it. He didn't actually remember why it was dishonest either, but since Beepers was doing it, he thought it must be. Bibsy was just glad they were on the same side. "Bit hard to walk like this?" Bibsy stomped around and the canister bumped his knees. "Ok, fine, just carry it. You can do it with one arm, so you can still hold the torch." "But you're much smaller, maybe if you carried it, it would be easier..." "How would that make it any easier?" "Well, maybe you could drag it on the ground in front of you where it can see..." "Drag it in front of me? Do you mean push it?" Beepers sighed. "Bibsy, you poor fool, do you know what would happen if this bumped into a rock that I couldn't see because I was pushing it along the ground because you were too lazy to do your fair share?" Bibsy's brow furrowed as he thought hard. "Er... explode?" Beepers slapped his forehead with his palm. "No! How many times do I have to tell you, it's not going to explode! The thing is empty! Why would you even think such a thing is supposed to explode! Do you see the front?" He tapped the large sign on the front of the container. In sloppily painted letters, it read'dragin repLant.' "That says'dragon repellent!' When a dragon is hurling fireballs at you, what good would it be to have dragon repellent that explodes? " "Oh. Boss... why aren't we bringing real dragon repellent?" "Because there's no such thing as dragon repellent. But the dragon doesn't know that." Beepers tapped his nose with his forefinger. "Oh." Bibsy forgot to ask again why Beepers couldn't carry the container. "Bibsy, you do the lifting, I'll do the thinking. We'll make a... great team." They continued up the mountain pass. Somehow, Bibsy had been made the Steward of the Land of Stews, which meant that Beepers had to find an innocuous way to get him killed so that Beepers could become the new, rightful Steward. The plan was simple in principle: claim they were going to steal back the Stewsland Staff from the dragon's lair, solidifying Bibsy's place in history as the best Steward there had ever been. In fact, Beepers was hoping to solidify him so well that Bibsy would never move again. The dragon's job was easy. The difficult part was getting Bibsy to the lair. And of course, if Beepers could pick up a few things while the dragon was occupied with his companion, so much the better. They soon came upon a glowing red portcullis in the side of the mountain. The undefined uneasiness grew in Bibsy as they approached the entrance. "Ok, after you, like we planned." Beepers nudged Bibsy forward. Suddenly, Bibsy could place exactly what had made him uncomfortable about this idea. "Boss, why do I have to go first again? What if the dragon sees me?" "You're not going first, you're going second. You've got the repellent in front of you. Any dragon sees that, he'll get right out of your way. And you've got me to guard the flank." Bibsy hesitated. ..."Are you sure?" "Sure I'm sure. Just make sure to hold the torch in front so the dragon can read the sign. Yep. There you go. I'll be right behind you." ..... On the walkway below, a single point of light disappeared behind a pillar, paused, and then hurriedly ran behind the next pillar. A smaller figure was in the middle of the walkway a few paces behind the torch, strolling easily. "Would you stop doing that? We're still nowhere near the lair." The figure holding the torch looked back and whispered, "But I read that dragons are sneaky! They could get you when you least expect it!" "First of all, you can't read. Second of all, do you know why they call it the dragon's lair instead of, say, the lair where the dragon isn't? " The first figure frowned. "Well, I've never thought about it..." "They call it the dragon's lair because that's where the dragon is. " "Oh. I learn so much when I'm around you, Boss." Bibsy looked back and smiled. It was pathetic. At that moment, Bibsy tripped and the canister hit the ground and rolled into a pillar. "Boss, careful! It might explode! I'll protect you!" Bibsy tackled Beepers. Beepers couldn't stand it anymore. " Bibsy, for the last time, nothing is going to explode! " A new voice purred from the darkness above. "I wouldn't say that." Their hearts stopped. Moments passed. Although at first he wanted to seep into the floor, Beepers slowly raised his body off of the ground. There was nothing for it. As he stood, he channeled through himself the deep wells of courage that had flowed through his bloodline in ancient days, when goblin kings ruled over the world and the dragons were young and tame. Fire burned in his eyes as he threw back his head and cried into the darkness, "I am Gondolfin Bartholomew Beepers Stout-shield the Third, Lord of the Far Hills! Conqueror of the Forbidden Lands! Blight of the Eastern Shores! Wielder of Excuse me," The voice above interrupted him as it resounded once more in the chamber, "your name... what was the middle bit?" "Bartholomew?" "No, no. The one after that." ..." Beepers?" Several little tufts of flame illuminated the tip of an enormous snout as they furled out of a pair of nostrils several times larger than the canister that now lay on the floor below. The creature in the darkness giggled. Deflated, Beepers hung his head. He hadn't even gotten to the best parts. Feeling like he had to defend his companion, Bibsy stepped forward defiantly. He only had one fancy title to say, and after Beepers' display that now felt inadequate. He groped for a convincing lie and looked around for inspiration. His eyes fell on the canister. "And I am Bibsy, uh, Stewer of Stews Steward, you idiot Steward of Stews, Slayer of Drag Beepers' hands were instantly cemented over Bibsy's mouth. Time seemed to freeze. Two tremendous orbs of fiery red light pierced the darkness above them as the dragon slowly opened his eyes. Beepers wished again that he could melt into the floor, and indeed he felt the odds of that reality increasing rapidly. "Ah, what was that last part?" "Er... we've got... dragon repellent..." Beepers pointed feebly. The dragon's eyes neared as he swung his head lower. "And how is that working out for you?" "Er..." Beepers said. The dragon turned to Bibsy. "You said that dragons are... sneaky." "Er..." Beepers said again. He was desperately trying to navigate to a course forward in this conversation that did not involve Bibsy speaking again, but his tongue seemed stuck in his mouth. "How about we play a little game," the dragon said. It wasn't a question. Beepers gulped. Bibsy considered. "Well, we were actually in the middle of something..." Light erupted into the chamber, revealing a beast of terrible size, larger than either had ever imagined possible. Dark red scales glimmered as the wall beside them exploded in fire and ash. Smoke billowed from the dragon's mouth. When they had regained their vision, the canister marked'dragin repLant' was no longer to be seen. Bibsy looked around him then jabbed Beepers in the side. "Psst, Boss, I think I misplaced the dragon plant. We might need another in case we do find a dragon when we get to the lair." He scratched his head. "Though, come to think of it, I think I read that dragons aren't afraid of plants." Beepers wanted to weep. The voice above them spoke. "The game is this..." ..... article: So much has changed since I were a maggot, things just seem colder and time seem somehow stretched these days. When I was first born I was a small maggot, pushed aside by my brothers and sisters and ignored. I remember two of the older flies talking about me as if I wasn't there, saying it'd be amazing if I even managed to pupate. I vowed that day that I would live and grow and survive and I did. I was the last to transform into pupae but that meant I was finally able to eat the food I had been denied so long. I began my metamorphosis 52 hours after hatching, the longest any fly has been known to live as a maggot. I knew I was supposed to begin but I forced myself to stay whole, to resist the change. I resisted our gift, our transformation, God's reward to the maggot. I resisted and I was cursed. I lived a good first life, I travelled, ate well and even mated. I saw my maggots born and grow up and as my thirty cycles grew to an end I prepared for my parting. Everyone I knew was dying, but not me, I guessed I would be last of my generation to die I stayed a maggot so long but I soon realised the truth. 40 cycles, 50 cycles, the young flies now called my immortal, but this was my punishment, penance for not metamorphosing quickly enough. Now I am old and tired and I have nowhere to go so I seek release, I fly high where the birds fly and low where the frog wait. I seek release.
